News.title: Brit tourist, 58, arrested for spitting on Turkish flag after heated row with hotel staff
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FLAG FRENZY Brit tourist, 58, arrested for spitting on Turkish flag after heated row with hotel staff

A BRIT man has been jailed after allegedly spitting on a Turkish flag.

The holidaymaker, believed to be Stephen Kerr, 58, had been staying at a popular meditteranean sea resort in Turkey when the chaos unfolded.



The Brit reportedly got into a heated spat with hotel employees – before spitting on the flag hanging in the lobby.

Outraged staff held the Brit and reported him to the police.



Cops raced to the resort in Turkey’s southern Antalya province – a paradise haven of blue seas, beaches and mountains.

Officers cuffed the Brit – in luminous yellow shorts and a blue vest – and escorted him to the Alanya courthouse.



Once there, a judge formally charged the hapless tourist with “insulting the symbols of the state’s sovereignty”.

The holidaymaker needed a translator to give his statement in court.

Kerr has reportedly been locked behind bars in Alanya L-Type Closed Prison.

Under repressive Turkish laws, disrespecting the national flag holds a jail term of up to three years.



The British Embassy in Turkey states on its website that they cannot get people out of prison – even if they are British citizens.

It is unclear precisely when the 58-year-old was arrested.

A spokesperson for the Foreign Office said: “We are supporting a British man arrested in Turkey and are in contact with the authorities.”

The Sun has contacted the British Embassy in Turkey for comment.

Last summer a tourist was blasted by prosecutors for pole dancing on a Turkish flag mast in Cappadocia – a region famed for its hot air balloon excursions.



And earlier this year, a British “drug mule” was arrested and thrown into jail for nearly ten years upon landing at Istanbul airport in Turkey.

Taylor Johnson, 20, was reportedly caught smuggling 19kg of cannabis in vacuum sealed bags from Thailand.

The young Brit claimed he’d been forced to transport the bags by a man who threatened him – and that he had no idea there were drugs inside.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A court in Istanbul nonetheless jailed the Brit for nine years and two months.

Heartbroken family members have claimed Johnson was thrown into an overcrowded cell and beaten up by thugs behind bars.

News.title: Driver in hospital with ‘serious injuries’ after crash during police pursuit as cops search for dog walker
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

SMASH HORROR Driver in hospital with ‘serious injuries’ after crash during police pursuit as cops search for dog walker

A MAN has been seriously injured in a crash during a police chase – as cops search for a dog-walker who narrowly missed the collision.

Police were pursuing a VW Golf which had failed to stop on the A6007 in Heanor, Derbyshire, just after 12.15pm on Tuesday.



As it reached Hardy Barn in Shipley, heading towards Ilkeston, the Golf crashed into a VW T-Cross travelling in the opposite direction.

The Golf driver suffered severe injuries and remains in hospital, Derbyshire Police confirmed today.



Neither the driver nor passenger in the VW T-Cross suffered serious injuries, the cops said.

A Ford Fiesta was also damaged during the collision.



Derbyshire Police are now looking to speak with an elderly man who was walking his dog and was almost hit when he crossed the road between Ilkeston Hospital and the Shipley Garden.

The force also said it will make a mandatory referral to the Independent Office for Police Conduct since the accident happened during a police chase.

Anyone with information has been urged to contact the force through their website or 101.

It follows another tense police chase in Hampshire in August, which saw a reckless female driver hit speeds of up to 130mph.



Tia Paget, 34, was caught on dashcam racing past other cars on the motorway and swerving between lanes before cops eventually caught up with her.

News.title: Andy Burnham hints new vote on Scottish independence COULD happen if there’s enough public support
News.content:
ANDY Burnham has indicated a new vote on Scottish independence could happen if there is public support for a break away.

The PM had previously told the country’s First Minister John Swinney that a second referendum was “off limits”.



But he told MPs that clear public support could trigger a vote in the same way a border poll could take place in Northern Ireland.

His response came after Scottish National Party’s Chris Law said the Good Friday Agreement made clear a poll would take place when there is a clear consensus for a vote.



The PM said: “I would say exactly the same situation in Scotland.”

“I am not aware that there is a majority of public support for another referendum and until that changes there won’t be one.”



But Mr Swinney said: “To go from ‘off limits’ to this is an acceptance of the reality that the people of Scotland will decide their own future – not the UK Government.

“For the first time since 2014, a British Prime Minister accepts that majority support for a referendum should mean one takes place.”

But Downing Street insisted there had been no change in the Prime Minister’s position.

Mr Burnham’s press secretary said: “The PM’s been repeatedly clear on this.”

News.title: After Andy Burnham’s performance at PMQs, it’s clear he is playing a dangerous game of chicken with UK’s security
News.content:
At Prime Minister’s Questions today, Andy Burnham was asked a simple question: Would he reform welfare to fund our armed forces properly? He said no.

His weak-willed answer will have been noted in Moscow and Tehran

Labour’s addiction to spending ever more on welfare is a poor shield against missiles, drones and cyber attacks.



The bond market has also heard it, on whom Britain’s parlous finances rely.

Under Chancellor Healey the Second, Britain borrows more expensively than any other G7 country.



The people who lend us that money are not interested in what plays well with Labour backbenchers.

They only care whether the government has the guts to make tough decisions to protect the nation’s physical and financial security.

I will never shirk that duty. In my first week as Shadow Chancellor, Kemi and I found the money for defence by cracking down on working-age benefits and the flawed Motability scheme.

We found the funding for defence in a fiscally responsible way.

That’s a plan Burnham could copy for free, but the Prime Minister is not interested.

Having spent 25 years in business before entering Westminster, I’ve learned you don’t solve problems by denying they exist.



Nettles are best grasped, and tough decisions made.

After yesterday’s performance by the Prime Minister, it’s clear he is playing a dangerous game of chicken with the nation’s security.

News.title: Jealous husband avoids jail after running over wife’s lover on the pavement
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

REVENGE ATTACK Jealous husband avoids jail after running over wife’s lover on the pavement

A JEALOUS husband has avoided jail after running over his wife’s lover on the pavement.

Paul Rudd, 58, waited for the pair to leave a pub then drove at Adrian Boakes at 10mph.



Ex-Royal Navy officer Rudd had warned his wife earlier: “I’m going to run the c*** over.”

Mr Boakes suffered a broken nose, torn kidney and concussion.



Rudd called 999, claiming: “He stepped in front of me.”

Mr Boakes was hit in Dodleston, Cheshire, in February.



Chester crown court heard the affair had ended weeks earlier.

Business consultant Rudd pleaded guilty to GBH and causing serious injury by dangerous driving.

He was sentenced to 17 months in prison, suspended for 18 months.

Rudd, from Broughton, near Wrexham, who braked before impact, was also banned from driving for two years.

News.title: I sat feet from Lindsay Clancy at her trial – but what I discovered away from the cameras left me sick to my stomach
News.content:
AWAY from the cameras and courthouse frenzy surrounding Lindsay Clancy’s sensational murder trial, I saw firsthand how the deaths of three young children had shattered a tight-knight community.

The killer mom’s case was inescapable almost as soon as I arrived in Massachusetts.



Shopkeepers, waitresses and even staff at the Hertz rental desk wanted to discuss the evidence and extraordinary attention surrounding the case, while several were frustrated by the wild internet conspiracy theories engulfing Clancy’s ex-husband Patrick.

I spent nearly two weeks covering the final stages of the trial, moving between Plymouth Superior Court and Duxbury, where the tragedy unfolded.





Once in the state, I headed straight to the courthouse and got there just minutes before Clancy’s defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, emerged to face a mob of reporters.

The scene was far more controlled than the frenzy it would become.

I’d already watched Reddington’s distinctive Boston “side-bahs” go viral, turning the veteran lawyer into an unlikely internet celebrity with memes.

Later, as the crowd thinned, I muscled in for some one-on-one questions as he walked towards his distinctive green Ford Bronco, its personalized “NG” plate shorthand for “not guilty.”



But some of the moments that stayed with me most happened away from the courthouse, on the quiet streets of Duxbury, where I pulled up as close as I could to the Clancys’ former home.

I had to park half a mile away and trek across the grass, with only rustling trees and the occasional car breaking the silence.

I’d seen countless photographs of the house, but seeing it in person was completely different.

The large New England-style property sat behind a sprawling lawn and trees, but my thoughts immediately went to the basement where three young children had been strangled with exercise bands.

It made me feel sick to my stomach.



The house had already been sold a year after the murders, but standing there, it was impossible not to picture the ambulances and police descending on the street on January 24, 2023.

How could anyone make that room feel ordinary again?

Following the case from afar could sometimes feel like watching a Netflix documentary before one had even been made, complete with viral clips, memes, and competing theories.



But looking at the house, all of that suddenly fell away.

I then walked the neighborhood, speaking to people who had actually lived through what happened, including Mark Shortt, 62, who lives two doors down.

His neighbor’s son was among those who saw Clancy after she jumped from the second-floor window, and Shortt told me he believed she was severely mentally ill and belonged in a psychiatric hospital rather than prison.



A new homeowner whose property backed onto the house was unnerved to learn its history, until Shortt reassured him that serious crime was rare in Duxbury, where even a bar fight was unusual.

From the neighboring properties, I could see through the trees what appeared to be the eerie remains of children’s play equipment near the garden, as well as the window from which Clancy jumped.

Across the road, Ruth Hearson, 81, recalled four ambulances arriving that night and initially believing there had been carbon monoxide poisoning.

I also approached paramedics who were friendly but unable to talk, and watched the blood drain from their faces when I mentioned the trial, a clear sign of how deeply what they had witnessed still affected them.

Hearson told me some first responders had been traumatized: “The police, they were all traumatized. Coming down, seeing the babies, and some of them couldn’t go back to work.”



Most people I spoke to felt Clancy belonged in hospital rather than prison, but one woman opposite the house stood out, looking visibly disturbed as I asked questions.

She said: “I don’t have good feelings about her [Clancy], and what she did. I just want it over with. I don’t want to see her face anymore.”

Like the lone juror who would ultimately prevent a unanimous verdict, she was the exception.

I visited Kingsbury Club & Spa, where the children had gone swimming days before their deaths, and other places around Duxbury, finding many people following the case closely and believing Clancy was not criminally responsible.

As deliberations dragged on in Plymouth, the chaos outside the courthouse intensified, with Clancy supporters booing prosecutors and clashing with protesters.



When Reddington emerged each day, it was the biggest media scrum many of us had ever seen, as I fought to keep my microphone near him while trying not to fall into a concrete trash receptacle.

By the final day, the jurors looked like they had run a marathon and still had miles to go, having been sent back repeatedly to deliberate as they remained deadlocked.

When the judge read out their last message saying “with a heavy heart” that they were still unable to reach a unanimous verdict, the courtroom fell silent.



Eleven jurors had reached the same conclusion, but one would not budge.

The judge said he had no choice but to declare a mistrial, and gasps rang out around the courtroom.

In the back row of the jury, a woman dressed in pink closed her eyes and leaned forward.

Then, just as we thought it was over, Reddington was given an hour to take an emergency appeal to Massachusetts’ highest court, sending everyone back into limbo.

Reporters returned to the floor outside the courtroom, hammering out updates while constantly darting their eyes towards the door.



Supporters, many dressed in pink, crowded into the back of the floor, still waiting and hoping to get into court for the last moments.

When the appeal was rejected, we were called back in, and the mistrial was formally declared.

The jurors shook their heads as Clancy appeared to stare blankly ahead from her wheelchair.

After weeks of waiting for a verdict, there was a strange flatness to it all, with people looking completely crestfallen.

Reddington appeared disappointed but also as though he had done everything he could, sipping a Dunkin’ coffee and shaking the hands of Clancy’s family.



There was no conviction, no acquittal, and no final answer for the family after more than three years of waiting.

Then we spilled out of the courthouse into the blazing heat, gathering around the podiums as cameras and reporters jostled for position.

Reddington took aim at the lone holdout juror, claiming it had been an 11-to-1 split in favor of finding Clancy not guilty by reason of criminal responsibility.

I asked Reddington how Lindsay was.

“Not good,” he replied.



Tears filled his eyes as he described the former nurse as being like a daughter and said her family had been “robbed.”

But District Attorney Tim Cruz made clear the case may not be over, saying his priority remained to “fight for Cora, Dawson and Callan” as prosecutors consider whether to put Clancy on trial again.

As the cameras packed away, it was strange thinking that after six grueling weeks, we could all be back here again for another trial.

My thoughts returned to that quiet street in Duxbury, and to Cora, Dawson, and Callan, whose deaths changed everything for the families involved, the first responders who found them, and the community they left behind.

If you or someone you know is affected by any of the issues raised in this story, call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988, chat on 988lifeline.org, or text Crisis Text Line at 741741.

News.title: Britain strikes breakthrough deal with Belgium to stop people smugglers launching migrant boats from its shores
News.content:
BRITAIN has struck a deal with Belgium to stop people smugglers launching migrant boats from its shores.

Belgian cops will join British and French officers going after the gangs sending dinghies across the Channel.



The deal will also let police on both sides swap vital intelligence faster.

It comes after smugglers turned to Belgium to launch “taxi boats” which sail along the coast picking up migrants bound for Britain.



Belgian cops spotted 32 suspected attempts between January and April – up from just two in the whole of last year.

The pact is the first of its kind between Britain and an EU country since Brexit.



More than 50 suspected smugglers have already been arrested in joint UK-Belgian operations this year and more than 40 vehicles have been seized.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said: “The migrant smuggling trade doesn’t start and stop on the beaches of northern France.

“These gangs operate across borders, so we’ll work with every international partner available to track them down, shut them down and bring them to justice.”

The deal will also target gangs smuggling drugs and guns.

News.title: PC Andrew Harper killer is also convicted sex offender – yet was STILL deemed fit for early release
News.content:
ONE of PC Andrew Harper’s killers is a convicted sex offender — yet was still considered fit for early release by Labour.

Albert Bowers, 24, is believed to have committed the crime before the brave cop’s death in 2019.



Bowers, still at Frankland jail, Durham, after a public outcry, is listed as a “sex offender”, “violent” and “racist” on its records.

A source said: “This is outrageous and shows he is a danger to society and to women in particular. It likely means he offended on the outside before he was jailed.



“That would mean he would have been under 18 and not named in public records because children have right to anonymity in relation to crimes.

“But the authorities know about it and that’s why it’s marked on files. It is a disgrace he was ever slated for release.”

PC Harper, 28, was dragged to his death as Henry Long, Jessie Cole and Bowers, then 17, fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.

Bowers is on an enhanced regime at HMP Frankland, meaning he gets £33 a week to spend in the canteen plus extra gym and workshop access and time out of his cell.



The revelation comes after we told how Bowers’ accomplice Cole had been listed as a “risk to staff” by bosses at high-security Whitemoor Prison, Cambs where he is held.

Bowers is held alongside murderers including Levi Bellfield, ex-cop Wayne Couzens and Sally Anne Bowman’s killer Mark Dixie plus a raft of terrorists.

A separate source said: “He is quite feared in Frankland because he is young and a trained boxer. He is always in the gym and can lift more than anyone else in there.



“He is also living quite a comfortable life by prison standards because he has behaved, so he gets all the privileges including 24-hour TV.”

Newlywed Thames Valley Police officer PC Harper, 28, was dragged to his death in August 2019 as Long, Cole and Bowers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.

Bowers and Cole were both 17 at the time and passengers in the car driven by Long, who was caged for 16 years and not eligible for early release.

They were jailed for manslaughter in July 2020 and handed 13-year terms.

The revelation in July they could have been freed next January after serving half the sentence – instead of two-thirds – sparked fury and prompted the government to act to keep them inside.



PC Harper’s widow Lissie campaigned for harsher sentences for the killings of emergency workers after her husband’s tragic death.

And she has blasted Government plans to free the killers under the Sentencing Act, saying her work had been “forgotten”.

PC Harper’s mum, Debbie Adlam, has called flip-flopping over their release “gut-wrenching”.



More than a million people have signed a petition demanding that Bowers and Cole – who laughed and sneered during their trial – stay behind bars.

Lord Chancellor and Justice Secretary Alex Norris MP said: “We moved quickly to exclude rape and many serious child sex and grooming offences from our sentencing changes, and we have gone further still by excluding all unlawful killing offences—including death by dangerous or drink-driving, causing or allowing the death of a child, and manslaughter.

“This means hundreds more dangerous criminals staying behind bars for longer, including those who killed PC Andrew Harper in the line of duty.

“It is the right thing to do, and I pay tribute to his wife Lissie and his mother Debbie, who campaigned for this.

“We would like to have gone further, but we were unable to do so due to the lack of investment by the previous Government over 14 years.”



A representative for PC Harper’s widow, Lissie, was contacted.

News.title: 'Reform UK is forever demanding tougher rules for everyone else - now it must face same scrutiny'
News.content:
'Reform UK is forever demanding tougher rules for everyone else - now it must face same scrutiny'

'Reform has built its entire base around sovereignty, hard borders and suspicion of those coming from abroad. Yet when foreign money appears anywhere near its own political operation, those principles suddenly appear to be far less rigid.'

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

The Metropolitan Police is investigating claims that Reform UK may have broken donation rules after polling commissioned by the party was allegedly paid for by a US company.

‌



Nigel Farage says no law was broken and has brushed off comments his aides were caught on camera saying as “loose pub talk”. That defence does little to disguise the rank hypocrisy.

‌



Reform has built its entire base around sovereignty, hard borders and suspicion of those coming from abroad. Yet when foreign money appears anywhere near its own political operation, those principles suddenly appear to be far less rigid.

‌



There is nothing trivial about this. Foreign companies are barred from funding political parties because British democracy should not be bought or shaped from abroad.

Reform is forever demanding tougher rules for everyone else. Now it must face the same scrutiny. A party that shouts so loud about protecting Britain should be held to the highest standard if there is speculation of foreign cash coming anywhere close to its coffers.

‌



Safety for all

There can be no uncertainty about the rise in antisemitic abuse and attacks on Britain’s Jewish community. It is both vile and frightening, and it must be confronted wherever it appears. But compassion cannot stop at one community’s door.

Palestinian families in the occupied West Bank are entitled to the same dignity, rights and protection from violence. The government is right to act against illegal settlements and the violence linked to them. Jewish people who fear sanctions could fuel hatred deserve to be heard, and those fears should never be dismissed.

Criticism of the Israeli government must never be confused with hostility towards Jewish people, just as concern for Palestinians is not support for Hamas. Our principles must be consistent. Antisemitism must be condemned without qualification, while Palestinian suffering, intimidation and dispossession demand equal moral judgement.

Article continues below

Life support

The hardest battles are often the ones nobody else can see. Prince William, Harry Kane and some of Britain’s biggest sporting names are right to use sport’s extraordinary reach to help people speak before crisis becomes tragedy. One conversation can bring hope, support and, at the darkest moment, a lifeline.

News.title: Andy Burnham urged to target banks' bumper profits with windfall tax to ease cost-of-living pain
News.content:
Andy Burnham urged to target banks' bumper profits with windfall tax to ease cost-of-living pain

EXCLUSIVE: Trades Union Congress chief Paul Nowak tells The Mirror in an interview a windfall tax on banks' profits would be a 'game changer' to help those struggling with energy bills

View 3 Images TUC chief urges Andy Burnham to go further and faster on cost of living measures (Image: Thomas Krych/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

Andy Burnham has been urged to ease the cost-of-living pain by slapping a windfall tax on the eye-watering profits of the big banks at next month's Budget.

Paul Nowak - one of the country's most powerful union figures - welcomed the new Prime Minister's cost-of-living blitz in his first weeks in Downing Street. But in an interview with The Mirror, the Trades Union Congress (TUC) chief said Mr Burnham and his Chancellor John Healey must go "further and faster" on the cost of living.

Ahead of his organisation's annual Congress in Brighton this weekend, the TUC has published new polling showing 68% of voters support cutting energy bills with a tax on banks' profits. It is among the measures the TUC are calling for at the crunch Budget on October 28.

Andy Burnham rules out Tory benefit cut plan to fund extra defence spending READ MORE :

View 3 Images TUC General Secretary Paul Nowak speaks to The Mirror ahead of his organisation's annual Congress (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

Mr Nowak told The Mirror the measure could be "a real game-changer in terms of supporting people with those heating bills, at the same time as driving down on inflation" He said: "It's less than two decades since we bailed the banks out during the financial crash. I don't think it's unfair to ask the banks to help out the British public at a time when their profits are absolutely soaring.

"And they're not soaring because they've become incredibly competitive overnight or leaner, meaner organisations. It's because interest rates are high. They've done well out of Trumpflation. While our members have been hit by it, they've done well, so I think it's right to ask them to pay a fairer share."

He added: "I think what's clear is Britain's banks are doing incredibly well at the moment. I mean, a billion pounds a week for the big four banks between them every single week. The biggest ever bonus pool in the City of London last year: £25billion."

Britain's 'big four' banks - HSBC, Lloyds Banking Group, Barclays and NatWest - announced over the summer combined half-year pre-tax profits jumped to more than £29billion. Their estimated annual haul is £55.3bn, equal to about £1,750 a second.

Earnings have been partly fuelled by the Middle East war, which has driven up energy and other household bills and kept interest rates elevated for longer. The TUC argued over the summer increasing the surcharge paid on banks' profits - on top of the 25% corporation tax they pay - could raise billions.

Reinstating the 2023 rate under the Tories alone would bring in £9billion over four years while a 16% charge could bring in £24billion and 35% a staggering £60billion. The TUC has proposed the cash could be used to help fund a social tariff to cut typical bills by between £345 and £517 a year for millions of households.

View 3 Images Britain's 'big four' banks - HSBC, Lloyds Banking Group, Barclays and NatWest - announced over the summer combined half-year pre-tax profits jumped to more than £29billion (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The TUC boss said it will be for the PM and Chancellor to "make judgements about where the right level sits." But he added: "What is clear - if you're paying out £25 billion in bonuses, you can afford to pay a little bit more in tax."

Pressed on whether the government should also end the Tories' freeze on income tax thresholds - a plan abandoned by ex-Chancellor Rachel Reeves - Mr Nowak said it was a concern of a lot of working people. But he added: "I think it's very hard to see how the government can move on that in the short term.

"But, you know, looking ahead, you want to sort of rebalance our tax system away from taxing work to taxing wealth. And at the moment, it often feels for the people that we represent—working people who go out and work hard each and every day—that their taxes go up. But if you're generating your income from shares or from property, your taxes don't. So, I think that rebalancing has got to be part of it."

Mr Nowak also said there was a case for looking at "more effective taxes on wealth" ahead of next month's crunch Budget, which could include equalising capital gains tax with income tax. He added: "I think people would expect there to be a level playing field for those who are incredibly asset-rich, and who, as I say, effectively can find clever ways to avoid paying tax, and those who go to work every single day where we've got no option — it's PAYE.

Article continues below

"So, yeah, more effective taxes on wealth, absolutely. You know, I think there are a whole range of options the government could look at."

While Mr Burnham announced policies in the summer to give families breathing space - including cutting VAT on electricity bills - Mr Nowak said: "I think the key message for the Prime Minister is he needs to go faster and further to help people through the cost-of-living crisis. Clear poll after poll shows that the number one issue that the British public care about is the cost of living."

He added: "The Prime Minister has done some important things, like breathing space policies, as he described them, you know, VAT on energy bills, a cap on bus fares—all welcome stuff. But we think he needs to go further and faster, and he needs to demonstrate with every single decision he takes, including right up to the budget and beyond, that he's on the side of working-class people and their families and communities."

News.title: Prince Harry source blames King's royal status letter as Uganda pulls out of Invictus Games
News.content:
Prince Harry source blames King's royal status letter as Uganda pulls out of Invictus Games

Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, the son of the Ugandan president, said the nation were no longer taking part in the Duke's Invictus Games due to the ‘Harry-Meghan nonsense’

View 3 Images Harry and Meghan are back in the UK - and the Palace issued a letter of 'guidance' (Image: Getty Images)

Uganda's decision to withdraw from Prince Harry's Invictus Games is a 'consequence' of the King's cutting letter on the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's royal status, it has been claimed.

‌



Buckingham Palace issued the 'guidance' on the monarch's behalf on Monday, declaring in no uncertain terms that the couple have not returned to the UK as working royals.

‌



A spokesman or the Sussexes quickly hit back at the announcement, claiming: "We were a little surprised not to have been told about this in advance" with the publication of the letter said to be catching the returning Sussexes off-guard.

‌



View 3 Images The Games are precious to Harry - and his team have hit out at the withdrawal (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Prince Harry has not spoken to King Charles since bombshell return to UK with Meghan READ MORE :

Uganda today are no longer going to be taking part in the Games, the country’s military chief has said, out of respect for King Charles amid division over the “Harry-Meghan nonsense”.

But a source linked to the Sussex's camp told ITV: "Intended or unintended, this is clearly a consequence of the Lord Chamberlain’s guidance regarding the Duke and Duchess of Sussex that was rushed out without consultation on Monday.

‌



“Sadly, the only people who will suffer are the Invictus Games competitors.”

Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, son of the Ugandan president, made the withdrawal announcement in a post on social media.

View 3 Images Harry's return to the UK has not been low key (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Kainerugaba wrote: “In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games. We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty’s approval.”

General Kainerugaba, speaking to The Times, said he made the decision to withdraw Uganda from the Invictus Games due to his support for King Charles.

He said: "I have factions in the Ministry of Defence that support that Harry-Meghan nonsense. I had to quash it straight away. I support the monarch. Period."

‌



The King issued a letter to "senior stakeholders" on Monday where he has made it clear that - despite being back in the UK - his son and Meghan should be considered "private citizens".

In a firm letter statement on his behalf, it stated that the Sussexes' should not use their HRH styles, which are still in abeyance, and that they "do not represent the sovereign" while out making public appearances.

Article continues below

The guidance was sent under the King's instruction by his most senior official, the Lord Chamberlain, to offer clarity over Harry and Meghan's royal status after requests for guidance. It has been issued to those in government, the military and lord lieutenants up and down the country.

In the run up to the Sussexes' return to Britain, the King was said to be glad to be able to spend more time with the family, but remained adamant they would not be working royals and there was no half-in, half-out option.

News.title: Woman stabbed to death at Lidl checkout in Germany before knifeman attacked by customers
News.content:
Woman stabbed to death at Lidl checkout in Germany before knifeman attacked by customers

The horror attack happened at a supermarket in Ratzeberg, northern Germany when around 20 customers were also shopping

View Image The attack happened at a Lidl in Germany (Image: Google)

A woman has reportedly been stabbed to death at a Lidl checkout in Germany despite the heroic efforts of two construction workers who struck the knifeman with bottles.

‌



Around 20 customers were in the supermarket in Ratzeberg, Northern Germany, when the horror attack happened at around 3.45pm, according to German news outlet Bild.

‌



The two men who tried to stop the attacker slammed him to the ground and eventually managed to overpower him.

‌



"A suspect has been seriously injured," Lübeck police said. Bild reports that he is a 44-year-old man who is now recovering from his injuries at University Hospital Schleswig-Holstein.

One witness told another German news outlet Kieler Nachrichten that he did not think the perpetrator knew the woman he allegedly stabbed to death.

Article continues below

The local homicide squad and public prosecutor's office have launched an investigation into the suspected murder. The Lidl remains cordoned off and cops have said there is no danger to the public. They said they had received multiple emergency calls.

News.title: UK economy could get £14bn boost by tackling youth employment Neet crisis
News.content:
UK economy could get £14bn boost by tackling youth employment Neet crisis

The hospitality sector is calling on a package of tax cuts from the government to help it get more 'Neets' into work for the first time, which cost boost the economy by more than £14billion

View 3 Images Hotel receptionist Hannah Carolan, 20, spent two years unemployed (Image: Provided)

Tackling a first jobs crisis could give the economy a more than £14billion boost, it is claimed.

‌



Nearly one million young people aged 16 to 24 are classed as Neets - not in employment, education or training, or about one in eight people in that age group. The figure has fallen from the start of 2026 but has risen over the past year.

‌



The Labour government has vowed to find ways to address the problem on the back of final recommendations from former minister Alan Milburn. However, research suggests getting more of the near one million Neets into work could also help grow the UK economy; one of PM Andy Burnham and Chancellor John Healey’s key priorities.

‌



View 3 Images The hospitality sector has appealed to the government for sector specific help to reduce costs to then enable it to take on more young people (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Analysis by hotel chain Hilton and consultants WPI Economics estimates that each Neet who gets a first job generates around £152,000 in economic value per year through higher output, tax revenues, lower benefits spending and reduced long-term scarring effects. Yet many young people struggle to take their first step into work due to a lack of prior experience, leaving them caught in an “experience trap”.

Recent data from the Office for National Statistics showed 400,000 Neets are actively looking for work, yet separate research suggests one in four cite a lack of experience as their biggest barrier to getting a job. WPI calculated that that this “experience trap” could be costing Britain up to £14.4billion a year in lost economic output.

‌



And on Wednesday, Children's Commissioner Rachel De Souza warned that tens of thousands of college teens are hidden from official Neets figures as they only attend for less than half the time. Hilton says it is part of an industry that can help tackle the problem given that hospitality remains one of the industries that offers young people without experience the opportunity to enter the workforce.

View 3 Images Hotel giant Hilton says getting each Neet young person into work is worth £152,000 to the economy (Image: Getty Images)

It, and trade body UKHospitality, are calling for a package of measures from the government specifically targeted at this sector, including reducing employer national insurance contributions, halving hospitality VAT to 10% in line with Europe, and scrapping the proposed holiday tax. Steve Cassidy, senior vice president for Hilton in the UK and Ireland, said: “Hospitality has always been one of the UK’s strongest routes into employment and we see firsthand how taking that first step into work can have a lasting impact on a young person’s confidence, skills and future career prospects.

‌



“This research backs up just how valuable those first-job opportunities continue to be, not only for young people but for the wider economy. Yet too many young people are now caught in an experience trap, unable to get the experience employers are looking for because they cannot access that crucial first opportunity.”

Allen Simpson, chief executive of UKHospitality, said: “The ‘experience trap’ thousands of young people are caught up in is the result of the last two years adding billions of costs onto critical employment sectors like hospitality. Hospitality is the sector of experience and opportunity, regardless of your background, qualifications or circumstances, but the jobs it creates and supports are being taxed out of existence.

"It’s costing the economy and taking away the first step on the career ladder for a whole generation. The benefits of backing hospitality are clear. Billions in economic benefit, opportunities for young people and thousands of people back in work.

Article continues below

"The new Prime Minister should continue to show his support for hospitality, reduce its tax burden and allow the sector to fulfil its potential to drive economic growth and create new jobs in every postcode.”

Hannah Carolan, 20, a receptionist at Hilton London Metropole, got her job after going on the firm's Springboard programme. She said "After leaving college I applied for dozens of jobs but found it difficult to secure interviews. After spending two years unemployed, my confidence began to suffer and I wondered whether I would be able to find a career that was right for me. Employers wanted experience, but I was unable to get a first job that would give me my first taste of work – it was a catch 22.”

News.title: Lawyer who witnessed horrors of 9/11 still providing for victims' families 25 years later
News.content:
Lawyer who witnessed horrors of 9/11 still providing for victims' families 25 years later

EXCLUSIVE: Helping youngsters with scholarships and jobs after witnessing the horrors of 9/11 is part of the vow Michael Barasch made after dozens of firefighters he knew were killed in the horror attacks he witnessed

View 6 Images Michael Barasch - providing jobs and scholarships for relatives of 9/11 victims 25 years on (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

It may be 25 years ago, but the horrific sight of seeing “dozens of people” jumping to their deaths from the World Trade Center is an image that has never left Michael Barasch.

‌



He also personally knew dozens of the firefighters who were killed. And he made a vow that day that whatever he could do to help the families of the victims in the future he would do so. He has certainly kept his promise.

‌



A quarter of a century on, he has given dozens of jobs at his Charitable Foundation to wives, husbands, sons and daughters of those who were died. Just last week another six teenagers, who lives were affected by 9/11, were given scholarships to help with their university fees.

‌



View 6 Images 9/11 - 25 years on Barasch & McGarry Charitable Foundation's still helping victims (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Iconic 9/11 briefcase man vows to never throw it away after World Trade Center horrors 25 years ago READ MORE :

As the victims’ children grew up many were able to seize the opportunity of employment at his offices - just a couple of blocks from the World Trade Centre. "It was the very least I could do,” said Michael, 71.

As we sat in his office he reeled off the names of members of his own staff who had fallen ill in recent years. Secretaries with skin cancer, lawyers with kidney cancer. He has been battling prostate cancer and skin cancer himself. He said: “We’ve given jobs to several dozen children and spouses of those who died on 9/11. It’s been great from a personal point of view and wonderful to help them after what they’ve been through.

‌



"It’s great to help those who are part of the 9/11 community. And they know what it has been like. When people call up to talk about issues surrounding 9/11 and they might say ‘you just don’t know what it’s like’. In fact our people do know exactly what it’s like and that a real help to them.”

View 6 Images Hero firefighter William "Billy" Gormley. (Image: firehero.org)

‌



Michael explained: “They come and perhaps work in the claims department or in various admin jobs. But some fall in love with law and then go off to law school.” He joked: “I tell them ‘I’ve given you a job and now you’re going and leaving me!’ But then some of them actually come back. We’ve got five or six lawyers with us now who all had their first start with us in different roles.”

He added: “It makes me so proud that so many of them end up going on to law school, or it's a way for them to spend some meaningful time giving back in honour of their parents who passed away. It makes me feel great to know that I'm putting my clients at ease, but I'm also giving these young people something meaningful to do with their careers.

“ I'm one of those people who believed the government when they said the air was safe to breathe. It wasn't. My office is three blocks from ground zero. I was exposed to the exact same toxins as the firefighters and cops. And not surprisingly, I got sick like so many others.

‌



"The office workers, the former students, the former teachers, the downtown residents, were all coming down with the same illnesses, the same cancers as the 9/11 heroes. And for me, I had prostate cancer and skin cancer, two of the most common cancers in the 9/11 community.

“Thankfully, both of them were diagnosed early, and that really is the key. I know it sounds corny, but the key to surviving cancer is early detection and early treatment. So I consider myself really lucky."

6 View 6 Images Barasch & McGarry Charitable Foundation's 'Giving Back' event 6 View 6 Images Some of the young scholars who have benefitted from generosity of Barasch & McGarry Charitable Foundation

‌



He heads the Barasch & McGarry charitable foundation. His legal firm represented many firefighters even before 9/11. They hosted an event last week on the 80th floor of 3 World Trade Centre called “Giving Back: Honouring the 25th Remembrance of 9/11”.

He invited the Mirror along to watch as they gave scholarships to Gabriella Abate, Sophia Cucuzza, Ian Dannenfelser, Domenick Masiello, Gianna Romano and Thomas Sheehan. They are all aged just 17 and 18.

Gabriella is honouring her grandad Joseph M Abate senior - a NYPD electrician who restored power at Ground Zero. She will attend Marist University where she study fashion merchandising. Sophia is honouring her mum Jaime Cucuzza who worked at Thomson Reuters downtown office. She will attend Hofstra University to study nursing.

‌



View 6 Images Bridget Gormley who lost her dad Billy to illness caused by 9/11 is one of Michael Barasch's key people (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

Ian is honouring his grandad a lifelong volunteer firefighter and Deputy Chief Marshall with Camden County Fire Marshal’s office. Ian is attending Penn State to study mechanical engineering. Domenick is honouring his grandad Domenick Zernone, a Local 3 electrician who helped restore critical systems after 9/11. He will attend Lafayette College to study mechanical engineering.

Article continues below

Gianna who honouring her granny Marie Erico who worked at Aon’s office in the South Tower. She will attend Penn State to study Communication Sciences and Disorders. Thomas is honouring his mum Delia Tanger who lived in Battery Park and later passed away from cancer. He will attend the New Jersey Institute of Technology.

Among those Michael helped with a job is Bridget Gormley. She lost her dad William “Billy” Gormley a hero firefighter who later died of bladder cancer. She said: “I’ve worked here for eight years. When I first started I was taking phone calls and now I work in a community liaison role.

“Michael likes to help people who can relate to the people he is trying to help. He has absorbed new generation - children who lost their parents at 9/11. People really are very grateful for the opportunities they’ve been given.”

News.title: Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan lose bid for jail release amid UK extradition battle
News.content:
Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan lose bid for jail release amid UK extradition battle

US Magistrate Lauren Louis denied a motion for release, meaning the Tates will remain jailed during a potentially lengthy extradition process that could take months.

View 2 Images The Tate Brothers must stay in jail (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate must remain in custody as they fight extradition to the United Kingdom, a federal judge in Miami has ruled.

‌



US Magistrate Lauren Louis denied a motion for release, meaning the Tates, who deny accusations of rape and sex trafficking, will remain jailed during what could be a months-long extradition process.

‌



The Tates failed to demonstrate that they do not present a flight risk or danger to the community or that special circumstances warrant their release, Louis said in her ruling.

‌



"Having failed to meet these three factors, Respondents' Motion for Release Pending Extradition Proceedings is DENIED," she said in the ruling.

The Tates' legal team said in a statement that the decision to keep them in custody creates a legal contradiction. The brothers are being detained in the United States because of a British extradition request while simultaneously being required to defend themselves against charges in Romania, the statement said.

View 2 Images Andrew and Tristan Tate deny accusations of rape and sex trafficking (Image: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP via A)

‌



Trump's travel halted as emergency plane slide seen deployed from Air Force One READ MORE :

Volodymyr Zelensky close call as drone narrowly misses his plane to Oslo READ MORE :

"They are now facing an extraordinary situation in which they are being held thousands of miles from Romania while Romanian proceedings continue, deadlines approach, an additional indictment is said to be imminent and their own Romanian lawyer says he cannot properly prepare," the lawyers said.

"No serious person can pretend that this can be reviewed properly through occasional conversations from a federal detention center in another country."

The attorneys said they are considering whether to appeal the judge's decision. The Tates have courted controversy with their promotion of wealth, male dominance and misogyny through their social media empire. Prosecutors say the brothers are a flight risk because they appear to have money and bragged about multiple passports.

‌



During a hearing last month in Miami, the brothers denied criminal accusations spanning several countries, blasted their critics and described their brash online personas as characters and not their true personalities. The Tates said they exaggerate their claims of wealth to boost their clout on social media.

The new allegations are the latest in the Tates' long-running international legal saga spanning the US, Britain and Romania. They have been held at the Federal Detention Center in Miami since making a brief court appearance two days after their July 18 arrest.

Lawyers for the Tates asked the judge to allow them to be freed from custody at least until an extradition hearing can be held on their UK rape and trafficking charges.

Article continues below

They have repeatedly argued that Britain's request is out of line because their criminal case in Romania is going first. Romanian officials have let the brothers remain free until the proceedings conclude, and they have not tried to flee and are complying with all court restrictions. Earlier this month, Romanian prosecutors indicted the brothers on additional charges.

News.title: Volodymyr Zelensky close call as suspected Russian drone narrowly misses his plane
News.content:
Volodymyr Zelensky close call as suspected Russian drone narrowly misses his plane

Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky's plane was nearly hit by a drone - believed to be Russian - as he travelled to Oslo for the funeral of King Harald, the Norwegian Prime Minister said

View 2 Images Volodymyr Zelensky pictured after landing in Oslo (Image: PRESIDENT OF UKRAINE/APAImages/Shutterstock)

Volodymyr Zelensky's plane was nearly hit by a drone thought to have been launched by Russia.

‌



The incident happened while the Ukrainian president was on his way to Oslo for the funeral of King Harald. Norwegian Prime Minister Gahr Støre said that it was the "reality" the Ukrainian President is facing amid the war with Russia.

‌



Zelensky regularly travels the world pushing Western leaders for their support in the war against Russia and this was a reminder of how perilous it is for him to travel.

‌



"His plane was ⁠almost hit by a drone as it was about to take off from Moldova" said Støre.

View 2 Images Volodymyr Zelensky with his wife at the funeral of King Harald (Image: Shutterstock)

Moldova's Defense Ministry reported that a Shahed-type drone had invaded the country's airspace at around 4.20pm local time. It was monitored by the Moldovan military until the drone crossed into Romanian airspace at around 4.37pm.

‌



The drone incursion triggered airspace closures, emergency alerts, and the scrambling of NATO fighter jets. The timing of the drone violation corresponded with Zelensky's flight from Moldova, a source told the Kyiv Independent.

Russian drones and missiles have routinely violated the airspace of both Romania and Moldova in recent months.

Anti-migrant protesters targeting Poole RNLI training centre met with heavy police presence READ MORE :

Ahead of the King's funeral today (Wednesday), the leaders met along with defence companies to discuss the FREYJA anti-ballistic missile programme – an initiative aimed at building alternatives to the US-made Patriot interceptors.

‌



Støre said that in another meeting today he had asked how Zelensky's night had been and he replied to say "it wasn't a good night, because he had been on the phone receiving news about where the missiles had hit".

Meanwhile, Zelensky has urged countries to step up pressure on Russia. "Unfortunately, there has been too little response from the international community to these strikes, which are taking people's lives practically every day," he said on social media.

"But a response is needed — Moscow must not go into the winter believing that it can get away with missile and drone terror without consequences."

Article continues below

The United Nations said last month that increasing Russian aerial attacks killed or wounded more Ukrainian civilians in July than in any month since March 2022, with 437 killed and more than 2,600 wounded.

In all, more than 16,800 Ukrainian civilians have been killed and more than 51,000 wounded since the Russian invasion, according to the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine. Moscow always denies it aims at civilians and says it is targeting military-related facilities.

News.title: Police launch criminal investigation into Reform UK donations
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police is carrying out a criminal investigation into Reform UK over allegations it broke foreign funding laws, following a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week.

An undercover reporter recorded two senior Reform aides apparently suggesting a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations, one of which would have totalled Â£500,000.

The police investigation by the Met's Special Enquiry Team is being folded into an inquiry that has been under way into other donations to the party.

A Reform UK spokesman said the party "denies any wrongdoing and will fully cooperate with the investigation".

"We won't be commenting further while a live investigation is under way."

A Met spokesperson said it had received "a number of reports relating to donations and polling involving a political party", after the film by Channel 4 News and Verbatim Investigations was shown on Thursday evening.

In its statement, the Met Police said: "All allegations under investigation relate to potential offences under the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000."

"Detectives continue to liaise closely with the Electoral Commission and Crown Prosecution Service as enquiries progress."

The police spokesperson said detectives were seeking to obtain footage relating to the broadcast.

An Electoral Commission spokesperson said the Channel 4 News report included "serious allegations of wrongdoing", adding: "It is right that these are properly and thoroughly investigated by the police.

"In parallel, we are also considering all relevant information and regulatory steps."

The film overshadowed the party's conference in Birmingham and led to the party losing two key figures - Dan Jukes, chief of staff to the leader Nigel Farage, and James Orr, head of policy.

News.title: Air traffic failure was avoidable, says transport secretary
News.content:
A technical failure of the UK's air traffic control system that has caused widespread flight chaos was avoidable, according to the Transport Secretary.

Heidi Alexander told the Commons she had ordered an independent investigation by the aviation watchdog into the system operated by Nats, which went down for four hours on Tuesday.

More than 2,000 flights have been cancelled as disruption continued for a second day with passengers stuggling to fly out of and into the UK.

After meeting with the boss of Nats, Martin Rolfe, Alexander said a cyberattack could be ruled out, but she added: "I do not believe this issue was unavoidable."

Nats has apologised for its third major technical fault in three years.

Alexander said she discussed with Rolfe how Nats, which is 49% owned by the government, "responded to resolve and minimise the disruption as quickly as possible".

She said there had to be "tough questions about resilience of Nats systems", adding: "We also need to think about consumer redress issues."

Earlier on Wednesday the government said it had confidence in Rolfe, who has led Nats for 11 years as airlines such as Wizz Air and Ryanair called for him to step down.

Nats has been asked to investigate the incident and report back in one week. But Alexander said she has also asked the Civil Aviation Authority to conduct an independent review and present an update in six months' time.

Airlines UK, which represents the country's carriers, said it had written to Alexander to "register serious concerns over yesterday's technical failure at Nats - the third major system failure in three years - which has caused major disruption across the UK's aviation network".

Airlines UK's chief executive Tim Alderslade, said: "The result is a system where airlines pick up the bill for the mistakes of others, while the organisations responsible face little or no financial consequence.

"Accountability should sit where responsibility lies and the Civil Aviation Bill offers the opportunity to address this."

The UK Civil Aviation Authority said passengers are unlikely to be entitled to compensation - though it reminded airlines of their responsibilities to look after passengers who flights had been delayed or cancelled.

It added that the disruption caused by the Nats issue is "likely to be considered the result of 'extraordinary circumstances'", meaning passengers "are unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays or cancellations that were directly caused by the incident."

News.title: Muted US response to UK's West Bank sanctions may reflect simmering frustration
News.content:
As the UK unveiled sanctions against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday, Israel responded with fury, declaring it would shutter Britain's diplomatic mission to the Palestinians, kick out UK military staff from an international coordination base near Gaza and ban nearly a dozen left-wing British members of parliament from entering Israel.

It was a blaring signal of defiance and a remarkable diplomatic escalation.

The UK had taken the action arguing it had a moral imperative to stop the "destruction" of the two-state solution - a future independent Palestinian state - at the hands of the Israeli government. It accused Israel's government of turning a blind eye to the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians by settlers.

The standoff, which by the afternoon extended to a further 11 mostly European countries set to join the settlement trade ban, raised a crucial question: When Israel becomes isolated, the US as its superpower backer often steps in to provide a diplomatic shield. Was the US, too, going to condemn Britain's policy?

Such a reprimand had been previewed by some observers. It felt even more likely when the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, appeared on the BBC before the UK announcement suggesting American "sanctions, repercussions or retaliations" could be coming for Britain, albeit that he didn't know what these were and hadn't spoken to President Trump.

But as Tuesday wore on, Washington's response was notably muted.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, asked about the UK move by reporters on the way to Colombia, said: "Obviously, we're not going to do what the UK did. We saw their announcement today but I don't have any comment on it right now."

He added that Britain had notified the administration ahead of time (most likely during a phone call Trump had with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Monday) and said the US shared "the goal of stability" at a tense time in the region and didn't "want to see some uptick in violenceâ¦ in the West Bank".

It was hardly a withering rebuke of the British move, let alone any kind of punishment. In fact, Washington seemed to be sharing some of the concerns that motivated the move.

Asked about it on Wednesday, Trump said he would be speaking to Israel to understand their thinking, adding: "I understand exactly what's going on, but I want to find out why all of a sudden has that happened."

My understanding is that discussions about the US response were taking place at a high level within the administration on Tuesday. The baseline position appeared to be against any moves that could negatively impact American companies.

News.title: Prince William, Kane and Shearer in campaign to use sport to prevent suicide
News.content:
The Prince of Wales is launching a scheme that aims to use the influence of sport to help prevent suicides, with the support of sports stars including Harry Kane, Kelly Holmes and Alan Shearer.

"Sport has the ability to reach people who may never walk through the door of a mental healthcare service," Prince William is expected to say at an event at Everton's football ground on Thursday.

"People who may never seek support themselves and may be struggling in silence," the prince will say later.

The On Your Side project wants to give people confidence to start the "difficult conversations" with friends, relations, teammates or colleagues who might be struggling with their mental health.

It aims to use the reach of sport to raise awareness about suicide and to show people the help available in a crisis, with the Football Association, Premier League and Team GB providing support.

Thursday's event will be Prince William's biggest public appearance in the UK since the return of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

Earlier this week, he attended the funeral of Norway's King Harald in Oslo and brought his son Prince George to his first day as a boarder at Eton College.

The level of suicide is disproportionately higher among men than women - it's the biggest cause of death for men under the age of 50 in the UK.

"My hope is that every sporting organisation in the country will look at what is being launched today and ask a question: 'What more can we do?' Because the opportunity before us is enormous," Prince William will say.

A film has been made, featuring England football captain Harry Kane and boxer Carl Frampton, talking about the importance of stepping in and offering help if people see someone who seems to be facing mental health problems.

Prince William helps to narrate the video, which aims to tackle the stigma around mental health and suicide, with 7,000 lives being lost to suicide each year in the UK.

The initiative has a practical toolkit, on a free website, for people who are worried or embarrassed about what to say to someone if they have concerns about their wellbeing.

It offers a sports-themed way of approaching the topic, called GOALS, representing G: get ready; O: open the conversation; A: ask the question; L: listen and respond and S: support and signpost.

Alan Shearer, former England football star and TV pundit, described it as "the first suicide prevention toolkit designed for the whole of UK sport".

"You don't have to be an expert. You don't have to have all the answers," said Shearer. "But we can all be better at asking, listening, and helping someone find the right support."

Shearer said it was particularly poignant that the launch would be at Everton, one of the clubs where Gary Speed had played, a friend of Shearer's who died by suicide in 2011.

News.title: RNLI volunteer targeted online and branded 'traitor' after Portsmouth protests
News.content:
An RNLI volunteer who was targeted with abuse online after being wrongly identified as having helped small boat migrants reach land in Portsmouth has told BBC Verify he is not a "traitor".

Neil and his colleagues were filmed wearing their lifesaving gear on a lifeboat by anti-migrant activists near the harbour on Sunday night, after hundreds of protesters descended on the area and shut down roads in response to dozens of asylum seekers being brought to shore.

The lifeboat crew's images were later used in posts accusing them of assisting what some users on X described as "an invasion", several of which also called for them to be "named and shamed".

These posts, which were collectively viewed at least two million times, also incorrectly claimed Neil and another colleague were two entirely different RNLI crew members whose names were available online.

News.title: BBC drops Drag Race UK after eight series
News.content:
RuPaul's Drag Race UK is leaving the BBC after eight series, the broadcaster has confirmed.

A spokesperson for the channel said it was facing "very difficult choices" in the face of "significant financial pressures".

The show is currently broadcast on BBC Three and iPlayer. Future series - as well as its spin-off vs The World - will be broadcast on Wow Presents Plus, a streaming platform owned by the production company behind the show.

At its peak, the UK version of the international drag competition averaged at around 1.5 million viewers per episode.

A spokesperson for the BBC said it was "proud [...] of this groundbreaking show" and thanked "RuPaul, World of Wonder and everyone involved, both on and off screen".

Started in 2019, Drag Race UK brought British drag into mainstream entertainment in the UK, and has made household names of drag performers such as La Voix, Danny Beard, and Tia Kofi.

The show sees drag queens compete in a series of challenges to impress judges RuPaul, Michelle Visage, Graham Norton and Alan Carr, and often features big name celebrity guest judges.

It has become a staple of LGBTQ+ culture and has been praised for its portrayal of the distinct style of British drag.

The corporation is currently rolling out plans to make Â£500m of savings, with director-general Matt Brittin previously telling staff "the scale of savings requires tough choices".

A BBC spokesperson said: "As the BBC continues to navigate significant financial pressures and deliver the savings required of us, we have had to make some very difficult choices, none of which have been taken lightly."

Announcing the news on Instagram, Wow Presents Plus said a "new era" of Drag Race UK was on the way.

A new series, Drag Race UK All Stars, which sees previous fan favourites return to compete again, will premier in Autumn 2027 exclusively on Wow Presents Plus.

BBC News understands the current series of Drag Race UK, which launched in September 2026, will continue to air as normal on BBC Three and appear on iPlayer, and all existing series will continue to be available once the move is complete.

The BBC declined to comment on whether future series of other international versions of the show, including Drag Race Canada and Drag Race Down Under, would continue to air.

Earlier this year, the BBC announced it was dropping LGBTQ+ dating show I Kissed a Boy - which made history as the UK's first gay dating show - and I Kissed a Girl.

Jordan Burrow, a contestant on series two of I Kissed a Boy, said the decision was an example of "where we're at within the queer community".

The corporation said at the time that it was "exceptionally proud" of the shows but they had to make "difficult choices in light of our funding challenges".

News.title: Apple's new boss starts with big gamble on costly first folding iPhone
News.content:
John Ternus has entered his second week as Apple's chief executive and the company has revealed the first major change to the iPhone since it was released almost 20 years ago.

Ternus, who took on Apple's top job after Tim Cook stepped down, was onstage on Wednesday at the company's annual product release event in front of huge images of the first foldable iPhone.

With a book-style format, the new iPhone, dubbed the Duo, is the largest ever size of the product. And with a US starting price of $1,999 (Â£1,475) going up to $3,200, it is also the most expensive. UK prices start at Â£1,999.

Ternus said the Duo was "inspired by the iPad" but called the folding features "fluid and completely intuitive."

The foldable phone has been a work-in-progress inside Apple for several years.

When unfolded, the new Duo has the look of a small iPad. When folded in half, it has the look of a wider iPhone.

Ternus said during the event that Apple wanted to avoid the look and feel of other foldable smart phones on the market, which he said "feel like two phones stuck together... making a larger screen feel much smaller."

The Duo, he said, is the "result of a series of remarkable innovations that we think will redefine the experience of using a foldable phone."

Ternus was directly involved in developing the foldable iPhone as he spent many years as a top executive inside Apple's hardware division before being tapped earlier this year as Cook's successor.

News.title: Miliband rejects chief rabbi's claim British Jews in greater danger after sanctions move
News.content:
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has rejected the chief rabbi's warning that British Jews are at greater risk after the UK announced sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Miliband said that as a "proud British Jew" he disagreed with UK Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis, who described the move as a "truly dark day" that would "succeed only in bolstering the very extremism they seek to target".

"We all need to do more to tackle antisemitism," Miliband said, "but I believe we can do that and stand up for British values".

The sanctions on trade with illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank come against a backdrop of rising antisemitic incidents across the UK.

The Community Security Trust (CST), an organisation that provides security support to the Jewish community, recorded 1,926 incidents of anti-Jewish hate across the UK in the first six months of 2026, a 21% increase on the same period in 2025.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham defended his government's decision, telling MPs that "Britain has to stand for fairness against injustice".

"Where people are being bullied out of their homes... we will always stand with the underdog," he said.

While a strong reaction against the move had been expected from the US - Israel's most powerful ally - President Donald Trump was relatively muted in his first public comments on the matter on Wednesday.

He told reporters he would speak to both Israel and the UK to "find out... their thinking" and ask why the decision had been made "all of a sudden".

News.title: National security can't come at expense of social security, Burnham says
News.content:
In the Commons session, Burnham repeated that the government would meet the Nato target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, with a target date for hitting the 3% figure set out in the spending review in the spring.

The PM said he had appointed John Healey, who resigned as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary over the government's failure to commit to a 3% increase by 2030, "because of his strong commitment to the defence of this nation".

However, Badenoch hit back that 2035 was "a decade away" and "the threats are now".

She questioned whether Burnham was "unable" or "just unwilling" to meet the 2030 target.

In response, Burnham insisted: "This chancellor of all chancellors will be willing to provide that funding to our armed forces."

However, he rejected a Conservative plan to partly fund increased defence spending by saving at least Â£4bn through reforms to housing benefit.

"I don't think, myself, that taking Â£4bn out of housing benefit is going to get the right consensus around this issue because that would create levels of homelessness in this country... that we wouldn't have seen before, hundreds of thousands of children in temporary accommodation," he said.

"Yes, we do everything to support our national security, but it can't come at the expense of social security."

He added: "This side of the House will not be forced to choose between the two and we will set out a plan to get to 3.5% by 2035 at the spending review."

Badenoch said Burnham's comments were "unbelievable", adding: "We need to fund our defence, not spend all of our money on welfare."

Burnham insisted he would "bring the welfare budget down" by tackling the number of young people not in education, employment or training.

"That's the Labour way to get the welfare bill down," he said.

"That is the right way to fund defence."

Badenoch accused Burnham of being "continuity Keir".

"He's pretending that he's the change candidate. But the fact is, he's still failing to cut welfare," she said.

As prime minister, Sir Keir attempted to cut disability benefits but was forced to row back on the plans in the face of opposition from Labour MPs.

Cutting the welfare bill is a key part of Tory proposals for funding increased defence spending.

Spending on benefits has ballooned in recent years and is forecast to rise to Â£408.6bn in 2030/31, according to figures from the Department for Work and Pensions.

There is particular concern about the nearly one million young people in the UK who are not in education, employment or training â known as "Neets".

The government has asked former minister Alan Milburn to look into the issue and he is expected to publish his final recommendations for how to tackle the problem shortly.

News.title: Man charged with assisting Russian intelligence service
News.content:
A 31-year-old British man has been charged under the National Security Act over alleged contact with Russia's military intelligence agency.

Joshua Cammidge, from Swindon, allegedly received instructions from an individual believed to be linked to the GRU Volunteer Corps, a group controlled by Russia's military intelligence agency, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said.

He has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct.

He is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Thursday.

Cammidge was arrested at an address in Swindon on Friday by Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) London officers, supported by officers from Wiltshire Police.

He was taken to a London police station and searches were carried out at a different address in Swindon, the Metropolitan Police said.

He was further arrested and detained under the National Security Act on Saturday.

The force said he has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service contrary to Section 3 of the National Security Act 203 and preparatory conduct contrary to Section 18 of the National Security Act 2023.

Frank Ferguson, chief crown prosecutor for the CPS's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said: "Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue criminal proceedings.

"We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial.

"It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information online which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings."

Security Minister Dan Jarvis said: "The police have taken action against a potential threat, and I thank them for the vital work they do every day to keep us safe.

"Whilst it would be inappropriate to comment further on the specifics of this case, I know people will be concerned about recent incidents across Europe, intended to sow fear, create disruption and undermine support for Ukraine. They will not succeed."

News.title: Hundreds mourn police officer killed in A66 crash
News.content:
Hundreds have turned out for the funeral of one of the police officers killed in a wrong-way crash.

PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, died when a Volkswagen Passat collided with their marked armed response car on the A66 at South Bank, near Middlesbrough, on 22 August. Five young men were also killed.

A full ceremonial police funeral took place for PC Blades in Hartlepool earlier, with hundreds of officers from Cleveland and forces across the country lining the street in a guard of honour.

Speaking on behalf of his family, Cleveland Police Federation chair Lauren Somerville said "life feels unbearably quiet" without the father-of-two's "silly jokes" and laughter.

Members of other emergency services were present at St Joseph's Roman Catholic Church, alongside community leaders and politicians.

Cleveland Police chief constable Victoria Fuller greeted mourners at the entrance to the church.

Policing minister Sarah Jones and Home Office minister Anna Turley also attended.

News.title: Failures 'contributed to' death of Sir Richard Branson's wife
News.content:
A private hospital's failure to provide preventative medication contributed to the death of Lady Joan Branson, an inquest has concluded.

The 80-year-old, who was married to Sir Richard Branson, died on 24 November last year after suffering a cardiac arrest at the private Lister Hospital in Chelsea, west London.

Senior coroner Professor Fiona Wilcox told Westminster Coroner's Court on Wednesday that Lady Joan did not receive prophylactic anticoagulants at the hospital despite a "very high risk of developing deep vein thrombosis".

"I do find her death would have likely been prevented and the lack of anticoagulation did cause or contribute to her death probably," she said.

The coroner's court heard that Lady Joan was admitted to the hospital on 17 November after a fall weeks earlier on Necker Island, a British Virgin Island owned by her billionaire husband.

She died after suffering a pulmonary embolism, a sudden, dangerous blockage in a lung artery, resulting from deep vein thrombosis.

Haematologist Dr George Adams told the inquest that Lady Joan was "extremely high risk" for blood clots and the "biggest risk factor by far was her immobility and her fracture".

From her hospital admission to her death, Glasgow-born Lady Joan did not receive any prophylactic anticoagulation, which is used to stop blood clots from forming.

The hospital's admitting doctor, Dr Basir Kunduzi, did not complete a bleeding risk assessment on the day of her admission, the inquest heard.

Dr Kunduzi said Lady Joan's death led him to "reflect on my role as a doctor" and the importance of "good communication between team members".

Giving her conclusion, Professor Wilcox said it was "not a case of neglect" and there "wasn't an absence of treatment".

After her death, Sir Richard described his wife as the "shining star around which our family's universe has always orbited".
