World.title: Gambia: Gambian President Declares Power Emergency Amid Protests
World.content:
President Adama Barrow has declared the country's prolonged electricity crisis a national emergency and promised to increase power generation as protests over rolling blackouts intensify ahead of the December presidential election.

Barrow urged citizens to remain calm over prolonged power cuts. He said that the country is not alone in facing an electricity crisis that has affected several parts of West Africa.

Demonstrators in Banjul and surrounding areas burned tyres, erected roadblocks and called for Barrow to resign after some communities experienced outages lasting up to 48 hours during the hot season.

Police used tear gas to disperse protesters gathering near Barrow's residence and the headquarters of the National Water and Electricity Corporation.

Barrow has promised a 24-megawatt generation machine by the end of October. He announced plans for a further 50-megawatt solar power plant. The electricity provider has blamed soaring temperatures, climate change and wider geopolitical disruptions for the crisis.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - September 9, 2026
World.content:
press review

Kenya Launches Crackdown on Foreign Informal Traders

Kenyan officials have started to crack down on foreign nationals running small businesses in the informal economy. This comes after President William Ruto backed measures reserving activities such as hawking and petty retail primarily for Kenyan citizens. Ruto said that foreign investors should focus on bringing capital, creating jobs and supporting local production rather than competing with citizens in businesses requiring little capital. Kenyans have reacted with mixed feelings to the move, with some welcoming it as a way of protecting jobs amid high unemployment. Others fear it could fuel xenophobia and discourage foreign investment. Political economist Sheila Owigo Olang questioned whether removing foreign traders would create more opportunities for Kenyans, describing the policy as potentially populist ahead of elections. The government has insisted that foreign nationals who comply with immigration, work permit and licensing requirements remain legally protected. Questions remain over who will ultimately be affected and how the policy will be enforced.

Gambia Declares Power Crisis a National Emergency

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Gambian President Adama Barrow has declared the country's prolonged electricity crisis a national emergency and promised to increase power generation as protests over rolling blackouts intensify ahead of the December presidential election. Demonstrators in Banjul and surrounding areas burned tyres, erected roadblocks and called for Barrow to resign after some communities experienced outages lasting up to 48 hours during the hot season. Police used tear gas to disperse protesters gathering near Barrow's residence and the headquarters of the National Water and Electricity Corporation. Barrow has promised a 24-megawatt generation machine by the end of October. He announced plans for a further 50-megawatt solar power plant. The electricity provider has blamed soaring temperatures, climate change and wider geopolitical disruptions for the crisis.

Funding Cuts Push Sudan's Health System to the Brink

Sudan's already fragile health system is nearing collapse as international funding cuts force healthcare facilities to close amid the country's devastating civil war, said Médecins Sans Frontières. More than 33 million people now require medical assistance following the conflict between the Sudanese army and the Rapid Support Forces. The loss of USAID funding and reductions in European aid have left many humanitarian organisations unable to sustain their operations. MSF reported a sharp increase in patient admissions at facilities it supports and said the closure of dozens of healthcare centres is placing enormous pressure on the hospitals that remain open. In some displacement camps, maternity and surgical services have shut down, forcing patients to travel long distances for treatment. The crisis is compounded by attacks on healthcare facilities, widespread hunger and continuing violence, prompting MSF to urge world leaders gathering at the UN General Assembly to increase support.

WFP Says Food Aid Key to Fighting DR Congo Ebola Outbreak

The World Food Programme has warned that food assistance must form a central part of the response to the rapidly spreading Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, where conflict, displacement and severe hunger are making it harder to contain the disease. The outbreak, declared in May and caused by the rare Bundibugyo species, has become the fastest on record, with more than 5,500 cases and 2,642 deaths reported in its first 100 days. WFP said that people struggling to feed their families cannot easily comply with the health measures needed to prevent transmission, particularly in remote areas far from treatment centres. More than 500,000 people in the affected Ituri province are facing severe food insecurity, while poor infrastructure and ongoing conflict complicate efforts to deliver assistance. The WFP is calling for more international funding to expand both food assistance and Ebola treatment services, noting that adequate nutrition in addition to medical treatment can greatly increase a patient's chances of survival.

Nurses' Strike Deepens Pressure on Kenya's Health System

Kenya's prolonged nurses' strike is placing increasing pressure on the country's public health system, with essential services disrupted as nurses demand the implementation of long-standing labour agreements. Hundreds of nurses have demonstrated in Nairobi, calling on the national and county governments to address salary arrears, allowances, staffing shortages, promotions and career progression. At the heart of the dispute is the 2017 Collective Bargaining Agreement, which the Kenya National Union of Nurses and Midwives says remains largely unimplemented despite provisions for nursing service allowances and improved working conditions. The union has said negotiations alone are no longer sufficient and insists that signed agreements must be honoured before members return to work. The government and county authorities continue engaging with the union, including on the permanent employment of UHC workers. Nurses argue that years of unfulfilled promises and poor working conditions have damaged morale and undermined their ability to provide safe and effective patient care.

Close 

Zimbabwean Vendors Vow to Defy Harare Street Clearance Order



Zimbabwean authorities have intensified efforts to remove illegal vendors from Harare's Central Business District. They declared that uncontrolled street trading is no longer acceptable and ordered traders to use designated markets and vending bays. Local Government Minister Daniel Garwe said illegal vending was contributing to congestion, blocked pavements, litter, poor sanitation and public health risks, including the potential spread of water-borne diseases such as cholera. The government insists that the crackdown is not a war against informal traders. It argued that significant investment has already been made in designated vending infrastructure that remains underused. The move has, however, been met with strong resistance from vendors, who say informal trading is their only means of survival in an economy with limited formal employment opportunities. The order is a seven-day ultimatum to vacate the streets, and vendors have vowed to resist. Traders' representatives have urged the government to implement reforms guided by the National Informal Economy Formalization Strategy of Zimbabwe, rather than just chasing traders off the streets.

World.title: South Africa: Fake Toys Raise Safety and Job Concerns - South African News Briefs - September 9, 2026
World.content:
press review

Fake Toys Raise Safety and Job Concerns

Concerns are mounting over counterfeit toys flooding the South African market, reports EWN. Fake products are now estimated to account for 25% of sales. Farrel Frank, managing director of the South African Toys and Games Association, warned that counterfeit toys can pose serious health and safety risks and cost jobs. He said the growth of online sales platforms has contributed to the problem. Some major platforms are working with the industry to remove suspicious listings. Consumers are also being urged to remain vigilant after a recent complaint involving a toy with a strong chemical smell that allegedly caused burning and tingling when it touched a consumer’s face.

More Witnesses to Testify in Anele Tembe Inquest

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

More witnesses are set to testify in the inquest into the death of Anele Tembe, who fell from the 10th floor of a Cape Town hotel in April 2021, reports SABC News. Lawyers representing Tembe's family questioned witnesses about whether her fiancé, the late rapper Kiernan "AKA" Forbes, had asked for her family to be informed of her death. Two police officers told the court they had no knowledge of whether the family had been contacted. One officer said Forbes did not ask police to contact them. The inquest has also heard from a nearby resident who reported hearing an argument between a man and a woman shortly before Tembe’s death.

Tshuma Extradition Hinges on Plea Deal

Extradition proceedings against UK fugitive Ndodana Tshuma could depend on whether the Johannesburg Magistrates Court accepts a plea agreement between him and the State, reports EWN. Tshuma, who is accused of murdering his wife and two young daughters in the UK before fleeing to South Africa, pleaded guilty to firearm and immigration-related charges following his arrest in Johannesburg. Details of the proposed plea deal and sentence have not been disclosed. The magistrate must still decide whether the agreement is just and appropriate. A custodial sentence could further complicate his extradition to the UK, where he is expected to face the murder allegations.

World.title: Nigeria: Nigerian Army Redeploys Top Generals, Appoints New Person to Lead Boko Haram War
World.content:
A Wednesday statement by army spokesperson Appolonia Anele said the deployments were approved by the Chief of Army Staff, Waidi Shaibu, a lieutenant general.

The leadership of the Nigerian Army has redeployed several top generals, including the person leading the war against Boko Haram terrorists in the North-east

A Wednesday statement by army spokesperson Appolonia Anele said the deployments were approved by the Chief of Army Staff, Waidi Shaibu, a lieutenant general.

A major-general, IA Ajose, will now head Operation HADIN KAI (OPHK), the army's main operation against Boko Haram and other terror groups in the North-east. Mr Ajose replaces another major general, AE Abubakar, who was redeployed to the Nigerian Army Heritage and Future Centre (NAHFC) as Dean, Faculty of Operational Research.



Read the full statement by the army below.

NIGERIAN ARMY REPOSITIONS SENIOR LEADERSHIP TO STRENGTHEN OPERATIONAL EFFECTIVENESS, NATIONAL SECURITY

The Chief of Army Staff (COAS), Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu, has approved the strategic redeployment of senior officers to key command, operational and staff appointments across the Nigerian Army (NA), as part of ongoing efforts to enhance operational effectiveness, strengthen leadership and align the Service's command structure with Nigeria's evolving security environment. The exercise prioritises critical operational theatres and strategic appointments to ensure the right leadership, experience and expertise are positioned to deliver decisive effects.

In the new postings, Major General IA Ajose moves from Army Headquarters (AHQ), Department of Army Operations, to Theatre Command Joint Task Force (JTF) North East, Operation HADIN KAI (OPHK), as Theatre Commander, while Major General AE Abubakar has been redeployed from OPHK, to the Nigerian Army Heritage and Future Centre (NAHFC) as Dean, Faculty of Operational Research. Major General AM Alechenu moves from Defence Headquarters (DHQ) Garrison to the Nigerian Army Heritage and Future Centre, while Major General RT Utsaha moves from AHQ Department of Army Standards and Evaluation to DHQ Garrison as Commander.

Similarly, Major General AM Umar moves from AHQ Department of Civil-Military Affairs (DCMA) to Army War College Nigeria (AWCN) as Commandant, while Major General UM Alkali moves from AWCN to AHQ DCMA. Major General GS Muhammed moves from the Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA) to the Nigerian Army Finance Corporation (NAFIC) as Director General, while Major General JE Osifo moves from NAFIC to the Military Pension Board (MPB) as Chairman and Major General IE Ekpenyong has been redeployed to DHQ Department of Defence Logistics as Director Engineering Services.

At the operational level, Brigadier General AA Bello moves from 6 Division Garrison/Sector 3 JTF South-South, Operation DELTA SAFE, to DHQ Department of Defence Operations. Brigadier General MS Adamu has been redeployed from Nigerian Army Women Command to the newly established 8 Brigade as Commander, while Brigadier General MS Sule moves from Special Task Force Operation ENDURING PEACE to 27 Task Force Brigade as Commander.

Close 

Similarly, Brigadier General I Sule, has been redeployed from the Directorate of Recruitment Management to 6 Division Garrison as Commander while Brigadier General E Azenda, moves from Land Forces Simulation Centre to 2 Division Garrison as Commander and Brigadier General AS Bugaje, moves from 2 Division Garrison to the Land Forces Simulation Centre as Director Administration.

The COAS has charged the newly appointed officers to justify the confidence reposed in them through exemplary leadership, operational innovation, professionalism and unwavering commitment to duty and relentless focused on the constitutional mandate of defending Nigeria's sovereignty, protecting its territorial integrity and supporting civil authority in maintaining peace and security.

The NA remains resolute in sustaining a dynamic leadership and force-employment framework that enhances operational outcomes, strengthens joint and inter-agency coordination and improves the capacity of the Service to respond decisively to contemporary and emerging threats in furtherance of Nigeria's national security objectives.

APPOLONIA ANELE

Colonel

Acting Director Army Public Relations

World.title: Dolly Parton 'could not bear negative things' and kept her cancer diagnosis from fans and family

Dolly Parton's sister is sharing why the legendary singer kept her cancer diagnosis a secret.

In an interview with "CBS Mornings'" set to air on Thursday, Sept. 10, her sister, Stella Parton, didn't go public with her cancer diagnosis because she "did not want people sad," revealing she didn't even share the news with her entire family.

"Well, Dolly did not want anybody to tell that, because Dolly could not bear negative things, and she would not have wanted her fans worried about it," she shared. "She didn’t want a lot of the family worried about it. Some of us knew, the ones that were closer, but not every relative."

The "Jolene" singer died at the age of 80, on Tuesday, Aug. 25, following a "brief battle with cancer."

DOLLY PARTON OFFERED TO TRY EXPERIMENTAL DRUGS IF ‘NO HOPE’ FOR CANCER BATTLE TO HELP OTHERS, SISTER SAYS

News of her death was announced on her Instagram by her nephew, Bryan Seaver, in which he highlighted her incredible body of work as a musician, as well as her philanthropic work with the Imagination Library.

Her death inspired tributes on social media from fans around the world, including musicians and actors alike, something Stella says the "9 to 5" star would have been happy with.

"She’d be really happy and delighted that people have shown her so much love because she knew that that would make us feel better as her family," Stella said. "Bottom line, end of the day, her family and Carl’s family and probably Judy’s family are the people that she would want to say, ‘See, everything I did, they cared. They really loved me."

Dolly rose to stardom in 1967 when she began appearing on "The Porter Wagoner Show." During her time on the show, the two released many iconic duets and were nominated for many Grammys together.

World.title: Surrogate who refused abortion takes fight to Supreme Court as baby's life hangs in balance
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A surrogate who defied a California couple’s demand to abort their baby after a devastating heart diagnosis is taking her fight to the U.S. Supreme Court, arguing a lower court ruling has left her powerless to advocate for the medically fragile newborn.

Attorneys for Alaska cardiac nurse McKenna West filed an emergency application Wednesday, asking Justice Elena Kagan to temporarily block a Los Angeles court ruling that declared the California couple the baby’s legal parents.

Kagan handles emergency matters arising from the Ninth Circuit, which includes California. She has not ruled on the request.

SURROGATE GIVES BIRTH IN TEXAS TO BABY WITH HEART DEFECT AFTER PARENTS REQUESTED ABORTION

West carried the child under a surrogacy agreement with California couple Nausheen Gilkar and Omar Ahmed, who call the baby Rumi. West calls him Gabriel.

The baby was born in Texas on Aug. 12, with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, or HLHS, a rare condition in which the left side of the heart is severely underdeveloped.

KAGAN RECALLS LINDSEY GRAHAM'S VOTE THAT HELPED SEAL HER SUPREME COURT CONFIRMATION

The legal war began after the condition was detected during a 20-week ultrasound. West alleges Gilkar and Ahmed asked her to terminate the pregnancy under a provision in their surrogacy agreement covering serious fetal abnormalities.

West refused, telling the surrogacy agency she could not abort "this precious baby" after feeling him move and learning treatment was available, according to the filing.

She offered to raise the child herself or arrange an adoption if the couple no longer wanted him, while allowing them to walk away from any further financial obligations.

Her attorneys allege West was then warned that continuing the pregnancy could expose her to more than $250,000 in financial penalties.

CONSERVATIVE GROUPS SAY JUSTICE KAGAN CANNOT BE IMPARTIAL IN UPCOMING SUPREME COURT CLIMATE LITIGATION

Gilkar and Ahmed later turned to a California court to establish their legal rights as the baby’s parents. West argued the case belonged in Alaska under the surrogacy agreement and said she appeared in California solely to challenge the court’s jurisdiction.

The Los Angeles Superior Court determined that West had effectively consented to its authority by submitting a 147-page filing that addressed the "substance of the issues," according to the application.

West’s lawyers said most of those pages were exhibits supporting her jurisdictional challenge and that she had repeatedly refused to argue the underlying case.

"Any reasonable view of consent would recognize that ‘no’ does not mean ‘yes,’" they wrote.

West also claims she was never properly served. Her filing says a FedEx package containing the court papers was delivered to her babysitter, who allegedly was not told what was inside.

The California court declared Gilkar and Ahmed the baby’s legal parents June 22, and West failed to persuade three state courts to put the ruling on hold.

SURROGATE GIVES BIRTH IN TEXAS TO BABY WITH HEART DEFECT AFTER PARENTS REQUESTED ABORTION

The judge acknowledged during the California proceedings that the dispute "[m]ay be a question of life and death" for the unborn child, according to West’s application.

The fight then moved to Texas, where West traveled so the baby could be delivered at a hospital equipped to treat his condition.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton secured an emergency order before the birth directing the hospital to provide life-saving care and preventing the child from being removed from the state.

West previously said she had only about one minute with the newborn while his umbilical cord was still attached before he was taken from her. A court order later barred her from seeing or holding him.

The baby underwent the first of three anticipated open-heart surgeries Aug. 17. He was later returned to a breathing tube after his condition declined, according to court filings previously reviewed by Fox News Digital.

Gilkar said during a hearing last month in Dallas that the couple had remained at their son’s bedside and accused West of trying to take him.

"He’s our child," Gilkar said, according to The Associated Press. "He’s the love of our lives."

She also told the court the newborn was "suffering a lot" as he struggled to breathe, choked on tubes and required a blood transfusion following surgery, according to the AP.

West has said she would abandon her custody effort if a court determined the intended parents were committed to providing the child with life-saving care.

But on Sept. 2, a Texas judge upheld the California ruling and removed West from the case. Paxton has also stepped away from the legal fight.

HHS WARNS TEXAS HOSPITALS AGAINST DENYING LIFE-SAVING CARE TO NEWBORN WITH DISABILITY

West’s attorneys argue she is now barred from receiving information about the baby or defending the order requiring his continued treatment. They allege Gilkar and Ahmed are challenging that medical-care order.

The couple previously agreed to the baby’s first surgery and said they would approve life-saving care if doctors determined he was a candidate.

West is now asking the Supreme Court to temporarily block the California ruling, which could give her a path back into the Texas case. Her attorneys argue the dispute raises a broader constitutional question over whether challenging a court’s authority can itself be treated as accepting that authority.

Her lawyers stressed that temporarily blocking the ruling would not decide who the baby’s legal parents are or direct doctors to provide a particular course of treatment. Instead, it could allow West to ask the Texas court to bring her back into the case.

Without Supreme Court intervention, her attorneys warned, West will remain shut out of decisions and updates about the baby’s condition as the appeals process plays out.

"Unless this Court provides relief from that judgment, M.W. will have no access to information about Baby G.’s condition," West’s attorneys wrote.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

They argued that a victory later could come too late to protect the child.

"Relief later in Texas proceedings may only restore her right to protect a child that has already passed," the filing states.

Fox News’ Shannon Bream and Bill Mears contributed to this report.

World.title: Potential Dem presidential contender crashes GOP convention, tries to snatch spotlight from Trump
World.content:

DALLAS - Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois is urging voters to ignore the Republicans' first-ever midterm convention.

"Voters can see through the BS that Republicans are spewing," Pritzker told reporters at a Democratic National Committee-hosted counter programming news conference across the street from the American Airlines Center in Dallas, the site of this week’s first-ever Republican midterm convention.

With less than two months until the midterm elections — and early voting just weeks away — President Donald Trump and the GOP kicked off their convention on Wednesday as Republicans fight to keep control of Congress.

The GOP's playbook for the convention, which comes as Republicans face energized Democrats and political headwinds as they defend their slim House and Senate majorities, is to motivate the party's base and boost turnout in key races that will determine control of Congress.

GOP MIDTERM CONVENTION: CAN THE 'BEST SHOWMAN IN POLITICS' DELIVER AGAIN?

"We are putting the president on the ballot," Republican National Committee (RNC) Chair Joe Gruters emphasized in a Fox News Digital interview on the eve of the gathering. "That's exactly what we're doing with this midterm convention."

But Pritzker, a potential 2028 White House contender, blasted the two-day GOP confab.

"This bizarre Republican midterm convention here can't paper over the fact that Republicans have done nothing to earn your vote. Donald Trump is hoping that a flashy primetime event will make you forget that, well, his trade war is killing costs for families at the grocery store. His war in Iran is killing ranchers and farmers and their way of life, and his war on people, on the working people, the working families of this country are raising the costs of health care and housing."

FIRST ON FOX: WHO'S SPEAKING - AND WHEN - AT THE GOP'S HISTORIC MIDTERM ELECTION

The governor also charged that Republicans are trying to "rig" the midterm elections, arguing that Trump is aiming to use the U.S. Postal Service to restrict mail-in balloting across the country.

"Republicans know that they can't win on the merits of their unpopular policies. So, they're working to rig the 2026 election," Pritzker charged.

Pritzker also warned that "if Democrats don’t win, if they don’t win in this election, we may not have other elections, or certainly we’re going to have future elections, every single one of which will be rigged."

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

The White House has defended Trump's executive order on mail-in voting as a "commonsense measure" aimed at ensuring secure elections.

Pritzker, who is running for re-election this year for a third term steering Democrat-dominated Illinois, is seen as a possible presidential contender in the 2028 White House race to succeed Trump.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

But the governor pivoted when asked by Fox News if his stop in Dallas should be seen as a 2028 signal.

Standing alongside some top Texas Democrats, Pritzker said, "I care a great deal about what happens in Texas. Voters everywhere in the country should care about what happens in Texas. So, I'm pleased to be here for that reason. If I can advance the cause, that's why I should stand here."

World.title: Manhattan prostitute pleads guilty to killing 3 men with fentanyl-laced drugs in robbery scheme
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

headlines

A Manhattan prostitute who killed three johns when she fed them fentanyl-laced drugs to rob them pleaded guilty Tuesday.

Tabitha Bundrick, 39, admitted to giving her customers the powerful synthetic opioid between April 2023 and February 2024 and then taking their personal belongings—including their cell phones, sneakers, money, and watches, the Manhattan District Attorney's Office said.

"The defendant knowingly killed three people by providing them fentanyl-laced drugs," said District Attorney Alvin Bragg. "As they lay unconscious, she robbed her victims and left them to die. In several instances, the victims’ bodies were found by their friends or family members."

FENTANYL DEATHS COULD NOW COST DRUG DEALERS THEIR LIVES UNDER NEW GOP PROPOSAL

Bundrick showed a "shocking indifference" to the lives of her victims, Bragg said.

She is expected to be sentenced to 27 years to life for three counts of second-degree murder and one count of second-degree assault.

Bundrick's crimes began on April 30, 2023, when she met Mario Paullan, 42, and his friend on the street and offered to sell them soap. She then offered to have sex with them for money and took them to an apartment she broke into, prosecutors said.

NEW YORK BODEGA WORKER KILLED LESS THAN A YEAR AFTER EXPRESSING FEAR TO REPORTER OVER VIOLENCE

After taking the fentanyl-laced drugs she gave them, Paullan's friend woke up to find him dead the next morning and their belongings missing, authorities said.

Months later, she met Miguel Navez, 39, and gave him drugs at his apartment. He was found three days later by his brother, with his belongings also stolen.

The third incident occurred on Feb. 25, 2024, when Abrihan Fernandez, 34, died in his apartment. Bundrick was caught entering and exiting the Upper Manhattan apartment several times with large bags.

She is scheduled to be sentenced on Oct. 6.

World.title: Gavin Newsom expresses 'openness' to packing SCOTUS, calls Electoral College system 'perverted'
World.content:

California Gov. Gavin Newsom expressed "openness" to reforming the Supreme Court and claimed the Electoral College "perverted" politics during an interview with former CNN host Don Lemon on his podcast Tuesday.

Near the end of the interview, Lemon directly asked Newsom, a rumored 2028 candidate, whether he believed the judicial branch needed to be expanded, an idea pushed by several Democratic figures, including former Vice President Kamala Harris.

"My initial instinct — me, a year ago, I would have said no out of concern that it will continue to be expanded," Newsom said. "And I was making a case for the ethical reforms and term limits, 18 years, which I was making a case a year ago. I'm more open to it on the basis of those district court arguments, which are not terrible arguments."

DEMOCRATIC SENATOR CLAIMS GOP 'STOLE' TWO SCOTUS SEATS IN 2016, 2020, CALLS FOR EXPANSION

"Is that a yes?" Lemon asked.

"I'm finding myself evolving on it. I normally have very clear conviction on things. I've been open to argument and interested in the evidence on this," Newsom answered.

He described his position as "caution on expanding it, but openness," adding that he believes reforms like term limits are a "no-brainer."

HARRIS LABELED 'INSTITUTIONAL ARSONIST' FOR PLAN TO FUNDAMENTALLY TRANSFORM SCOTUS AND ELECTORAL COLLEGE

The California Democrat had harsher criticism of the Electoral College, suggesting that it has "perverted" U.S. politics.

"California has already been a leader that's already gone out front saying it's time to change that system. Which state's more burdened by it than my state? We're the size of 21 state populations combined. Come on. And we have two representatives in the Senate? Come on. And the way that thing favors...it's perverted, I think, our politics. The Constitution is a living document, and it was conceived to be amended, and I think it's time to make that amendment," Newsom said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for comment.

CARVILLE TELLS DEMS TO QUIETLY PREPARE POWER GRAB WITH DC, PUERTO RICO STATEHOOD AND SUPREME COURT PACKING

Though Newsom has not explicitly supported expanding the Supreme Court, he made similar comments suggesting an openness to it during an interview with Brian Tyler Cohen on his podcast in June. Cohen was arguing in favor of court expansion, and Newsom remarked that Cohen was "getting me closer to your point of view."

During an interview with "PBS NewsHour" on Monday, Newsom also said that the Democratic Party is "pretty aligned" with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) on issues like universal healthcare, climate change and moving off fossil fuels. The DSA's goals include eliminating the Supreme Court and replacing it with a judiciary that would be selected by Congress.

House Democrats recently voted against a constitutional amendment to cap the number of justices on the Supreme Court off at nine. Rep. Andy Biggs, R-Ariz., who introduced the measure, warned Congress about the downsides of expanding the court.

World.title: Beauty school moms caught in accreditation crossfire as Trump administration weighs consequential decision
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Trump administration is weighing the future of an accreditor overseeing roughly 1,300 beauty and cosmetology schools and more than 120,000 students, in a decision that could test how the president’s push to overhaul higher education accreditation is applied beyond the diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) battles that have dominated the issue.

President Donald Trump promised during the 2024 campaign to "fire the radical left accreditors" and called accreditation his "secret weapon" against colleges and universities he argued had been captured by the political left.

But the case now before the U.S. Department of Education (DoE) is different.

Rather than allegations involving DEI requirements, it centers on whether the National Accrediting Commission of Career Arts and Sciences, or NACCAS, has complied with federal requirements and what consequences should follow if it has not.

MCMAHON TELLS HOUSE PANEL TRUMP ADMIN MOVING TO DISMANTLE ‘FAILED’ $3T EDUCATION BUREAUCRACY

That distinction matters to students because recognition by a DoE-approved accreditor is generally necessary for schools to participate in federal student aid programs. NACCAS says it accredits approximately 1,300 institutions serving more than 120,000 students in cosmetology, beauty and related career programs.

DoE staff identified deficiencies with NACCAS but recommended continuing its federal recognition with restrictions, additional reporting and monitoring while it works to come into compliance.

The National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity, or NACIQI, took a harder line at its July meeting, voting 9-3 to recommend that the department deny NACCAS renewed recognition.

TRUMP ADMIN TIGHTENS VISE ON STUDENT AID FRAUD IN ‘GHOST STUDENT’ CRACKDOWN

The DoE has not made a final decision.

The Department of Education told Fox News Digital that accreditor recognition is reviewed every five years through a three-step process: DoE staff make a recommendation; the independent bipartisan NACIQI makes its own recommendation; a senior department official makes the final judgment based on both.

"We will not comment on details as the process is ongoing," the DoE said.

For some students, the federal process has raised concerns about a source of funding they say they could not have attended beauty school without.

TRUMP ADMIN URGES RETURNING EDUCATION TO STATES, CITING $3 TRILLION OF TAXES SPENT AND POOR PROFICIENCY SCORES

Aliyah Fernandez, a recent Hollywood Institute cosmetology graduate and mother who now works as an assistant in a salon, said federal aid made her education possible.

"I could not have afforded beauty school without federal financial aid," Fernandez told Fox News Digital. "It was because of that, that I could attend at all."

Fernandez said she chose cosmetology in part because she wanted a career that would allow her to earn a living while remaining present in her daughter's life.

"I knew that if I worked full-time 9 to 5, I wouldn't barely have any time to see her grow up," Fernandez said. "I really just wanted to be there for her."

"I wanted an opportunity to financially support her and be present in her life at the same time," she added. "I wanted to have both."

I’M A UNIVERSITY PRESIDENT. TRUMP IS RIGHT TO MAKE COLLEGES DELIVER FOR STUDENTS

Blythe Fields, an expectant mother who is studying cosmetology while working in salons, said she previously paid for esthetician school herself and spent roughly two years saving her tips to continue her education.

"I paid out of pocket for esthetician school, and it made me go broke," Fields told Fox News Digital.

Fields said she now works during the day and attends school at night, describing her schedule as "literally 12-hour days."

She said federal financial aid allowed her to continue her education and that the flexibility of cosmetology will become even more important when her baby arrives.

"The first year is so important, and I need to be able to have that flexibility to raise a child," she said.

Fernandez and Fields both said they helped start a petition asking the DoE not to adopt NACIQI's recommendation outright. The petition calls instead for a monitored improvement period that would allow NACCAS to address the government's findings while maintaining recognition.

Fernandez said she understood why federal officials raised concerns about NACCAS but believed denying recognition would go too far.

FOX NEWS POLL: FAITH IN HIGHER EDUCATION IN THE US IS COLLAPSING

"Having done the research myself, I can completely understand, you know, the side of the board," Fernandez said. "However, I do not think a full termination of accreditation is reasonable considering how many people rely on this."

Fields was more pointed when asked what she would tell Trump before his administration makes the final decision.

"I would ask him who cuts and colors his hair and how did they get there?" Fields said.

The disagreement over NACCAS centers on whether the deficiencies identified during its federal review warrant continued oversight or denial of recognition.

Education Department staff recommended that NACCAS be prohibited from accrediting additional institutions until it demonstrates compliance, complete corrective action within 12 months and submit additional reports to the department.

NACIQI instead recommended denial.

Zakiya Smith Ellis, a former Obama administration DoE official who serves on the advisory committee, made the motion to deny NACCAS renewed recognition.

Michael Poliakoff seconded the motion, which passed 9-3.

Smith Ellis argued during the July meeting that NACCAS had been given opportunities to address compliance problems and questioned whether giving it additional time would be sufficient. She also raised concerns about debt and earnings among students at NACCAS-accredited institutions.

Three committee members voted against denial, including Robert Eitel, who served in the DoE during Trump's first term.

Eitel argued that NACCAS should be required to correct its deficiencies rather than lose recognition and raised concerns about the potential consequences for the schools and students it oversees.

The proceeding also creates an unusual contrast with the accreditation practices Trump highlighted in his April executive order.

The order directed the DoE to investigate whether accreditors require schools to engage in unlawful discrimination, including through DEI-related standards. The federal findings at issue in the NACCAS proceeding concern compliance and oversight rather than an allegation that NACCAS imposes DEI requirements.

Smith Ellis, meanwhile, has publicly defended DEI policies and previously served as a senior DoE official during the Obama administration.

Fox News Digital asked Smith Ellis why she favored denying recognition rather than the corrective measures recommended by DoE staff and what she would say to students concerned about the potential consequences. Smith Ellis did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Fields told Fox News Digital she believes beauty careers can be overlooked in ways that other skilled trades are not. Asked whether she thought the same fight would be playing out around traditionally male-dominated trades such as plumbing or welding, she said she did not.

"I think it's because they're like male fields, like mainly men are involved in," Fields said. "They don't think about that. They just think, ‘Oh, they went to hair school. It's easy.’"

For Fields, however, the training will give her the career she hopes will allow her to earn a living while raising her child.



The White House, NACCAS, and the Hollywood Institute of Beauty did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

More than 1.7 million free eggs have already been delivered to Texas food banks, with another 5.3 million slated to arrive in the coming weeks as part of an antitrust settlement with three major egg producers, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton announced Tuesday.

The Houston Food Bank is expected to receive the largest allocation with 1,544,400 eggs, followed by the North Texas Food Bank in Plano and the Tarrant Area Food Bank in Fort Worth, which will each receive 842,400 eggs. Other participating food banks are located across the state, including Austin, San Antonio, Tyler, Corpus Christi, El Paso, Laredo, Odessa, Pharr, Beaumont, Amarillo, Lubbock, Victoria, Abilene and Wichita Falls.

World.title: Stephen A Smith blasts SEC for threats to kick LSU out of the conference: 'Sit your a-- down'
World.content:
The 2026 college football season is off to a surprisingly controversial start. Out of nowhere, the Western Michigan-Michigan game became one of the most contentious finishes in recent memory, with replay review adding an additional second to the fourth quarter after the game had seemingly ended.

That sparked a formal appeal from the MAC to the FBS Oversight Committee and the College Football Playoff to recognize the Broncos as the official winners, due to improper replay review procedures.

Then there’s the human element: new LSU head coach Lane Kiffin. Kiffin drew criticism for his lengthy, drawn-out decision-making process after LSU offered him the job in Baton Rouge. His eventual decision to leave Ole Miss before the College Football Playoff made him public enemy No. 1 in Oxford. Somehow, the questions surrounding Kiffin have only deepened over time.

LSU’S LANE KIFFIN FIRES BACK AT NFL RETURNEE BACKLASH: BLAME THE NCAA, NOT US FOR RECRUITING PRO ATHLETES

Kiffin set about reshaping the Tigers' program through the transfer portal, then apparently had an even more unique and extreme idea: bring players who had signed with NFL teams but failed to make the regular season roster back to college football. Obviously designed to give LSU an advantage by adding more physically advanced and developed players, that tactic was immediately disparaged by opposing coaches, NFL coaches and, more importantly, the SEC itself.

A war of words and policies ensued with multiple conferences, including the SEC, immediately passing a policy to prevent "pro" players returning to the collegiate ranks. LSU fought back, even winning an injunction to allow two players, Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris, to confirm their eligibility.

That led to some extreme measures being discussed, including reports this week that the SEC was prepared to vote imminently to expel LSU from the conference entirely. As shocking and extreme as that sounds, it's clear that the SEC wanted to ensure that their commitment to "amateur" athletics remained unblemished.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Some supported the potential vote as a punishment for Kiffin and the Tigers program pushing the limits of eligibility. And further SEC filings implied that the athletic director had little control of the football team, with Kiffin alone running the ship.

But Stephen A. Smith, apparently, strongly disagrees, saying that just signing a contract in the NFL does not make you an "NFL player."

"Just because you enter a draft — if you haven’t signed a contract with the NFL team, you are not an NFL player," he said during a recent episode of "First Take" on ESPN. "If you haven’t been on a practice field, if you haven’t competed against NFL players, you are not an NFL player. You should be able to go back to college. That’s the one thing that I do feel."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Smith wasn't done there, saying that LSU being pushed into independence may actually help the program.

"And oh, by the way, Notre Dame, and we got love for Notre Dame, they’re an independent," he added. "LSU, you wanna throw them out the SEC? Go ahead and do it. Watch, they ain’t gonna lose. They’ll be just fine…Could you imagine Lane Kiffin as an independent? Out there in the open market for the LSU brand? Please, they’ll get paid…The SEC, sit your a-- down! Sit your a-- down!"

The Tigers seemingly backed down from their plan this week, signaling by adding two other players to their roster that they wouldn't bring in those former "NFL" players. But Smith seems to have a different perspective on this than most fans or rival administrators and coaches. Once you leave college and sign with an NFL team, that's it. You're done. That's how it's always been, and changing it now opens up a can of worms.

Would a player who’s, say, only made the practice squad be considered an "NFL player" in Smith’s view? Or would they still be eligible to return? What about another who is on an active roster, but never enters a game? Or someone who plays just one game before getting hurt? Defining who and who isn't a professional becomes a game of Whac-A-Mole that shouldn't be necessary.

Stephen A., though, clearly doesn't see it that way. He's wrong.

World.title: Apple announces long-awaited foldable phone, iPhone Duo
World.content:
Apple on Wednesday unveiled its first foldable phone, called the iPhone Duo, a device that opens like a book into a wide screen. The announcement marks the biggest change to the iPhone since it was introduced in 2007, and an entry into a category that Samsung has dominated for years.

In its announcement, made by Apple’s new CEO John Ternus at the company’s Cupertino, California, headquarters, Apple emphasized that it took time to develop the idea after rivals embraced it years ago.

Apple CEO John Ternus speaks during the keynote address at Apple’s “Surprise and Shine” event in Cupertino, Calif., on Wednesday. Benjamin Fanjoy / Getty Images

“Others have created foldables that just feel like two phones awkwardly stuck together,” Ternus said in the livestreamed event. He described the Duo as having “a larger display that feels as natural and intuitive as iPad.”

Ternus said it was the “largest display ever on an iPhone, while still fitting easily in your pocket.”

Apple said the device would sell for a base price of $1,999. Preorders would start Oct. 16, and the device will be available at stores on Oct. 23, the company said.

Once opened, the double-wide screen is 50% larger than the size of the iPhone Pro Max and measures 7.6 inches on the diagonal, said Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice president for worldwide marketing. He said the device is made of titanium, has speakers on the top and the bottom, and initially will come in two colors: “star white” and “night sky.”

World.title: Missouri redistricting fight heads back to Supreme Court
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The no-holds-barred redistricting fight in Missouri has returned to the U.S. Supreme Court for the second time, with opponents of a new GOP-drawn congressional map urgently asking the justices to prevent it from being used in the midterm elections.

At issue is how to resolve two competing rulings, with the Missouri Supreme Court finding last week that the new map could not be used based on state law while a voter referendum that could veto it moves forward. The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to block the state court ruling.

But in a separate case, a federal court on Tuesday ruled that the new map must be used in order to prevent violations of the U.S. Constitution, raising questions that were not put to the U.S. Supreme Court in the state case.

The Missouri Supreme Court has also opened a contempt probe into Secretary of State Denny Hoskins. A hearing is set for Thursday morning.

All of this is playing out after Tuesday’s deadline to finalize Missouri ballots ahead of this fall’s elections. First ballots are set to go out in the state on Sept. 19.

In the new U.S. Supreme Court filing, brought by a group called People Not Politicians, led by activist Richard von Glahn, lawyers said the federal judge’s ruling is in “direct conflict” with the state Supreme Court.

Hoskins has made it clear that “election officials will continue to implement a congressional map that Missouri’s highest court has held is not and never has been law,” they wrote.

Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark ruled on Tuesday that the state must use the map that people voted in during the primary.

The St. Louis-based 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals declined to put that ruling on hold.

Separately, the Missouri Supreme Court issued an order asking Hoskins, a Republican, to explain “why he should not be held in contempt” for violating the ruling last week that said the state cannot use the new map. Despite the ruling, Hoskins has continued to push to use the new map.

The court also ordered Hoskins to appear in person at Thursday’s hearing.

Hoskins indicated in a post on X that he would not back down.

“I look forward to my day in court,” he said.

A congressional map Missouri Republicans enacted in 2025, part of a nationwide redistricting push led by President Donald Trump, sought to eliminate one of the state’s two Democratic-held seats, currently held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.

Should the Missouri Supreme Court’s ruling remain in effect, a map drawn in 2022, with six Republican-held seats and two Democratic-held seats, would be in place for the general election.

The legal fight was kick-started when von Glahn’s group gathered signatures in support of a state referendum that would undo the GOP-drawn map and put it on hold for the 2026 election.

But Hoskins refused to put the measure on the ballot, arguing that redistricting plans are not subject to voters’ approval. The Missouri Supreme Court, which has a majority of Republican appointees, disagreed, saying there was nothing in state law that exempted congressional maps passed by the Legislature from being vetoed by voters via the referendum process.

World.title: Bessent’s move to tamp down rising rates backfires, as bond yields jump and stocks tumble
World.content:
Bonds sharply sold off and stocks tumbled Wednesday after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s latest effort to tamp down what he called market “fever” backfired.

At 11 a.m. ET, the Treasury Department announced that it would repurchase $6 billion worth of 10- to 20-year government bonds, in the hopes that fewer bonds on the market would drive up demand, pushing down rates, or yields, that have soared to levels not seen in decades.

But that’s not what happened. Instead, most Treasury yields sharply jumped on the announcement. The 10-year bond yield surged to as high as 4.85%, its highest level since November 2023. The 20- and 30-year bond yields surged to as high as 5.3%. When Treasuries fall, their yields rise.

By 4p.m. ET, bond yields had pulled back slightly from the highest levels of the day but remained sharply elevated.

The Nasdaq Composite, which is sensitive to interest rates given the high number of major tech companies it tracks, ended the day down 0.6%. The S&P 500 tumbled 0.5%.

The reaction from Wall Street underscores the limits of the power Bessent claims to exert over markets. It also comes as the Trump administration is running out of tools to gain leverage over major parts of the U.S. economy, from gas prices and bond yields to retaliatory tariffs.

Yields have been rising steadily since the start of the year. But they began to surge in late July, when President Donald Trump’s newly-installed Federal Reserve chairman, Kevin Warsh, held a press conference at which he didn’t sound fully committed to using the Fed’s tools to help curb inflation.

That spooked bond markets, which saw inflation climbing as the Iran war dragged on and Trump’s trade policies raised the prices of many imported goods.

World.title: Hurricane Lowell leaves trail of destruction across Kauai
World.content:
POIPU, Hawaii — On Kauai’s south shore, Hurricane Lowell lifted a home off its foundation and split it in two, the storm’s powerful winds thrusting part of the structure across the street.

At a nearby Sheraton hotel, the hurricane carried several cars across the parking lot and destroyed the hotel’s oceanfront restaurant. Its pool sits full of sand.

These are just two of the many scenes of destruction the hurricane has left in Hawaii after lashing the state’s western islands with heavy rain, widespread flooding and tropical-storm-force winds on Monday and Tuesday.

Now the extensive recovery efforts begin.

World.title: ‘Trumpapalooza’ and another primary night: From the Politics Desk
World.content:
Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, we dig into the GOP’s midterm convention and the next round of primaries in Rhode Island. Plus, Andrea Mitchell writes that the aftermath of 9/11 is still being felt 25 years later.

— Adam Wollner

Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here.

‘Trumpapalooza’ and another primary night

It’s a big night on the sports calendar, with the NFL season kicking off and more action at the U.S. Open.

But it’s also a big night on the political calendar, with Republicans meeting for a midterm convention in Dallas, and Rhode Island holding its primary (yes, on a Wednesday, to accommodate the late Labor Day holiday this year).

🎉 ‘Trumpapalooza’: Republicans are kicking off a two-day gathering today designed to boost enthusiasm for the party in the final stretch of the midterm campaign. In addition to hearing from the party’s candidates on the ballot across the country this fall, President Donald Trump is set to speak at 9 p.m. ET tonight, while Vice President JD Vance will address convention-goers tomorrow.

As Sahil Kapur reported, congressional Republicans have been split on whether to attend. On the one hand, speaking at a gathering headlined by Trump could help them turn out his MAGA base in key races. On the other, being tied to an unpopular president amid widespread discontent over the state of the economy and the Iran war could repel swing voters.

The latest NBC News Decision Desk poll found that Trump’s job approval rating sits at 80% among Republicans, but 24% among independents.

According to an NBC News tally, 32 House Republicans have said they will be at the convention, while 35 said they will not.

“We’ve been working really, really hard here, and it just doesn’t get out. So I’m going down there because this is a fantastic platform to tell people what we’ve been doing,” GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden, who represents a battleground district in Wisconsin, said in an interview. “We have been accomplishing things, and it’s just so under the radar, unfortunately.”

🦀 Rhode Island primary: On the Democratic side, Gov. Dan McKee is at risk of becoming the first sitting governor to lose a primary in eight years, Adam Edelman notes.

McKee is facing a challenge from former CVS executive Helena Foulkes, who has outspent him on the airwaves 3-to-1, according to AdImpact. Foulkes also narrowly lost the 2022 primary to McKee, who replaced Gina Raimondo in 2021 when she was selected by President Joe Biden to be commerce secretary.

While there has been a wave of anti-incumbent energy in Democratic primaries throughout the year, Rhode Island’s contest hasn’t broken along generational or ideological lines. Rather, the race between Foulkes, 62, and McKee, 75, has been defined by hyperlocal issues — most notably the closure of a major bridge in Providence in 2023.

The last sitting governor to lose a primary was Republican Jeff Colyer in Kansas in 2018. He was defeated by then-Secretary of State Kris Kobach, who was backed by Trump.

🎥 Tune in to the Kornacki Cam at 7:45 p.m. ET to watch Steve break down tonight’s results.

🗳️ New Hampshire recap: As for last night, Republican former Sen. John Sununu and Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas won their Senate primaries, setting up a battleground state race, Bridget Bowman writes.

A lingering lesson, 25 years after 9/11

Analysis by Andrea Mitchell

Those of us who covered the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks 25 years ago had reported early warnings, although there was no immediate proof.

The Environmental Protection Agency, then led by former New Jersey Gov. Christine Todd Whitman, issued the first official “all clear” about the air quality and safety of drinking water a week later, on Sept. 18. The air from the collapse of the twin towers for the first responders working in the still smoldering pit was safe, tests showed. There were reassuring pronouncements from the city’s mayor, Rudy Giuliani, and his immediate successor, Michael Bloomberg.

On Sept. 21, Whitman said that the “EPA has been very aggressive in monitoring for potential environmental problems in the aftermath of the World Trade Center attack. … New Yorkers and New Jerseyans need not be concerned about environmental issues as they return to their homes and workplaces.” She continued: “More recently, we’ve also tested drinking water supplies and found no sign of asbestos bacterial contamination, PCBs or pesticides.”

Were government officials at the local and federal level — from both political parties — misled by the experts? Or, perhaps, overly eager to reassure the public and Wall Street? Partisans on all sides still disagree. Anecdotally, residents, health officials and first responders were reporting discomfort and more serious respiratory concerns from visible dust and larger debris during the aftermath.

More definitively, the 9/11 Commission reported in 2004 that the EPA “did not have sufficient data and analysis to make such a blanket statement” one week after 9/11. Congress still resisted appeals for survivors’ benefits, even as firefighters and other first responders began succumbing to lung ailments.

On NBC News on Feb. 25, 2019, former first responder and advocate John Feal, a demolition supervisor at ground zero, told me: “Everybody knows these cancers and these respiratory illnesses have different latency periods. I mean, come on, I mean, it’s just insulting. We’re sick and dying, but we’re not stupid.” By then, he had already attended 181 funerals of fellow responders.

It took years after the attacks for Feal and his high-profile fellow advocate, Jon Stewart, to persuade Congress to approve health benefits for surviving first responders and their families, and years more to extend those family benefits until 2090.

“As I sit here today, I can’t help but think what an incredible metaphor this room is for the entire process that getting healthcare and benefits for 9/11 first responders has come to,” Stewart said in June 2019 during congressional testimony. “Behind me a filled room of 9/11 first responders and in front of me a nearly empty Congress.”

“Sick and dying, they brought themselves down here to speak to no one,” he continued. “Shameful. It’s an embarrassment to the country and a stain on this institution and you should be ashamed of yourselves, for those who aren’t here, but you won’t be because accountability doesn’t appear to be something that occurs in this chamber.”

And now, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has released 170,000 pages of documents providing substantial evidence of the environmental fallout from ground zero, including asbestos found in air samples half a mile from the twin towers 10 months after the buildings collapsed.

It perhaps serves as a cautionary tale for public policymakers who have long focused on the counterterrorism lessons of 9/11, but not the impact on first responders and others living in the shadow of the twin towers.

Owen Hayes contributed.

World.title: Trump admin fires prosecutor in dropped case against politically linked billionaire
World.content:
WASHINGTON — A federal prosecutor who had been assigned to the now-defunct case against a politically linked Indian billionaire has been fired by the Trump administration, two people familiar with the firing tell NBC News.

The prosecutor, who had been with the Justice Department’s Fraud Section in Washington, was one of two who previously asked to withdraw from the Gautam Adani case two days after Principal Associate Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter moved in May to dismiss the case against Adani.

Adani was charged in November 2024 in connection with an alleged scheme to defraud U.S. investors and pay off Indian government officials to win a bid to develop the country’s largest solar power plant. He called the accusations baseless.

Adani pledged to invest billions of dollars in the U.S., and Democratic lawmakers raised questions of a quid pro quo with the Trump administration to avoid prosecution. The federal judge hearing the case ordered Adani to explain whether any deal was made in connection with the government’s significant reversal. He denied it, and so did the Justice Department.

U.S. District Judge Nicholas Garaufis of the Eastern District of New York eventually agreed to toss the case against Adani, though he blasted the Trump administration’s “highly unusual” conduct.

The prosecutor’s firing came a month later, the people said. The Trump administration has fired numerous federal employees without explanation, beyond citing Trump’s executive powers in letters, which Justice Department alumni have come to refer to as “Article II letters,” referring to a clause of the U.S. Constitution.

A spokesperson for the Eastern District of New York declined to comment. The prosecutor did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Last week, Garaufis let stand some counts against some of Adani’s co-defendants, saying the Trump administration had “not provided sufficient factual information to support the stated reasons” for dismissing the charges.

Gautam Adani, chairman of Adani Group, at the company's headquarters in Ahmedabad, India, in 2024. Sumit Dayal / Bloomberg via Getty Images file

Adani had pledged to invest billions of dollars in the United States but said in a sworn statement filed in July that he was “not aware of any agreement involving any person or entity exchanging anything for the dismissal of the indictment.”

An email from May from U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella referenced a slide deck presentation from Adani’s defense team that included a proposal to invest $10 billion in the United States, and Nocella wrote that the proposal was “categorically rejected” by the office.

The Justice Department has defended the decision to forgo its case against Adani, with McCotter saying the case was “indefensible” and that he “would have sought dismissal of the securities charges regardless of any mentions of investments, regardless of whether the civil case (or any other matter) was settled or otherwise resolved.”

An attorney for Adani couldn’t be reached for comment about the prosecutor’s firing.

World.title: Lindsay Clancy rejects conspiracy theories accusing her ex of their children’s deaths, lawyer says
World.content:
Lindsay Clancy rejects the internet conspiracy theories accusing her ex-husband of killing their three children in 2023 and believes he has been unfairly targeted by online sleuths since her murder trial, her defense attorney Kevin Reddington told NBC News on Wednesday in a wide-ranging interview.

“She knows, and it’s readily apparent that Patrick has been set upon and his life has been turned upside down into a nightmare that he doesn’t deserve. Period. Full stop,” attorney Kevin Reddington said Wednesday.

Patrick Clancy’s lawyers released a statement Tuesday responding to the online allegations and slamming the true-crime creators behind the theories. The statement called the theories and online storylines a “campaign of misinformation” that was “publishing what they know to be outright falsehoods that Patrick was somehow involved in the death of his young children and other vile claims.”

His lawyer added that “every appropriate measure will be pursued to hold them accountable, including legally,” and that “law enforcement has been notified.”

Reddington told NBC News that Clancy is aware of how the case has taken off on social media as online sleuths pushed conspiracy theories and broke down testimony about the broadcast trial and as conversation around postpartum psychosis captured the nation. She also disagrees with the theories.

On Friday, Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial at Plymouth Superior Court after the jury deliberating whether Clancy was criminally responsible for the strangulation deaths of her three children said it was deadlocked three times. Reddington sought a last-minute emergency stay to send the jurors back to deliberations, but a justice at Massachusetts’ Supreme Judicial Court swiftly denied it.

Since then, Clancy is “not very good” and remains “suicidal” after her high-profile murder trial, Reddington said.

“She’s strong. She has incredible family support,” he added of his client. “But she is suicidal. I mean, she’s on 24/7, one-on-one suicide watch. I worry about her every day.”

Despite the dramatic end to the trial that leaves Clancy’s legal case in limbo, Reddington says his client does not hold any anger toward prosecutors, jurors or even witnesses who testified against her.

“She was hurt by the way they would talk about her and the way they would attack her. She was hurt, but she never once expressed anger towards anybody in the system,” he said. “She doesn’t have it in her DNA to be angry with anyone.”

Instead, he added, she talks about her children and often repeats one phrase constantly: “I want my babies.”

The sentiment is a stark contrast to the prosecution’s case throughout the trial, which argued Clancy was aware of her actions and planned the killings ahead of time. Reddington argued that she was compelled to act on auditory hallucinations that told her to carry out the murders, a symptom of the postpartum psychosis he said she was experiencing.

Both parties admit she killed the children: Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months old.

“That was not the Lindsay that is now living amongst us,” Reddington said Wednesday. “The person that committed this atrocious act was as a result of postpartum psychosis combined with the medications that she was provided.”

Postpartum psychosis is a rare but serious condition that can affect new mothers. More severe than postpartum depression, it can cause hallucinations and other intense psychological symptoms.

To prove their argument that Clancy was not actually experiencing psychosis at the time of the killings, prosecutors repeatedly pointed to the fact that she never told anyone she was hearing voices before that night and that she hasn’t heard any since — something said to be exceedingly rare for someone experiencing psychosis.

Reddington, however, said Wednesday that Clancy told her struggles to “anyone who would listen,” including Patrick Clancy and her mother. He conceded Wednesday, though, that “she should have” told more people about the voices.

The lawyer also challenged the notion that Clancy lied about how she was feeling and that she repeated a list of symptoms to doctors that she found online.

“If she was so smart, and Googling things like psychosis, why would she not have had exactly the symptomology that you can Google about psychosis, about postpartum psychosis, [including] the voices?” he said. “What are you supposed to say? How are you supposed to say it?”

He added: “If she was faking, she would have hit it on every single cylinder. She was telling the truth. She did the best that she could. She was failed by these doctors.”

A lone holdout

After 38 hours of deliberations, the jury on Friday said it could not reach a unanimous decision, remaining deadlocked 11-1. Jurors had the option to convict Clancy of first-degree murder, second-degree murder or manslaughter or acquit her owing to lack of criminal responsibility.

Had she been found not guilty by reason of insanity, she would have been sentenced to time in a state mental health facility.

Three jurors, including the foreperson, told NBC Boston on Tuesday that the majority favored finding Clancy not guilty by lack of criminal responsibility, while one holdout wanted to convict. But that juror expressed reasonable doubt, they said, and still wouldn’t agree with the remainder of the jury.

Reddington, however, defended the juror’s right to his opinion Wednesday, saying it “doesn’t matter” what was going through his head.

“He’s got every right to do that, and I would defend that right, but not to refuse to apply the law,” Reddington said. “This is where you draw the line.”

Now, prosecutors must decide whether to retry Clancy. The next hearing in the case is scheduled for Sept. 29.

Despite telling reporters multiple times last week that he was ready to retry Clancy’s case as soon as this week, Reddington said that is not the outcome he wants and that he will file a motion to dismiss charges. He also said he would be open to plea iscussions, but would not take a deal that landed his client in jail for even a day.

Reddington on Tuesday called on President Donald Trump to offer his client a pardon, even though Clancy was tried on state charges and the president can only pardon federal charges.

He explained Wednesday that he made the suggestion because Trump “felt compelled to comment on the case” and thought that maybe Trump could reach out to colleagues in the Justice Department to influence Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz to drop the charges. Or, he theorized, Trump might even reach out to Cruz directly on the issue.

Despite such strong attention toward the case, Reddington said, he felt that there was some fundamental misunderstanding about Clancy’s situation.

“They feel that if you determine that Lindsay was and is not guilty of this crime because of lack of criminal responsibility, that in some fashion you are ignoring the loss of these three children,” he explained. “That is as far from the truth as possible.”

Reddington added that Clancy, who is in a wheelchair and has been on suicide watch since the night of the murders, is “living in hell.”

“I look back over the years, and the people that I’ve represented — been able to help, not so much help — but yes, this is the one that really has moved me,” Reddington said, agreeing it was one of the hardest of his career.

World.title: Federal judge backs Missouri's new House map after Supreme Court rebuffs case
World.content:
A federal judge ruled Tuesday that Missouri should use a new congressional map that favors Republicans for now, hours after the U.S. Supreme Court left in place a ruling from the state's highest court directing Missouri to use an older map.

The Supreme Court rebuffed an appeal from Missouri officials who wanted to use new congressional districts backed by President Trump in the November election, marking a defeat for Republicans who had hoped the new map could help them hold on to their slim House majority. The justices let stand a decision by Missouri's top court, which said the new districts cannot be used in the November elections because they were superseded by a citizen petition demanding a statewide vote.

But shortly after, U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark issued a temporary restraining order in a separate challenge to Missouri's Supreme Court decision, writing that the plaintiffs faced "irreparable harm" otherwise because "many Missouri voters would have to cast their general-election votes for candidates whom they had no role in nominating."

Clark's decision was appealed late Tuesday by People not Politicians, a Missouri group against the redistricting effort. On Wednesday, however, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit rejected the request for a temporary stay of Clark's ruling, writing that the appeals court either lacks "jurisdiction over the appeal or, based on the briefing we have so far, the stay factors have not been met."

Immediately following the 8th Circuit Court's ruling, People not Politicians appealed the case to the U.S. Supreme Court. Justice Brett Kavanaugh has requested a response from the plaintiffs in the lawsuit — the proponents of the new redistricting map — by Thursday morning.

Clark's decision has added further confusion about which boundaries will be used in November.

The new House maps, passed by the state legislature last year, would dramatically redraw longtime Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver's Kansas City-area district, making it GOP-leaning.

Missouri's new districts were used in the August primaries. But the Missouri Supreme Court ruled last week that the state must revert to districts adopted after the last census.

Republican state Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, who appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, had argued it would violate federal rights to switch districts for voters between the primary and general elections. She also said it would cause confusion.

"A federal-election-administration disaster is unfolding in Missouri," Hanaway wrote in an emergency application for the U.S. Supreme Court to put the ruling on hold, warning it could lead to "unprecedented chaos" and render the primary "utterly pointless."

She continued: "Looking forwards, the State is genuinely unsure whether it can switch its governing congressional map in time to run a timely federal election."

Richard Von Glahn, who sued over the new maps, urged the U.S. Supreme Court not to intervene, writing that the state "waited as long as possible to manufacture the present dispute over Missouri's congressional districting map" by not moving to reject the petition for a referendum until last month.

Hanaway's request for the U.S. Supreme Court to step in was rejected by Kavanaugh on Tuesday.

Missouri currently is represented in the House by six Republicans and two Democrats who were elected under districts that Republican state officials approved in 2022.

But at Mr. Trump's urging, Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe called the Legislature into a special session last year to redraw congressional boundaries to their advantage ahead of the midterms.

The revised map targeted the 5th Congressional District, held by Cleaver. It reassigned portions of Kansas City to two neighboring districts represented by Republicans and stretched the remainder of Cleaver's district far eastward into rural Republican areas.

Cleaver was unopposed in the Democratic primary. State Sen. Rick Brattin won the Republican primary in the reshaped district.

On the same day as the primary, Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins rejected a petition with thousands of signatures seeking to force a November referendum on the map. Hoskins asserted that Missouri's Constitution doesn't allow a referendum on congressional redistricting. A lower court agreed, but the state Supreme Court reversed Hoskins' decision.

The state's top court said the new districts were retroactively frozen in December, when the petition signatures were submitted, and thus never became law. Hoskins on Tuesday assigned the redistricting referendum as Proposition A on the November ballot, in compliance with the state court order.

The Missouri Constitution does not specifically say that a referendum can be used for congressional redistricting. But the state Supreme Court said a constitutional provision allowing a referendum on "any act" of the Legislature encompasses congressional redistricting legislation.

Missouri was the second Republican-led state, after Texas, to respond to Mr. Trump's call last year to redraw congressional districts. Several other states followed. All told, Republicans had hoped to win as many as 16 additional seats from new House maps enacted in eight states — Texas, Missouri, North Carolina, Ohio, Florida, Tennessee, Louisiana and Alabama.

Democrats, whose counterattack faced several setbacks, think they could win up to six additional seats from new districts in California and Utah.

It remains to be seen whether the redistricting works as intended for Republicans. The president's party historically has lost congressional seats in the midterms, and Mr. Trump's poor approval ratings could provide an extra hurdle for Republican candidates.
