Today’s Hispanic Heritage celebration continues that approach, placing the cultural history surrounding the sport alongside the tennis itself as the US Open moves into its championship week.

World.title: BDF soldier ordered out of marital home after domestic dispute; granted $2,000 bail
World.content:
BDF soldier ordered out of marital home after domestic dispute; granted $2,000 bail

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize Defence Force soldier has been ordered to stay away from the Newtown Barracks home he shared with his wife after being charged with harm and damage to property following an alleged domestic dispute.

Justin Lincoln Flowers, 32, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday, where he was arraigned on one count of harm and one count of damage to property stemming from an incident on Saturday, September 5.

Flowers initially pleaded guilty to the charges but changed his pleas to not guilty after the allegations were outlined in court.

According to the complaint, Flowers’ wife, a 35-year-old general manager of a local hotel, alleged that the dispute began after another woman approached her and claimed she had recently been intimate with Flowers.

The hotel manager told police that during the confrontation Flowers allegedly damaged her Samsung A23 cellphone, punched her in the nose, grabbed her by the throat and damaged several personal items. She further alleged that he threatened to kill her and repeatedly referenced his training and position as a BDF soldier.

Among the items allegedly damaged were a cellphone valued at $600, an Asus laptop valued at $4,500, a Black & Decker iron, a Fossil watch, clothing, a purse and other belongings.

Flowers was granted bail in the sum of $2,000 with strict conditions. He is prohibited from contacting the woman or any prosecution witnesses, directly or indirectly, and must relocate from the Newtown Barracks residence.

The Senior Magistrate also warned Flowers that he is not to return to the home alone. He may only collect his belongings while accompanied by police, and any breach of the condition could result in his bail being revoked.

Flowers indicated that he would stay with his grandmother in the meantime.

A BDF representative was also present during the court proceedings.

Flowers is scheduled to return to court on November 4, 2026.

World.title: Growing up with AI: What it could mean for young brains
World.content:
Growing up with AI: What it could mean for young brains

By Zoila Palma: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life, children and teenagers are turning to AI tools for schoolwork, entertainment, advice and even companionship.

The American Psychological Association (APA) says research into youth and AI remains in its early stages, but psychologists are already examining how excessive or inappropriate use could affect cognitive, social and emotional development.

More than half of U.S. adolescents report using AI chatbots to help with schoolwork, according to a 2026 Pew Research Center report.

While AI can improve productivity and provide educational support, psychologists warn that relying too heavily on the technology may prevent students from engaging deeply with challenging material and developing important skills independently.

Research involving nearly 1,000 high school mathematics students in Turkey found that students using ChatGPT improved their grades by 48%, but when the AI tool was removed, they performed 17% worse than students who had never used it.

Researchers say the findings highlight concerns about “cognitive offloading,” in which students rely on technology to reduce the mental effort needed to complete tasks, potentially weakening learning and long-term skill development.

Psychologists stress, however, that AI itself is not necessarily harmful and that how and why students use it matters. AI can support learning by acting as a brainstorming partner, providing feedback, creating practice problems or helping with nonessential tasks such as formatting. Research has also found that specially designed AI tutoring systems with educational guardrails can produce stronger learning outcomes while reducing some of the negative effects associated with unrestricted AI use.

Concerns extend beyond academics as young people increasingly turn to AI chatbots for companionship, entertainment and personal advice.

Surveys cited by the APA indicate that 72% of children have used social AI, with some reporting that they have discussed serious problems with AI rather than with another person.

Experts warn that AI relationships could potentially displace real-world interactions and limit opportunities for young people to develop empathy, communication, conflict-resolution and other social skills.

The APA says parents, educators and policymakers should focus on helping young people develop AI literacy and establish appropriate safeguards.

World.title: International News: Stronger El Niño raises alarm for Galápagos wildlife and forests
World.content:
International News: Stronger El Niño raises alarm for Galápagos wildlife and forests

By Zoila Palma: Scientists in Ecuador are raising concerns over the potential impact of a stronger-than-normal El Niño on the unique wildlife and ecosystems of the Galápagos Islands.

The Pacific climate phenomenon is expected to bring significantly warmer waters and intense rainfall, threatening species found nowhere else on Earth.

According to the latest projection from the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), sea temperatures in the region could reach about 2.2 degrees Celsius above normal, a level considered a very strong El Niño.

Scientists warn that the warmer waters could cause plankton, algae and smaller fish to decline, disrupting the food chain and placing marine species at serious risk.

Among the animals considered most vulnerable are Galápagos penguins, blue-footed boobies, petrels, flightless cormorants, albatrosses and sea lions, while coral colonies and tuna fisheries could also be affected.

Scientists say food shortages can cause animal colonies to stop reproducing, disperse in search of food and, in some cases, die from starvation. The vertebrate population of the archipelago could decline by at least 20% if the phenomenon reaches its projected intensity.

The Galápagos penguin is being closely monitored as an indicator of El Niño’s impact.

Following the powerful 1998 El Niño, the penguin population reportedly fell from about 1,300 to just 400. Scientists are also concerned about the islands’ remaining Scalesia forests and coastal Opuntia cacti, which could be overwhelmed by heavy rainfall and invasive plants.

Conservation groups, the Ecuadorian government and nongovernmental organizations are preparing measures to protect vulnerable ecosystems, including removing invasive species, collecting seeds and establishing nurseries for threatened plants.

World.title: Blackouts again? BEL announces possible load shedding tonight
World.content:
Blackouts again? BEL announces possible load shedding tonight

By Zoila Palma: Belize Electricity Limited (BEL) has warned customers across the country to prepare for possible power interruptions tonight, Wednesday, September 9, 2026, as the company works to maintain stability of the national power grid amid high demand and limited electricity supply.

Power interruptions may occur between 6:00 p.m. and 9:00 p.m. in several areas, including parts of the George Price Highway, Ladyville, San Ignacio, Dangriga, Independence and Belize City.

A second round of possible interruptions is scheduled between 9:00 p.m. and 11:59 p.m., affecting areas in Corozal, San Ignacio, Dangriga and Punta Gorda.

BEL said the tentative load-shedding schedule is based on projected energy demand and generation, but conditions can change quickly.

The company noted that the situation is being driven by high power demand and limited supply from local sources and Mexico’s CFE.

World.title: International News: Sheinbaum says Mexico will not sign deal that threatens Sovereignty
World.content:
International News: Sheinbaum says Mexico will not sign deal that threatens Sovereignty

By Zoila Palma: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has declared that Mexico will not sign any agreement with the United States that compromises the country’s sovereignty, as negotiations continue over the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA).

Sheinbaum said that the United States has opted to conduct separate negotiations with Mexico and Canada rather than hold trilateral discussions.

She explained that Mexico is conducting its own consultations with Washington and is not participating in negotiations between the United States and Canada, ua reports.

The talks include US tariffs on Mexican steel, aluminum and automobiles, with Mexico seeking improved conditions for its exports and opposing additional tariffs on key economic sectors.

Other issues under discussion could include intellectual property and the recognition by Mexico’s health regulator of certain US pharmaceutical patents.

Sheinbaum stressed that Mexico is willing to discuss trade and economic cooperation, provided its ability to make independent decisions is not restricted.

World.title: Police, Ministry of Health launch Road-safety drive in Corozal to combat drunk driving
World.content:
Police, Ministry of Health launch Road-safety drive in Corozal to combat drunk driving

By Zoila Palma: Community Policing personnel, together with the Regional Patrol Unit (RPU), Traffic Police Unit (TPU), National Drug Abuse Control Council (NDACC), and Ministry of Health, conducted an awareness campaign in Corozal Town today.

As part of the campaign, officers conducted a checkpoint and distributed approximately 500 informational flyers reminding motorists and members of the public about the dangers of drinking and driving.

Car fresheners were also distributed to citizens as part of the initiative.

World.title: PSU sounds alarm as GOB limits SmartStream access amid ‘Mira Millions’ audit
World.content:
PSU sounds alarm as GOB limits SmartStream access amid ‘Mira Millions’ audit

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Public Service Union of Belize (PSU) is demanding the immediate reversal of new restrictions which it says have dramatically reduced Finance Officers’ ability to view government transactions through the SmartStream financial management system.

In a strongly worded statement issued Wednesday, September 9, the PSU said Finance Officers can now view transactions only within the ministry where they are posted, while their previous ability to examine payments and transactions across other government ministries has been withdrawn.

The union says the timing is particularly troubling because the restriction comes amid the ongoing investigation into the so-called “Mira Millions” affair, which emerged after leaked SmartStream records revealed numerous government payments connected to relatives of Belmopan Area Representative Oscar Mira. The PSU argues that viewing transactions across ministries is precisely what allows Finance Officers to identify suspicious patterns that may not be apparent when transactions are examined individually.

Public reporting on the controversy has shown that many of the transactions under scrutiny were below the $10,000 threshold, above which additional Treasury scrutiny is required. Financial Secretary Joseph Waight previously explained that payments below that amount can be processed within individual ministries, while larger payments require further levels of approval.

The Auditor General’s investigation has since widened to examine procurement and financial controls within the Ministry of Defence, Belize Defence Force and Belize Coast Guard. Auditor General Maria Rodriguez said last week that the first report from the investigation is expected by the end of September.

The PSU acknowledged that some restrictions on access to sensitive information, including payroll and personnel records, may be legitimate, but argued that removing cross-ministry visibility from all Finance Officers without publicly explaining the legal basis for doing so goes far beyond normal information-security controls. The union described the move as “a curtain” rather than an internal control.

Among seven demands, the PSU is calling for the immediate restoration of government-wide read access, publication of the instruction authorizing the restriction, assurances that officers will not face disciplinary action for reporting irregularities, and confirmation that the Auditor General, Integrity Commission and Public Accounts Committee retain unrestricted SmartStream access.

The union also renewed its call for passage of the Protected Disclosures Bill, commonly referred to as whistleblower legislation. The bill was introduced in 2021 but remains unenacted five years later, despite renewed pressure from trade unions following the SmartStream revelations.

“Finance Officers do not work for ministers. They work for the people of Belize,” the PSU concluded, calling on the Government to restore the access.

World.title: $2,000 reward offered for information in Belize City murder
World.content:
$2,000 reward offered for information in Belize City murder

By Zoila Palma: Crime Stoppers Belize is offering a $2,000 reward for information leading to the arrest of the person or persons responsible for the murder of 33-year-old Belize City resident Barry Johnson.

The incident occurred at approximately 11:15 p.m. on Monday, September 7, 2026 in the Kings Park area of Belize City. At least two armed men reportedly exited a dark-colored SUV at the corner of F and 7th Streets and opened fire.

The shooting left one man injured and claimed the life of Johnson.

Police are investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident and are seeking information that could assist in identifying and apprehending those responsible.

Anyone with information about the shooting is urged to contact Crime Stoppers Belize at 922, submit information through the P3 Tips app, or report directly to the nearest police station.

World.title: Grand Marshals Buju, Kes join Mamdani for New York Caribbean Carnival Parade
World.content:
Trinidadian social artiste Kees Dieffenthaller (left) and dancehall icon Buju Banton (left) with Mayor of New York City Zohran Mamdani (centre) at the 59th Annual New York Caribbean Carnival Week and Parade.

NEW YORK, United States — Grammy Award-winning Reggae artiste Buju Banton proudly represented Jamaica as an Honorary Grand Marshal of the 59th Annual New York Caribbean Carnival Parade.

Held on Labour Day, September 7, along Brooklyn’s Eastern Parkway, the event saw Buju sharing the honour with Kees Dieffenthaller of ‘Kes The Band’, bringing together two of the Caribbean’s most influential musical voices.

Representing Jamaica’s reggae and dancehall traditions alongside Kes’ Trinidadian soca and Carnival roots, the artistes reflected the spirit of “One Caribbean” and the cultural connections that unite the region and its diaspora.

The day began with the West Indian American Day Carnival Association’s annual VIP Breakfast at the Carlos Lezama Netball Court in Lincoln Terrace Park, where Buju Banton and Dieffenthaller were formally recognised as Honorary Grand Marshals.

The gathering brought together elected officials, community leaders and cultural ambassadors, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, New York Governor Kathy Hochul, New York Attorney General Letitia James, United States (US) Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, US House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, New York City Public Advocate Jumaane Williams, New York City Comptroller Mark Levine, Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso, New York City Council Member Farah N Louis and Irvington, New Jersey Councilwoman Charnette Frederic.

Following the breakfast, Buju Banton took to Eastern Parkway alongside Dieffenthaller and Mamdani, greeting spectators as the parade moved through Brooklyn in a vibrant celebration of Caribbean music, heritage and identity. His presence drew an enthusiastic response from paradegoers, many of whom carried Jamaican flags and celebrated the opportunity to see one of reggae and dancehall’s most respected voices representing the island on the Parkway.

Throughout the procession, Buju Banton also made stops to join the PIX11 crew for live on-camera moments, sharing the energy of the parade and the significance of the occasion with television audiences across New York.

The appearance marked another major cultural moment for Jamaican music in New York and reflected Buju Banton’s enduring connection with Caribbean communities across the diaspora.

His appointment also recognised a career spent carrying the sound, messages and cultural identity of Jamaica to audiences around the world. The honour comes as Buju Banton continues to promote his latest studio album, Too Too Bad, released on July 17 through Gargamel Music/VP Records. The 13-track project includes collaborations with DJ Khaled, Ari Lennox and Gramps Morgan.

For nearly six decades, the New York Caribbean Carnival Parade has transformed Eastern Parkway into one of North America’s largest celebrations of Caribbean culture.

Buju Banton’s participation as Honorary Grand Marshal stood as a proud moment for Jamaica while reinforcing reggae and dancehall’s lasting place within the wider Caribbean story.

World.title: SLB apologises for email distribution error
World.content:
The Students’ Loan Bureau head office in Kingston.

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The Students’ Loan Bureau (SLB) is advising customers of an inadvertent email distribution error that occurred on Tuesday, September 8, during the dissemination of its SLB Insights newsletter.

According to the SLB in a statement on Wednesday, the newsletter was being distributed to customers as part of its ongoing communication regarding loan repayment obligations. It said during the distribution process, a customer email distribution list was inadvertently attached to one batch of the mailing in place of the intended newsletter.

“This was an error on the bureau’s part in the execution of that distribution. The affected file contained a list of customer email addresses only. It did not contain separate fields with customer names, loan account numbers, loan balances, Taxpayer Registration Numbers (TRNs), dates of birth, residential addresses, telephone numbers, banking information, passwords or other account credentials,” said the SLB.

SLB said the error affected only one batch of the distribution.

“The file was not published on SLB’s website, social media channels or other public platforms. The bureau is continuing to verify the final scope of the affected distribution and whether there is any evidence of further dissemination. The incident did not alter any customer’s loan account, balance, repayment obligation or account status. There is currently no indication that the incident resulted from unauthorised access to SLB’s systems or from malicious activity. The matter was identified and escalated for investigation on the same day it occurred,” the bureau added.

The bureau said it has initiated a review of the incident and of the controls governing bulk customer communications, including confirmation of the scope of the affected distribution and the implementation of additional safeguards to reduce the possibility of a recurrence.

“Bulk email distributions using the affected process have been suspended while additional safeguards are implemented. The matter has been reported to the Office of the Information Commissioner in accordance with applicable requirements. Customers identified as affected are being contacted directly by the bureau,” the SLB said.

It noted that as a precaution, customers should remain vigilant for suspicious or unsolicited communications that may appear to originate from the bureau.

“SLB takes seriously the responsibility entrusted to us to safeguard customer information,” said Nickeisha Walsh, executive director. “Customers should not disclose passwords or one- time passcodes in response to unsolicited emails and should verify any suspicious communication directly with SLB through its official channels.”

The executive director added: “This was an error on the bureau’s part, and we apologise to the customers affected. Our customers are entitled to expect that information entrusted to SLB will be handled with appropriate care. We are addressing the immediate incident and strengthening the processes and system controls governing bulk customer communications to reduce the risk of a recurrence.”

The SLB said it remains committed to communicating transparently with affected customers while ensuring that information released about the incident is accurate and based on verified findings.

World.title: Cellphones, smart watches, baby food on approved list for US embassy visits
World.content:
US Embassy in Jamaica

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The United States Embassy says previously banned cellphones and smart watches will now be allowed inside the embassy following a September 1 advisory.

In the advisory, the embassy said visitors attending their visa appointments will now be allowed to take their phones inside the building but will have to abide by rules governing their usage.

The list of items that visitors are allowed to carry includes:

Cellphones, earbuds, smartwatches.

Medical devices and non-liquid medication (pills), which must be declared before security screening

Small quantities of baby formula, baby food, milk

Small quantities of diapers

Money (bills and coins)

Belts

Watches

Keys

Baby carriers and baby strollers that can be folded small enough to pass through an X-ray machine

There are certain items, however, that visitors will still not be allowed to enter with, including:

Computers, intelligent eyewear, and other electronic devices not specified below

Media devices such as compact discs (CD’s), thumb drives, memory cards, flash drives/USBs, headphones, speakers, etc.

Cameras or video equipment

Flashlights

Lighters and matches

Weapons (guns, pepper spray/mace, etc.)

Knives and other sharp objects

Purses and bags larger than 18” x 18”

Alcoholic beverages of any kind

Liquids, gels, aerosols, oils, lotions, or powder (exceptions above)

In the past, cellphones were prohibited inside the building, with visitors reporting having to pay vendors outside the embassy to hold onto electronic devices.

World.title: Costly prisons
World.content:
In this August 2021 photo George Williams appears to be pondering his future while standing in the doorway of his house in Linstead, St Catherine. Williams who spent over 42 years in prison on murder charges despite being found unfit to plead from 1971, was released in 2020. He sued the State and was awarded $120 million in damages.

WITH the majority of lawsuits against the State filed by inmates seeking millions in compensation based on complaints about lack of bathroom facilities, overcrowding and general prison conditions, the Attorney General’s Chambers has recommended that the Department of Corrections “address the systematic deficiencies and the administrative shortcomings in order to cauterise the influx of these types of cases”.

“We have a lot of cases before the court that highlight these challenges,” director of state proceedings in the Attorney General’s Department Faith Hall said Tuesday on day two of the 14th annual Association of Caribbean Heads of Corrections and Prison Services (ACHCPS) Conference.

The confab is hosted by the Department of Correctional Services (DCS), Jamaica at the AC Hotel Kingston.

According to Hall, there are currently 10 claims before the Constitutional Court awaiting a ruling on these matters.

Addressing the issue of how the DCS can implement policies or amend systems to stem the influx of civil cases, Hall said chief among the Chambers’ recommendations is that the institution should “allow, where reasonable, liberal use of bathroom facilities; discourage the use of buckets for disposal of excrement; create a system of oversight for cleaning parties or manage it more closely or reimagine what is there; create a system of oversight to increase food standards and implement rehabilitation programmes focusing on hygiene and behaviour”.

Another area of concern is inmates’ lack of knowledge about the channels through which they can access legal help from outside the prison walls.

“The thinking is that when an inmate comes in they get an orientation package that informs about their release date, for example,” Hall suggested, adding that information about how to file appeals should also be included.

She said while the prison’s Bail and Appeal Section offers inmates help in filing appeals, it needs to do more in pointing them to the source of legal advice. According to Hall, a lot of the complaints by inmates is that when they go to that division they are discouraged from filing an appeal. She noted, however, that these claims have not been proven.

Hall also urged the DCS to make a strong push to address unsafe conditions within prisons as there is a serious possibility that DCS would be blamed if an inmate is injured by another using contraband.

“The responsibility is a multi-stakeholder one, in terms of preventing these kinds of claims that we are seeing at the Attorney General’s Chambers which are many times difficult for us to defend in court in this current climate where the society has become more aware of their rights and the society has become more litigious. Once it is [that] their rights are infringed — and there are attorneys there who are seeking out these persons — a claim will be filed,” Hall warned.

She noted that while many of the systematic failures which trigger lawsuits do not rest with the DCS alone, “the fact remains that the DCS plays an important role in advocating for the resources needed to carry out the functions given to it”.

Highlighting other claims being brought because of breach of constitutional rights or systematic deficiencies, Hall said these come from individuals “found unfit to plead and mental health patients” in addition to claims hinging on the inhumane and degrading conditions of prisons and unsafe custodial conditions.

She referenced the cases of Noel Chambers, an 81-year-old Jamaican man who died in custody on January 27, 2020, after being imprisoned for 40 years without ever standing trial, and George Williams who was released in 2020 after he spent over 42 years in prison on murder charges despite being found unfit to plead from 1971. She said these were cases of individuals being lost in the system, due to a multiplicity of errors on the part of various State actors, which have caused taxpayers dearly.

“What is important to note is that there were review mechanisms in place specifically to prevent a mentally ill person from being indefinitely detained without judicial oversight. However, regrettably those safeguards were not implemented in Mr Williams’ case,” Hall said.

“The responsibility of bringing him back before the court is not the DCS’s, so to speak. He was being housed by the DCS; there should have been some alert to say this was the situation and this was happening,” she added, pointing out that those shortfalls led to approximately $120 million in damages being awarded to Williams following the ruling by the court.

She said the department has appealed the ruling but only in respect of the quantum.

“The issues in relation to the failings and the breach of his constitutional rights were clear and we really wouldn’t have any defence for that. But we do believe the judge was a little heavy-handed, in terms of the award. But what the decision reinforced is that there are consequences that the State faces when it fails to address deficiencies in the prison’s administration, especially where vulnerable persons with mental illness are concerned,” she said and mooted electronic systems for tracking inmates among the methods to prevent them from being lost in the system.

In the meantime, she said while the ruling in relation to Williams’ payout is being appealed, $35 million of the $120 million was paid over to him in August this year “as a portion of what we think the claim is worth… as a show of good faith”.

The three-day conference, which began on Monday, is being convened under the theme ‘One Caribbean, One Vision’ and brings together senior correctional leaders, policymakers, and technical experts from across the Caribbean to discuss innovations, legal governance, and rehabilitation.

World.title: More school mergers coming
World.content:
Education Minster Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon and Hydel Cumberland Principal Carlon Pitt unveil the newly merged school’s name, crest, and motto on Monday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness has signalled that more underpopulated schools could be consolidated or left off the Government’s reconstruction list, arguing that Jamaica cannot continue maintaining costly education facilities with too few students to fill them.

Speaking during Tuesday’s official launch of the Jamaica Reconstruction and Resilience Oversight Committee (JAMRROC) at Jamaica House in Kingston, Holness stressed the rebuilding of Jamaica after Hurricane Melissa would not simply mean restoring every damaged asset to its previous form.

He said some infrastructure would be rebuilt differently, some would be relocated, and some assets would not be rebuilt at all — a position he linked directly to the Government’s plans to consolidate parts of the education system.

“Please note they will not necessarily be rebuilt in the same place or in the same way, and there are some assets that will not be rebuilt. I think the public should become aware of that… We are in the process of consolidating our education infrastructure. There are… many schools that are underpopulated. And I know there is a great attachment to the schools because they signal the life of the community, but it is highly inefficient,” he said.

Holness argued that maintaining underpopulated schools places an unnecessary burden on taxpayers, as Government still has to cover fixed costs regardless of enrolment.

He said it was inefficient to maintain facilities designed for 1,000 students when only about 300 are using them, with taxpayers effectively footing the bill for space that remains unused because of sentimental attachment to the school.

Holness did not identify specific additional schools for closure or merger, nor did he announce a list of institutions that would be excluded from reconstruction. Instead, he described consolidation as part of a broader rethink of the country’s education infrastructure, against the backdrop of the massive rebuilding exercise triggered by Hurricane Melissa which ravaged sections of the country last year on October 28.

The prime minister’s comments come as Government has already begun restructuring schools where existing facilities and enrolment levels make consolidation a practical option.

On Monday, Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon officially unveiled the newly merged Hydel Cumberland High School in Portmore, St Catherine, bringing the two school communities together at the former Cumberland campus.

The move followed concerns about infrastructure at Hydel and the underutilisation of Cumberland, which had capacity for 1,200 students but was operating with just over 300 when Morris Dixon visited about a year earlier.

Morris Dixon said the merger was intended to make better use of existing resources and form part of a strategic restructuring of the education system.

“One of the things we had thought about was potentially moving the children in little groups to different schools, putting them all around St Catherine. But I think this is the best option. I think this was quite strategic in nature, and that’s how we’re going to continue to do this restructuring of education in Jamaica — be strategic — because now that we have one institution instead of two, it means we can direct more resources to one… that is our plan,” she said.

However on Tuesday, the prime minister acknowledged that schools are not simply buildings and that closing or consolidating one can have consequences for the communities around it.

He said the Government therefore intends to consult before making such decisions, while maintaining that public money must be used responsibly.

World.title: Caribbean Music Awards to host landmark weekend celebration in Trinidad
World.content:
King of Soca Machel Montano (left) shares the stage with dancehall artiste Ayetian during last year’s CMAs in New York.

AFTER three years of celebrating Caribbean excellence in New York City, the Caribbean Music Awards (CMAs) is coming home. For the first time since its inception, the awards ceremony will be staged on Caribbean soil, with Trinidad and Tobago selected to welcome artistes, industry stakeholders and music lovers for what is expected to be a landmark celebration of regional sound and culture.

The move will also usher in a new era for the CMAs as the event will move from a single celebratory evening to an immersive weekend featuring networking, industry discussions, cultural showcases and opportunities for fans to engage more closely with the people behind the music.

For Paige de Leon, regional public relations strategist for the CMAs, the expansion reflects the steady growth of an event that has increasingly established itself as a credible platform for Caribbean talent.

“I think that when you’re building a movement like this, you are going to find that if the quality of the offering and your product is really solid, and there is authenticity in your intention, you are going to see growth,” she said. “The growth is all positive. One of the things that I most appreciate about the Caribbean Music Awards, as a Caribbean woman, is that it is an intuitive entity that seeks to respond to the needs of its audience — the Caribbean Diaspora. That speaks very highly of its founders, and now to the fact that it will be held in Trinidad and Tobago.”

Since its launch, the CMAs has sought to provide a dedicated stage on which the breadth and diversity of Caribbean music can be recognised. Its growing reach was underscored last year when the awards were broadcast on BET, introducing the ceremony and its honourees to an even wider audience. Having strengthened its footing internationally, de Leon said the time had come to ensure that the people who live within the region and continue to fuel its musical movements could experience the ceremony for themselves.

“We’re bringing it to Trinidad because we want to make sure that the people of the Caribbean have the opportunity to experience the ceremonial splendour of their music in this way,” she explained. “We have spent the last three years or so building the event, and last year the CMAs were shown on a major network, BET, and that was a very significant moment for us. Now we want to connect our people with the music. We want the people who fuel this music to have access to this and how it is evolving.”

That connection will stretch beyond the awards stage. The weekend will begin with a Friday-night networking experience, allowing guests to engage with artistes, participants and other members of the entertainment industry. A celebration of the steelpan will also form part of the programme, paying tribute to an instrument born in Trinidad and Tobago that has become an enduring symbol of Caribbean creativity and identity. The weekend will also include a discussion forum bringing together various industry professionals to explore the Caribbean music industry’s place within the global entertainment landscape.

According to de Leon, the forum will provide space for serious conversations about the business, development and international integration of the region’s music.

“There is an intellectual side to the music that we must not forget,” she said. “That will make for a very robust and rounded weekend of activities.”

While several Caribbean destinations could have provided an appropriate backdrop for the historic occasion, de Leon said Trinidad and Tobago emerged as the most natural fit. Beyond its globally recognised Carnival and rich musical traditions, she explained that the twin-island republic possesses the infrastructure and expertise required to successfully stage large-scale entertainment events. Its reputation for celebration is also expected to bring a distinctive energy to the CMAs’ first Caribbean staging.

“We could have picked anywhere in the region to host the awards because, really and truly, the music is everywhere,” de Leon said. “However, we felt Trinidad and Tobago was a natural fit because we have the physical and human-resource infrastructure that routinely churns out shows of this nature. Trinidad is party central, so there will be a lot of activity that will make for a very interesting and vibrant weekend in the capital, Port of Spain. We’re all excited to have a successful weekend.”

The decision to bring the awards into the region also signals that the CMAs is no longer simply an ambitious new undertaking. Though entering only its fourth year, the ceremony is already being positioned as an institution capable of preserving legacies while acknowledging the contemporary artistes carrying Caribbean music into new markets.

“I think, over time, people realised that this wasn’t something that was going to stop and start again or fade away,” de Leon said. “There is a lasting, legacy-type feel to the awards, even though we’re just four years in.”

That commitment to legacy will be reflected in the recognition of Jamaican dancehall trailblazer Patra, whose commanding image and unapologetic expression helped introduce a new representation of Caribbean womanhood to international audiences.

For de Leon, the honour is also deeply personal. “Patra is one of those artistes who has had a really transformational impact on the music. She had such a significant impact on me as a young Caribbean woman when I saw how she handled herself and how authentic she was about her sensuality as a woman and her experiences,” she shared. “She has been a significant influence in spreading Caribbean music across the world. She’s very special to us because of what she changed in how we see ourselves, and we just want to give her her flowers.”

Although Trinidad and Tobago will be the first Caribbean destination to host the ceremony, organisers do not intend for it to be the last. The long-term vision is to rotate the awards throughout the region, allowing the countries that have shaped Caribbean music to participate directly in its celebration while benefiting economically from the event.

“The intention is most certainly to have the awards move around and have all the countries that contribute to the success of music in the region be a part of the celebrations,” de Leon said. “When you have an awards ceremony like this, it means you’re stimulating the economy in the country where that ceremony is being held, and we want that for every country in the Caribbean. We want the CMAs to become an important element of the global tourism product.”

World.title: $5-BILLION GROWTH DRIVE
World.content:
WISYNCO Group Limited is moving to spend up to $5 billion on its operations over the next three years to meet the growing demand for its manufacturing and distribution business lines.

That’s the update provided by Wisynco Group Chairman William Mahfood following the release of the company’s audited financials for the June 2026 financial year (FY). The next round of investments is focused on growing the company’s manufacturing capacity and warehouse space for its expanding proprietary and third-party product portfolio.

“If you were to lay it out on a map, over the next three years you’d see continued investment in capital in terms of buildings and equipment. We’re looking at even more factory and production [capacity] in the next year,” Mahfood told the Jamaica Observer during a recent phone call.

Wisynco spent $3.24 billion in capital expenditure (capex) on its property, plant and equipment for its 2026 FY, which saw $1.26 billion deployed on land and buildings and $1.13 billion for ongoing work.

Between the 2023 and 2025 FY, the company spent $14.65 billion in capex which supported its ability to meet domestic demand for its existing products, diversify into new packaging types and launch its alcohol portfolio, including its Legend beer. The company invested US$35 million ($5.47 billion) on its new brewery and manufacturing facility.

Mahfood revealed that the company recently acquired additional land at Lakes Pen, St Catherine, and is expected to complete a new 70,000 square foot warehouse by the end of the year which is near completion. This is on top of the new 60,000-square-foot distribution centre to be constructed in Lacovia, St Elizabeth.

“We acquired some land for further expansion across the road. So, we’re looking at building a new distribution centre. We’re going to submit the plans in probably six months,” Mahfood explained.

Wisynco’s expansion comes at a time when its revenue grew 14 per cent to $65.35 billion, underpinned by a diverse product mix and introduction of new products such as the manufactured alcohol and Stone’s Ginger Wine portfolios which contributed $397 million during the year.

However, the company also had to book $454 million related to the new special consumption tax on non-alcoholic sweetened beverages which it must book as revenue and deduct as an expense under cost of sales.

“We’re seeing steady growth every month on the new business, so that’s positive. Overall, we’re happy about the turnout. We’re excited about this year,” Mahfood explained on the new alcohol portfolio.

While the company is spending significant sums on marketing and promotions for its Legend and alcohol portfolio, it has not begun to significantly push this product in the export market.

Wisynco’s exports grew 26 per cent to $1.55 billion for the 2026 FY but represented 2.38 per cent of group revenue. Exports represented $628 million or 1.97 per cent of revenue in 2021, demonstrating how fast domestic sales continue to grow.

“Our main focus is still in Europe. We just started in Canada with a new partnership with GraceKennedy,” Mahfood noted while pointing to the USA and Eastern Caribbean as other focus markets.

The company’s operating profit climbed 12 per cent to $5.87 billion as it spent more on advertising, staff and property expenses following its recent expansion initiatives.

However, earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) improved 16 per cent to $8.62 billion for 2026. The EBITDA metric is used to remove certain non-cash expenses like depreciation which lowers the company’s operating profit and shows the business’ core profit capacity.

Although Wisynco generated $531.26 million in finance income from its cash and investment portfolio, the higher debt balance pushed up its finance costs by 2.5 times to $847.57 million. The company reported $87.16 million in share of profit from its 30 per cent stakes in Ringtail Holdings Limited and JP Snacks Caribbean Limited.

Ringtail, the parent company of Select Brands Limited, reported $8.07 billion in revenue and $711.46 million in net profit since the July 2025 acquisition. JP Snacks reported $2.19 billion in revenue and a net loss of $29.23 million for the reported period.

While Wisynco reported a two per cent rise in profit before tax to $5.64 billion, its net profit fell seven per cent to $4.12 billion due to the increase in deferred taxes. The earnings per share declined from $1.17 to $1.10.

Despite the slightly lower net profit, Mahfood is confident about the new year which will see the company ramping up initiatives to grow its manufacturing and distribution reach. This comes against the backdrop of the western Jamaica rebuild via the National Reconstruction and Resilience Authority, which will see increased spending in the economy.

“As long as we have no more hurricanes, I think this is going to be a very vibrant winter season going into next year. We’re very excited,” the Wisynco chairman noted.

Wisynco’s asset base improved eight per cent to $47.30 billion as its PP&E stood at $18.37 billion, inventory at $8.53 billion, investments at $5.46 billion and cash at $5.34 billion. Wisynco’s sole stage two investment was restructured in December 2025 while the remaining $4.36 billion in investments are carried at stage one.

Total liabilities increased six per cent to $17.09 billion with total debt of $6.52 billion, while equity grew nine per cent to $30.21 billion.

Wisynco closed Tuesday at $20.14, leaving the stock up eight per cent in 2026 with a market capitalisation of $76.58 billion. That translates to a price to earnings ratio of 18.18 times.

Director Francois Chalifour sold 2,655,000 ordinary shares during the 2026 FY while Chairman William Mahfood and CEO Andrew Mahfood had reduced direct stakes in the business. Executive Lelani Hunt sold 412,937 ordinary shares, but Assistant Corporate Secretary Vanessa Young acquired 3,629 ordinary shares.

GraceKennedy Pension Fund Custodian Limited acquired an additional 15,556,346 shares to become the fifth largest shareholder with 48,478,631 ordinary shares or a 1.28 per cent stake. SJIML A/C 3119 and DOMHAD Investments Limited acquired an additional 2,038,856 ordinary shares and 806,949 ordinary shares, respectively. Sagicor Pooled Equity Fund is now the 10th largest shareholder with 26,913,562 ordinary shares or a 0.71 per cent stake.

World.title: GET BACK ONSIDE
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino (centre) addresses a round table press briefing at the end of the FIFA Executive Summit at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James in January 2018. Also pictured are JFF President Michael Ricketts (left) and Concacaf President Victor Montagliani.

JAMAICA Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts is calling for unity between FIFA President Gianni Infantino and Concacaf President Victor Montagliani as tensions between the two reportedly continue to escalate.

The relationship between both men has come under scrutiny recently amid the fallout over Infantino’s scrapped proposal to sell stakes in FIFA competitions, including the men’s and women’s World Cup.

Montagliani, who is a Canadian and Infantino’s vice-president at FIFA, is being touted as a potential challenger for the presidential elections next year. Infantino, who is Swiss, is seeking a fourth term as head of football’s world governing body, and is the only candidate who has publicly declared his intention to run on Sunday, with nominations closing in November.

UEFA, however, have called on Infantino to step down while reports from Europe suggest its member associations would strongly back Montagliani should he enter the race. Several European football associations have publicly withdrawn their support for Infantino, who has been in office since 2016.

Last month, Concacaf, which governs North America, Central America, and the Caribbean, released a joint statement with UEFA, and the Asian Football Confederation strongly criticising Infantino.

“When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned,” the statement said.

Montagliani and Infantino reportedly had awkward moments after Infantino’s impromptu visit to the Caribbean Football Union Presidents’ Meeting and Under-14 Challenger Series in Dominican Republic last month, which Ricketts attended. Montagliani had written to Infantino asking him not to attend.

During the tournament, Montagliani said he stood by the statement” and was coy when asked by

Sky News if Infantino should resign.

“That’s his decision, not my decision,” Montagliani told Sky. “My view is we have to follow proper governance processes and I have to respect my colleagues with that. Once we follow that then those decisions can be made my individuals.”

Reports from Europe also say that Concacaf members were “infuriated” by Infantino’s behaviour.

Ricketts, though, told the Jamaica Observer that both presidents were welcomed equally.

“No truth that Infantino was snubbed,” Ricketts said. “We did show him a lot of respect. In fact, both gentlemen — Montagliani and Infantino — were treated with utmost respect. We showed both of them love.”

However, Ricketts is hopeful that two can come together for football’s development.

“What we really want is for both gentlemen, Infantino and Montagliani, to come together and put the differences aside because obviously right now there’s a strained relationship,” he said.

“I would love for them to just put these issues aside, rekindle the love and warmth and the camaraderie and let’s move on with the growth of the football because both gentlemen in their own jurisdiction and their own portfolio responsibilities have done very well for football and I just hate to think that they are not now seeing eye to eye. The most important thing for me right now is for both of them to come together, put the past behind, get over this strained relationship and both of them continue to do what they’ve been doing for football.”

Ricketts says the JFF board will ultimately decide on supporting Infantino in the upcoming election in Morocco next March. Infantino needs the support of at least 106 of FIFA’s 211 member associations to secure re-election.

However, at least 14 FIFA member associations have publicly withdrawn support, including England and Italy.

Ricketts, though, says he won’t be influenced by the views and stance of some of the established nations.

“When Infantino tried to increase the numbers [for the FIFA World Cup], some of the bigger countries say that he was trying to bring in weak Caribbean teams into the World Cup,” he said.

“When he decided that he would increase our subvention, a number of big countries say that the Caribbean countries can’t manage from a fiscal perspective. So I am not even watching some of these countries because like I say, that’s how politics is. People will have different views and different opinions for different reasons.”

Infantino won a contested election in 2016 to replace Sepp Blatter, defeating Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa but has since been re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023.

World.title: ‘Step backwards’: Union leader warns Burnham against political donations cap
World.content:
He wrote to ministers this week calling for a “comprehensive plan” to ensure workers have a say on AI practices at their own workplaces. He said: “I think at some stage it will require primary legislation.”

Nowak met Burnham face-to-face on Monday and said they discussed his promises to “reindustrialize” Britain and bring more public sector contracts in-house, as well as the TUC’s push for the government to deliver the Employment Rights Act — Labour’s flagship set of workplace reforms — “in full.”

Some unions will use next week’s Congress, where either Burnham or a senior Cabinet ally is expected to speak, to press the government for a second employment rights bill to go further than the first Act. This would prompt a backlash from many business groups, which argue the new law, passed last December, is already adding burdensome red tape.

Nowak suggested he would back a second bill as part of a future general election manifesto, given many policies from the first Act haven’t been implemented yet. “I think it’s entirely legitimate to say, at the next election, what is Labour’s manifesto going to say about employment rights?” he said. “The idea that the Employment Rights Act is the finished article in terms of U.K. employment law, that nothing else needs to change, I think clearly is not the case.”

Elsewhere, Nowak said the government “could listen more” to unions when drawing up trade deals, as they have “real concerns” about a recent pact with the Gulf Co-Operation Council and ongoing talks about upgrading the U.K.’s free trade agreement with Turkey. “I’ve got concerns about any trade deals that say nothing about labor standards, say nothing about respect for union rights, and say very little about environmental standards — and I’ve made this point directly to [the] government,” he said.

He also said that Burnham’s agenda to move power and resources out of Westminster is not a “panacea,” adding: “I think it’s part of the solution. It’s not the solution in and of itself. Simply devolving powers without devolving responsibilities and real resources I don’t think is going to benefit anybody.”

World.title: New EU taxes will cut countries’ payouts to Brussels, Costa says
World.content:
“All national budgets need to be respected,” he added.

Costa’s visit came only three days after the far-right Alternative for Germany secured a historic landslide victory in the regional elections in Saxony-Anhalt. The Euroskeptics’ success risks hardening Merz’s stance in the budget negotiations, according to several EU diplomats.

Speaking alongside Costa, the German Chancellor reiterated calls to cut “several hundreds of billions” from the Commission’s near-€2 trillion proposal.

He described the budget increase as “simply prohibitive because at the end it is the European taxpayer who has to foot the bill.”

Costa countered that EU-wide taxes, known as own resources, are needed to finance common European policy areas such as defense and competitiveness that cannot be addressed by individual governments.

The Portuguese leader has previously signaled that he intends to narrow down several potential taxes that are acceptable to EU governments during a leaders’ summit on Oct. 15.

New own resources were expected to be €66 billion per year according to the Commission’s proposal from last July.

But after over one year of negotiations, EU governments have only agreed to proposed levies on foreign polluters, known as the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, and on uncollected electronic waste, which are expected to jointly raise around €20 billion per year.

World.title: How Emmanuel Macron brought France’s AI darling to the world stage
World.content:
It’s not every AI company that can count the French president as its top salesman.

On June 11, 2025, the founder of French AI company Mistral took to the stage alongside Jensen Huang, the powerful CEO of chip giant Nvidia, to announce a partnership between the two companies. As President Emmanuel Macron joined them, the Taiwanese-American executive turned to Mistral’s young CEO Arthur Mensch and said something just audible to the Parisian audience of techies and public officials: “Your president worked really hard for you.”

The Nvidia boss was referring to the deal his company had just sealed with Mistral to roll out AI infrastructure across Europe. “I told the president that Arthur and Mistral needed support from France’s biggest companies. Mr. President said to me: ‘Which ones? Let me call them!’” Huang said.





By the time the deal was official, the companies could announce that BNP Paribas, Orange, SNCF and Thales had all expressed interest in the partnership — boosting Mistral’s official entry into the global race for computing power.

Even for the head of Nvidia, the world’s most valuable company, such presidential proactivity was remarkable, illustrating the French government’s dedication to championing its homegrown startup and showing how Mistral has leveraged ties to the executive branch in Paris to try and reach the level of some of the biggest generative AI companies.

Mistral’s rise over the past three years, according to a dozen public officials and representatives of France’s tech ecosystem interviewed by POLITICO, owes much to the privileged relationship it built with Macron — enabling the company to secure both strong ties with the French state and a seat at the table with the world’s leading AI companies.

Macron, DeepMind Technologies CEO Demis Hassabis and Mensch in London on July 9, 2025. | Pool photo by Ludovic Marin via Getty Images

Now, with a French presidential election bringing to a close Macron’s two-term reign, details on the depth of that relationship — many of which are reported here for the first time — also raise questions about Mistral’s future under a different president.

The company on Tuesday announced a new €3 billion funding round including investments from the European Union and South Korea’s electronics giant Samsung, valuing Mistral at more than €21 billion. While that falls well short of the valuations of Anthropic and OpenAI, the news confirms the French startup as the only serious European player in the AI race.

As Europe questions its ability to challenge Chinese and American tech giants, Mensch and his team must now plan for life after Macron.

‘Fairy godmothers around the cradle’

Launched in 2023 by three co-founders — Mensch, Guillaume Lample and Timothée Lacroix — Mistral AI set out to build a full-fledged large-language model to compete with the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic. To do so, the Paris-based startup put forward a clear strategy from day one: cultivate a relationship with the French executive, and Macron in particular.

From its first funding round, the startup — which declined to respond to questions for this article — made a point of forging ties with the public sector. First among them was Bpifrance, France’s public investment bank and one of its earliest investors.

“We were aware of the sovereignty issues linked to AI,” recalls Arnaud Caudoux, deputy CEO of Bpifrance. “We had a good idea of the few — a few hundred in the world at the time — credible experts in the sector, among whom were Mistral’s founders.”





The BPI investment was part of a record €105 million total for a French seed round. But Caudoux noted: “There were a lot of fairy godmothers around the cradle.”

Those looking out for the startup came from the cream of French business and tech, playing crucial roles as matchmakers, patrons and fundraisers. They included telecom billionaire Xavier Niel, as well as Jean-Charles Samuelian-Werve and Charles Gorintin, co-founders of insurance startup Alan.

They were driven by the same goal: helping a European AI giant emerge. They tapped their networks to identify the most promising French AI researchers. These three businessmen were the ones who played matchmaker, bringing together Mensch, Lacroix and Lample.

Mistral AI cofounders Timothee Lacroix, Arthur Mensch and Guillaume Lample in Paris on May 28, 2026. | Stephane de Sakutin/AFP via Getty Images

When the Alan team struck a deal with the three young co-founders, it secured a strategic recruit to forge ties with the public sector: Cédric O, a former digital affairs secretary of state and early Macron supporter, would play a crucial role in the startup’s launch.

It was O who went into battle in Brussels to try to secure looser rules under the European Union’s AI Act, first proposed in April 2021. For Mistral, the burgeoning legislation posed a threat: How could Europe build a giant of its own if it stifled innovation?

In 2023, O intervened on Mistral’s behalf in EU talks in an effort to influence the negotiations — to the point that some lawmakers accused him of a conflict of interest. He also drew a rebuke from Thierry Breton, then European commissioner for the internal market.





Mistral “is lobbying, that’s normal,” French-born Breton said during the final weeks of negotiations over the AI Act. “But we are not fooled by anything. It is defending its business today, and not the general interest.”

“Cédric O’s role was, in a way, that of a lightning rod,” said a private-sector official who followed Mistral in its early days. By taking the hits, O allowed Mensch “to grow and develop as a CEO.”

Behind the scenes

From the outset, Mistral played the French and European card. The three co-founders may have built their careers in U.S.-based AI labs — Google DeepMind for Mensch and Facebook AI for Lample and Lacroix — but the first concept notes drafted for the startup’s launch put technological sovereignty at the heart of the project.

At the time, Mensch was a discreet 30-year-old engineer who needed to transform himself into the public face of Mistral on the international stage. Just a few months after launching the startup, the alum of the prestigious École Polytechnique made his first public appearance at VivaTech 2023 — Europe’s largest annual technology event — alongside Macron, who had already begun making the appeal for European technological autonomy.

The two were clearly in sync. “How do France and Europe intend to enable European champions to emerge, and how do we make sure that AI regulation does not hinder innovation?” the young sneaker-wearing entrepreneur asked the French president on the main stage.

Mensch would himself be tasked with helping come up with the answers. A few months later, the prime minister’s office formed a committee of experts to devise a French AI strategy. Alongside Mensch and O, its members included Gaël Varoquaux, a top researcher at France’s national digital research institute and Mensch’s former Ph.D. supervisor, as well as future Nobel economics laureate Philippe Aghion and Meta researcher and Turing Award recipient Yann LeCun.

By 2024, the committee delivered its report and Mistral unveiled Le Chat, its rival to OpenAI’s ChatGPT. But the AI landscape was already changing rapidly — and Europe was having second thoughts.

German rival Aleph Alpha, the continent’s other great hope in generative AI, announced it was moving away from developing its own models. Its CEO, Jonas Andrulis, offered a gloomy assessment: “Simply having a European LLM is not enough as a business model. It does not justify the investment.”





Mistral was not spared those doubts. Many observers feared its technology could fall behind American or Chinese rivals — even raising concerns that the startup might be acquired from abroad.

In 2025, reports of talks with Apple sparked panic at the highest levels of the French state. France’s embassy in the United States and the Elysée presidential palace asked Mistral whether the reports were true, according to two advisers who spoke to POLITICO. The company eventually reassured them: There had been no discussions “at the highest level.”

The French champion instead turned to a partner closer to home, and at the heart of Europe’s drive for technological sovereignty: the Netherlands’ microchip-printing giant ASML. The Dutch pioneer in the chips supply chain poured €1.3 billion of fresh investment into Mistral in September 2025 in a bid to speed up industrial AI development and keep Mistral’s know-how in European hands.

The deal was a boon for politicians — including Macron — seeking to keep the United States out of Europe’s most prized critical technology players.

Strategic partner

Three years into the company’s existence, the French government is no longer simply promoting a promising young startup. The state is now prepared to bend over backward to preserve a company whose technologies are being integrated across government.

After signing a strategic partnership with France’s national employment agency in early 2025, Mistral secured a deal with the French Armed Forces Ministry to develop AI for defense. Since 2025, Le Chat has also been in the process of being rolled out to 10,000 civil servants.





In public, Mensch has played down the importance of public subsidies and government support for his company. But Mistral’s teams in private conversations readily acknowledge that this privileged relationship is a major asset.

With Macron’s help, the French company has also opened the doors to the world’s biggest international summits — all the way up to the G7.

Mensch has been brought along on almost every presidential trip abroad in the past two years, giving him repeated opportunities to sharpen and spread his AI counter-narrative to contrast with the all-powerful Silicon Valley vision.

Mensch and French President Emmanuel Macron, behind, after signing an agreement with Samsung executives at the Élysée Palace on Sept. 8, 2026. | Pool photo by Gonzalo Fuentes via Getty Images

For several months, the Mistral boss — who readily appropriates the École Polytechnique motto, “For the Nation, Science and Glory” — has hammered home a position aligned with Macron’s: Europe must promote technological sovereignty and offer the rest of the world a model that is more sensitive to cultural and linguistic nuances than American and Chinese rivals.

In February, on stage at the New Delhi AI summit attended by Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Demis Hassabis of Google DeepMind and Sam Altman of OpenAI, Mensch defended AI as “a tool for empowerment, not domination.” He spoke about the importance of deciding who controls the deployment of AI, who benefits from it and how to ensure that it serves the general interest, not just a few powerful players.

That landed as countries across the world were scrambling to get insights from U.S. firms and the Trump administration into how new AI models were creating major new hacking risks.





And in June, in Evian-les-Bains at Lake Geneva, Mensch had lunch with G7 leaders and AI executives, including Altman. He once again took on the role of maverick to confront his American rivals, who were calling for technological standards to be drawn up under U.S. leadership.

“We still need to be very wary,” Mensch told POLITICO in an interview after the meeting. “It’s true that American actors tend to make that argument, which is, ‘Trust us—we’ll set standards here, and then we’ll export them to you.’”

Succession planning

As Mistral moves into infrastructure by building data centers and continues rolling out its solutions at major companies, some are beginning to doubt whether it can remain in the race to produce “frontier” models — the most powerful models available.

For Macron, the June G7 meeting was one of the last opportunities to leave his mark on the global AI debate before his presidency ends next spring. For Mistral, its relationship with Macron’s successor has yet to be built.

Gabriel Attal, former prime minister and presidential candidate for Macron’s pro-business bloc, readily showcases his ties to Mistral and has put AI at the heart of his campaign platform — even incorporating Le Chat into his communications toolkit. Attal’s centrist rival Edouard Philippe would also almost certainly continue backing Mensch.





While Mistral does not publicly associate itself with the far-right National Rally of Marine Le Pen, the nationalist party sees the company as a sovereign asset. On the left, the parties have unanimously backed the company — and called for sovereign AI — in response to the risk of American models being weaponized against European countries.

Yet Mistral relies on international funding and major partnerships with American giants including Amazon, Nvidia and Microsoft. While bringing in ASML as a key investor meant Mistral would remain firmly rooted in Europe, it also shifted some of the power to ASML’s headquarters in Veldhoven, the Netherlands.

Macron takes a selfie with young French tech entrepreneurs, including Mensch, n Paris on Feb. 11, 2025. | Amaury Cornu/AFP via Getty Images

This detail could undermine the French consensus in favor of Mistral, just as AI is emerging as a key campaign issue for the presidential election.

“We need to kill this very bar room idea that it would be feasible to own the capital, and therefore finance on our own, at French or European level, the hundreds of billions that AI infrastructure requires. It’s simply impossible,” said Bruno Bonnell, a French businessman who runs a major public investment program, France 2030, under the prime minister’s office.

World.title: Europe pans ‘disturbing’ Trump map that shows all of North America as US territory
World.content:
“It’s disturbing and, in many ways, completely inappropriate,” Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen told broadcaster DR. “It’s obviously a sign that the U.S. president still harbors some kind of maximalist vision in his own mind. We need to rein that in.”

Icelandic Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir summoned U.S. Ambassador Billy Long on Tuesday, with her ministry saying it made clear that the post was “entirely inappropriate.”

The U.S. president has also repeatedly mixed up Iceland, a sovereign country, and Greenland, a self-governing Danish overseas territory. At the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, he referred to Iceland four times while discussing issues relating to Greenland, including blaming “Iceland” for a drop in U.S. stock markets.

Trump’s map also included French, British and Dutch territory. The French Caribbean and Saint-Pierre and Miquelon, off Canada’s coast, were covered by the U.S. flag. Left-wing presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon said Macron should “send the aircraft carrier to maintain control over our sovereignty and reassure the populations under threat.” Conservative politician Xavier Bertrand was more restrained in an X post on Wednesday: “Our sovereignty is not reshaped by a series of edited posts on social media.”

The latest post landed as European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Greenland on Monday, declaring the island was making a “clear choice” to deepen ties with Europe and unveiling a €200 million investment package.

The star-spangled map was part of a wider burst of Truth Social posts over recent weeks in which Trump claimed Apple Maps had joined Google Maps in renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America,” declaring the change “complete, ratified, and binding.”

World.title: Asylum applications plummet across EU as governments push for deportation hubs
World.content:
The EU earlier this year agreed on wide-ranging new rules allowing countries to establish “return hubs” in third countries like Albania and Rwanda, to which unsuccessful asylum seekers and other failed migrants can be sent to. It has also drawn up lists of safe countries from which would-be refugees are unlikely to be accepted apart from in exceptional cases.

With far-right parties gaining in the polls ahead of key elections in France, Germany, Italy and other EU countries, governments are pushing Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to use her State of the Union speech next week to demonstrate mainstream politicians can take effective action to address concerns about migration.

Germany, which is among the countries pushing for more powers to remove failed asylum seekers, saw applications fall by 50% year-on-year. Nonetheless, the anti-immigrant, far-right Alternative for Germany party continues to enjoy electoral success.

Sweden recorded just 8,485 applications last year, the lowest level in 40 years, while Denmark — one of the EU’s staunchest opponents of unregulated migration — had registered a historic low of 1,835 applications by the end of November. Austria saw the fewest applications in 23 years and has returned more failed asylum seekers than the number of new ones arriving.

At the same time, the statistics show, illegal border crossings have fallen by 55% in the past two years, with Brussels having struck agreements with neighboring countries like Turkey and Serbia to reduce irregular migration.

World.title: Even Trump-friendly EU countries back Brussels’ pact with Canada
World.content:
"There’s very strong support for [Commission President] von der Leyen making that outreach and for closer cooperation," said a third diplomat with knowledge of the preparations. That's despite a handful of countries, including Giorgia Meloni's Italy, Andrej Babiš's Czech Republic and Robert Fico's Slovakia, traditionally seeking close ties with the Trump camp and trying to avoid outright provocations.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney will address the European Parliament next week on a trip first reported by POLITICO, as part of a public campaign to pivot away from dependency on the U.S. and form a club of like-minded, pro-free trade democracies. The visit is designed "to clearly signal the intention and ambition on both sides to upgrade our partnership," a senior EU official said.

From the Arctic to the universities

Carney's trip, which coincides with von der Leyen's State of the Union speech, has sparked a search for concrete ideas on areas for closer collaboration. Participation in the EU's Erasmus student exchange scheme, alignment on security and defense in the Arctic region and military-industrial partnerships are among those areas being considered, according to nine EU officials and one diplomat familiar with the discussions.

No broad new partnership has been agreed, however, and officials cautioned that talks remain at an early stage. For now, the aim is to demonstrate political ambition and identify areas where the two sides can deepen cooperation, with Carney expected to set out more practical next steps in his speech.

The Commission is preparing an updated Arctic policy, currently expected on Oct. 20 and renamed the North Neighbourhood and Arctic Strategy to reflect its broader geographic focus. Von der Leyen, meanwhile, recently returned from Greenland saying Europe wanted to become “more engaged in the Arctic.”

That makes the region a potentially useful bridge between Brussels’ strategic priorities and Ottawa’s.

Another EU official said any reference to Canada in the speech could center on security, potentially through some form of Arctic security initiative. “Security and defense is always her happy place,” the official said when asked what form an overture to Carney might take.

Cooperation in the region could extend well beyond defense. A third official who has worked on the Arctic strategy pointed to existing and potential cooperation on critical raw materials, subsea cables and specialized equipment needed to operate in the High North, including icebreakers and other Arctic-capable vessels. Cleaner shipping is another area where the two sides’ interests overlap — and diverge from the U.S., which has lobbied against decarbonization in the industry.

World.title: Comment Macron est devenu le meilleur allié de Mistral
World.content:
Mistral AI et son patron Arthur Mensch ont tissé avec l’Elysée des liens que peu de start-up peuvent revendiquer. Cette relation survivra-t-elle au départ d’Emmanuel Macron ?

Nous sommes le 11 juin 2025. Alors que s’ouvre VivaTech, le patron de Mistral AI, Arthur Mensch, monte sur scène pour l’une des tables rondes les plus attendues du salon : l’à peine trentenaire, impeccablement cravaté, doit prendre la parole au côté de Jensen Huang, tout puissant PDG du géant des puces Nvidia, pour annoncer un partenariat stratégique entre les deux entreprises. Alors que le président Emmanuel Macron les rejoint avec quelques minutes de retard, l’Américano-Taïwanais se tourne vers le jeune patron français et lui glisse, d’un air entendu : “Your president worked really hard for you” [“Votre président s’est vraiment démené pour vous”].

Même pour le patron de la société la mieux valorisée au monde, ce volontarisme présidentiel surprend. Sur scène, le voilà qui fait rosir de plaisir le chef de l’Etat français, en illustrant son activisme : “J’ai dit au président qu’Arthur et Mistral avaient besoin du soutien des plus grandes entreprises françaises. Monsieur le président m’a dit : ‘Quelles sont-elles ? Laisse-moi les appeler !’”

Ce sera fait. Au moment d’officialiser leur accord, les deux entreprises et l’Elysée peuvent déjà annoncer que BNP Paribas, Orange, la SNCF ou encore Thales ont manifesté leur intérêt pour ce partenariat, qui a acté l’entrée de Mistral dans le domaine de la capacité de calcul informatique, maillon crucial de la chaîne de valeur de l’IA.





L’épisode relaté par le patron de Nvidia illustre tout à la fois l’inclinaison du gouvernement à promouvoir sa start-up nationale, et la manière dont Mistral a pris appui sur l’exécutif pour se hisser auprès des plus grandes entreprises d’IA générative.

Lancée en 2023 par trois cofondateurs, Arthur Mensch, Guillaume Lample et Timothée Lacroix, Mistral AI a d’emblée fait un choix : miser sur un lien étroit avec l’exécutif français, et en particulier avec Emmanuel Macron. Interrogés par POLITICO, une douzaine de responsables publics et de représentants de l’écosystème technologique décrivent ainsi la construction d’une relation privilégiée, qui a permis à Mistral de se faire une place auprès de l’Etat et à la table des leaders internationaux de l’IA.

Or, à quelques mois de l’élection présidentielle et alors que l’Europe s’interroge sur sa capacité à défier les champions technologiques chinois et américains et à gagner en indépendance technologique, Mistral AI est face à un tournant. L’entreprise, qui compte désormais plus de 1000 salariés, doit maintenant se projeter dans l’après-Macron.

Bonnes fées et millions

Dès sa naissance et sa première levée de fonds en 2023, la start-up — qui n’a pas souhaité répondre à POLITICO dans le cadre de cet article — a fait le choix de se rapprocher du secteur public. Ainsi, Bpifrance, la banque publique d’investissement française, fait partie de ses premiers investisseurs. “Nous avions conscience des enjeux de souveraineté liés à l’IA, et avions une bonne idée des rares — quelques centaines dans le monde alors — experts crédibles dans le secteur, dont les fondateurs de Mistral faisaient partie”, se souvient Arnaud Caudoux, le directeur général adjoint de Bpifrance. “C’était un montant record pour un tour d’amorçage français, mais il y avait beaucoup de bonnes fées autour du berceau”.

Les bonnes fées en question sont le gratin du capitalisme et du secteur technologique français, qui ont joué des rôles essentiels d’entremetteurs, de mécènes et de leveurs de fonds. Parmi eux, le milliardaire Xavier Niel, mais aussi Jean-Charles Samuelian-Werve et Charles Gorintin, cofondateurs de la start-up spécialisée dans l’assurance Alan. En 2022, ils sont mus par un même objectif : contribuer à faire émerger un géant européen de l’intelligence artificielle. Ils ont ainsi activé leurs réseaux pour identifier les chercheurs français les plus prometteurs du secteur de l’IA.

Les trois cofondateurs de Mistral AI, Timothée Lacroix, Arthur Mensch et Guillaume Lample, à Paris le 28 mai 2026. | Stephane de Sakutin/AFP via Getty Images

Ce sont eux qui joueront les entremetteurs pour former le trio Arthur Mensch, Timothée Lacroix et Guillaume Lample. Au moment de “toper” avec les trois jeunes cofondateurs, l’équipe d’Alan obtient un ralliement stratégique pour tisser des liens avec le secteur public : Cédric O. L’ancien secrétaire d’Etat au Numérique, soutien d’Emmanuel Macron de la première heure, jouera un rôle majeur au moment du lancement de la start-up. C’est même lui qui montera au front à Bruxelles pour tenter d’obtenir des assouplissements sur le règlement européen sur l’IA (AI Act), présenté par la Commission européenne dès avril 2021.

Car, pour Mistral AI, ce texte est dangereux : comment bâtir un géant européen si l’Europe bride l’innovation ? Dès 2023, Cédric O se retrousse les manches et s’inscrit, au nom de Mistral, au registre de transparence de l’Union européenne afin de peser sur les négociations — au point même d’être soupçonné de conflit d’intérêts par certains parlementaires.





Ce nouveau venu s’attire rapidement les remontrances de Thierry Breton, alors commissaire européen : la start-up Mistral AI “fait du lobbying, c’est normal. Mais nous ne sommes dupes de rien.
