World.title: The problem with replatforming Alfred ‘Krip’ Yuson
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – Filipino literature and the classics that have come out of it always deserve to be known, and it’s often made possible by efforts like republishing and circulating physical copies to make them accessible to even more readers. But when the author behind one of these books has caused more harm than good, it becomes an entirely different story.

Case in point: Alfred “Krip” Yuson and his 1988 novel Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café.

The book was supposed to have been given new life by Exploding Galaxies — with the publishing house even standing by its initial decision to republish the book despite drawing backlash from members of the literary community. Here’s what went down.

Yuson’s web of controversies

Yuson, a Carlos Palanca Memorial Awards for Literature Hall of Fame inductee, has been accused by several individuals of alleged sexual misconduct. His latest published work was the 2022 book The Mountain That Grew.

“Why re-platform a man who’s responsible for the harassment and suicide of women? I do not care how brilliant you think his book is. I DO NOT CARE. And I will NEVER understand,” writer Katrina Stuart Santiago said in a Threads post on August 26.

Santiago further attested that she knows of young female writers who have had their own share of “horrid” experiences at the hands of Yuson.

“I remember when writers were being ‘cancelled’ left and right for everything from minor indiscretions to horrible mistakes to bad decisions, my question then was: when do we talk about the dirty old men of the literary establishment? Because THAT is a list. And it also has a list of victims. Re-platforming one of them by reprinting his book seems like [a] signal, doesn’t it. Of many things, including that people think we forget who these men are. We do not. We cannot. WE SHOULD NOT,” she said in another post on August 27.

Santiago added that literary workshops fuel Yuson’s predatory behavior, given the power dynamics that exist in these spaces between mentors and their mentees.

In response, Exploding Galaxies had initially attempted to discredit Santiago’s commentary, stating that while sexual harassment isn’t something they take lightly, the allegations that have been thrown at Yuson “have not been proven or independently corroborated.”

“We republished Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café for its well-established literary merit, and we stand by our decision to publish the book,” Exploding Galaxies wrote in its first public statement on September 5.

“We also stand firm against dishonest and unfair attempts to discredit this republication, especially as it is coming from a person who has expressed a longstanding personal grudge against the author, and who has, over the years, leveled serious public accusations against others,” it added.

Public response

Other figures in the literary community were quick to weigh in on the matter, with award-winning writer Jose “Butch” Dalisay Jr. pondering on the topic of art being created by questionable individuals.

“Does moral or political purity translate to some kind of elevated prose, or more honest and insightful poetry?” he wrote in a Facebook post. “Can someone please put together a library of vetted literature (or otherwise a new Index Librorum Prohibitorium) to spare us the process, and so we can keep to the straight and narrow, and enjoy reading without guilt or shame?”

Dalisay had followed it up with another post apologizing for appearing to trivialize the plight of sexual harassment victims — adding that the phenomenon of enabling a culture of harassment in workshops was something he would take up with the UP Institute of Creative Writing.

“There was a specific context to my remark that sexual misconduct and plagiarism were “low-hanging fruit.” It was not to dismiss them but to suggest that they were, among human evils, among the most visible and most common (which makes them no less painful to those concerned). I was talking about the possible crimes writers and artists have been accused of, which include murder and treason, and other offenses that injure not just one but many,” Dalisay said.

“I apologize to those victims of sexual harassment who may have seen my remarks as dismissive; they were not meant to be. It is a serious problem we are confronting not only in literature but in society at large.”

2011 plagiarism case

But sexual harassment isn’t the only serious issue that Yuson has found himself involved in. Writer Jaemark Tordecilla had accused him of plagiarism in 2011.

Tordecilla noticed that Yuson lifted several paragraphs from sportswriter Rey Joble’s piece about former PBA commissioner Rudy Salud. Joble’s story was published under GMA News Online, while Yuson had passed off his own version of it to Rogue Magazine.

Yuson was serving as GMA News Online’s editor-at-large then, and was in charge of copyediting Joble’s draft. He explained that since he had rewritten portions of Joble’s work, he thought he was considered to at least be part-author.

While he apologized for his actions, Yuson had merely attributed them to his old age, being overworked, and the pressure of having to meet deadlines. He still continued to write more after, and had even published several more works, like Islands of Words & Other Poems (2015), The Music Child & The Mahjong Queen (2016), and In the Footsteps of St. Ignatius of Loyola (2017), among others.

Withdrawing the republication of Yuson’s book

On September 7, Exploding Galaxies eventually announced that it would no longer push through with promoting or publishing Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café.

“We hear you all. We are sorry for the hurt this has caused our community. We are no longer promoting or releasing this book. As a publisher, we will do better. Thank you for speaking up,” the publisher said.

Exploding Galaxies also promised to “do better” in its mission to put works of Philippine literature back into circulation. But this still begs the question: How can publishers and literary circles do their part in discerning whether or not it is appropriate to promote a piece of work when the individual behind it has caused hurt to many others in the past?

Yuson has yet to comment on the matter himself. – Rappler.com

World.title: Supreme Court acquits Imelda Marcos in 7 counts of graft
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – The Supreme Court (SC) 1st Division acquitted Imelda Marcos, the mother of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., in her graft cases related to Swiss foundations.

In a decision made public on Wednesday, September 9, the SC division overturned the Sandiganbayan’s November 2018 decision that convicted the 97-year-old former first lady of seven counts of graft.

Play Video

“Accordingly, the Appeal is granted. The November 9, 2018 Decision of the Sandiganbayan in Criminal Case Nos. 17287, 17288, 17289, 17290, 22867, 22868, and 22869 is reversed and set aside. Accused-appellant Imelda R. Marcos is acquitted for the prosecution’s failure to prove her guilt beyond reasonable doubt for violation of Section 3(h) of Republic Act No. 3019, in relation to Article IX, Section 8 of the 1973 Constitution,” said the 50-page ruling penned by Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda.

Associate justices Ramon Paul Hernando, Henri Jean Paul Inting, Ricardo Rosario, and Jose Midas Marquez all concurred in the ruling.

The Marcos matriarch is acquitted four years into the presidential term of her son, who won the presidency in 2022.

The ruling

In its decision, the SC division said the prosecution failed to prove Marcos’ guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Beyond reasonable doubt is the threshold needed to convict an accused in criminal cases.

Marcos was charged with alleged violation of Section 3(h), which has the following elements:

the accused is a public officer

they have direct or indirect financial or pecuniary interest in any business, contract, or transaction

they either intervened or took part in their official capacity or connection with such interest, or they are prohibited from having such interest by the Constitution or by any law

The SC said it’s undisputed that the first element is present, but the second and third elements are contested. The Office of the Ombudsman presented documentary and testimonial evidence that sought to prove Marcos’ financial interest, but the SC said they were “inadmissible and lack probative weight.”

In Marcos’ case, the Sandiganbayan found that she had a financial and pecuniary interest in the foundations based on the Swiss documents. The documents were retrieved from Swiss banks and had been authenticated in accordance with Swiss legal procedure.

However, the SC said the Sandiganbayan erred when it considered the Swiss documents duly authenticated.

“The Court has emphasized that the rule on authentication, more particularly as to private documents, is in place to prevent the inclusion of spurious documents in the body of evidence. Thus, it is settled that private documents are generally inadmissible in evidence unless they are properly authenticated,” said the ruling, adding that the prosecution was not able to present a credible witness who could have testified to the documents’ authenticity.

In addition, even if the SC would ignore the probative weight of the prosecution’s evidence, Marcos must still be acquitted, said the Court. The prosecution, according to the SC, failed to prove that the alleged pecuniary interest was “covered by Section 3(h) of Republic Act No. 3019 and Article IX, Section 7 (then Section 8) of the 1973 Constitution.”

“All told, the prosecution failed to establish that the subject foundations are businesses as the term is ordinarily understood. Any financial or pecuniary interest in the subject foundations is not covered by Section 3(h) of Republic Act No. 3019 and Article IX, Section 7 (then Section 8) of the 1973 Constitution. Doubts on the coverage of the term ‘business’ should be resolved against the State and in favor of the accused-appellant,” said the ruling.

2018 Sandiganbayan decision

In the 2018 decision, the Sandiganbayan sentenced Marcos to six years and one month, up to 11 years, for each count. It also meted the penalty of perpetual disqualification to hold public office.

According to the anti-graft court, Marcos participated in the management of foundations which was a violation of the country’s anti-graft law. The Office of the Ombudsman also found that the public money involved in the private organizations reached $200 million.



It involved seven Swiss foundations. When one foundation closes, the money will be transferred to another, then the foundation will be closed again.

“Pertinently, the [Sandiganbayan] noted that the documents and testimonies presented by the prosecution showed that she has a direct or indirect financial interest in the foundations and has participated in the management of the same,” said the 2018 ruling of the anti-graft court. – Rappler.com

World.title: P6.2 billion slated for fertilizer, fuel aid to ease El Niño impact
World.content:
MARKET. People buy different kinds of basic commodities at the Paco Market in Manila on March 11, 2026.

On top of this, the Department of Agriculture is asking Congress for an additional P10 billion in its 2027 budget in anticipation of severe El Niño impact

MANILA, Philippines – The government is set to distribute P6.2 billion worth of fertilizer and fuel assistance to help cushion the impacts of the global oil crisis and El Niño on farmers and fisherfolk.

The fund is under the Unified Package for Livelihoods, Industry, Food, and Transport, or UPLIFT, a comprehensive response to energy security and livelihood needs amid the Middle East conflict.

There is no identified number yet of beneficiary farmers and fishers, according to Department of Agriculture spokesperson Arnel de Mesa. To ensure good yield, much of the fertilizer aid will be distributed to places less affected by El Niño.

“One of the things that DA is really going to do is to maximize yield in areas not affected by El Niño,” De Mesa said in a press briefing on Wednesday, September 9.

De Mesa said the full impact of El Niño on crops and prices will not be felt until the first semester of 2027, and that these measures are preparatory before El Niño develops into a more severe state by the end of 2026.

“If the fund is released in October, it works exactly as support during El Niño,” said De Mesa.

The Department of Agriculture is also requesting an additional P10 billion in 2027 to augment cash assistance for farmers and fishers, in anticipation of El Niño impacts.

No impact on rice production, prices yet

The agriculture sector was left reeling from the effects of the southwest monsoon or habagat and past tropical cyclones, incurring production losses worth P4.38 billion. The palay sector lost P2 billion.

“Again, we do not see impact on rice prices because, in terms of volume, this is within our estimated losses every year because of typhoons, flooding, and other calamities,” De Mesa explained.

Estimated losses in rice production ranged from 500,000 to 600,000 metric tons, said De Mesa. The P2 billion worth of damage in the palay sector is “about only 70,000 metric tons of losses.”

In a bid to curb prices and support local production, the DA said it will not allow imports of high-grade rice in the meantime. According to reports, Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. talked with the rice industry to import only 25% (and above) broken rice. – Rappler.com

Quotes translated to English for brevity.

World.title: No travel tax, no budget: Can TIEZA keep its tourism projects alive?
World.content:
The pesky travel tax is easy to hate, but abolishing it could leave multi-year tourism infrastructure projects in limbo, especially with TIEZA not getting anything in the proposed 2027 budget

Even as the government keeps pitching tourism as a growth priority and jobs engine, the agency tasked with building much of its infrastructure is heading into 2027 with billions’ worth of ongoing projects and a proposed budget of exactly zero.

On top of this, if Congress succeeds in abolishing the travel tax, the Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority (TIEZA) could also lose the revenue stream that normally pays for almost everything it does.

A source familiar with TIEZA’s budget planning told Rappler that the agency initially sought around P5.2 billion in national government funding for 2027. That request covered infrastructure projects alone and did not yet include personnel services or maintenance and other operating expenses.

Budget Secretary Kim Robert de Leon informed TIEZA that the request could not be favorably considered because of the government’s limited fiscal space, the source said. Consequently, the proposed 2027 budget carries zero subsidy for the agency, compared with P248 million for general administration and support in 2026.

The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) echoed this stance during the budget hearing of the Department of Tourism (DOT).

“TIEZA’s proposal for National Government Subsidy in FY2027 is in view of several legislative measures proposing the abolition of the travel tax. However, as these bills remain under deliberation in the Senate and have yet to be enacted into law, the TIEZA’s requested subsidy was not considered in the FY [2027] NEP,” DBM Assistant Director Lulu Vispo said.

A zero budget may come with consequences on the tourism infrastructure pipeline. TIEZA chief operating officer Mark Lapid told lawmakers during the tourism department’s budget hearing that almost all of its projects are multi-year, with around P5.2 billion needed in 2027 alone to keep them moving.

The DBM, however, pointed to P2.355 billion in supposedly available TIEZA funds: P810.25 million in unobligated allotments as of March 31 and another P1.545 billion in unreleased 2025 appropriations.

“TIEZA may continue to utilize its travel tax collections to fund tourism-related infrastructures or projects,” Vispo added on Monday, September 7.

Meanwhile, TIEZA says that money is not sitting idly. Lapid told lawmakers that the roughly P2 billion cited during the hearing could not simply be used to pay for its infrastructure commitments as it was being used to fund the agency’s payroll.

“The P2 billion is for our personnel services in our office operations. So technically, we wouldn’t have any funds for infrastructure from the amount mentioned,” Lapid told lawmakers in Filipino.

The travel tax problem

The problem is that the pesky P1,620 travel tax that travelers love to hate is also what keeps much of TIEZA running.

Congress is now moving to abolish it. The House has already approved House Bill 8464, while Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said in August that the Senate is targeting abolition within the year.

Under the current setup, 50% of tax collections go to TIEZA, 40% to the Commission on Higher Education, and 10% to the National Commission for Culture and the Arts. TIEZA’s share from those travel taxes makes up roughly 95% of its funding, an agency source told Rappler.

The House bill does anticipate the problem by requiring the national government to replace those funds through the annual budget. The tricky part is timing. TIEZA is being told to prepare for a future in which the travel tax disappears, but it has yet to receive approval for replacement funding.

Photo from a TIEZA presentation shown during the House budget hearing for the DOT.

The tax cut could also have a very human cost inside the agency that needs consideration. A TIEZA presentation showed that around 300 travel tax personnel may be displaced out of its 1,045-strong workforce. Of those, 115 may have difficulty finding new work because of their age, while some 270 families could be affected.

Lapid told lawmakers that TIEZA cannot simply absorb the workers elsewhere because they are spread across international gateways nationwide and the agency does not have enough plantilla positions at its main office. Some could be terminated, while others may receive separation incentives.

Five projects may get a lifeline

During Monday’s budget hearing, the DOT made its case for Congress to restore an allocation for at least P1.3 billion for five TIEZA projects.

The list obtained by Rappler from a source includes:

P328.9 million for improvements of the Banaue Hotel and Youth Hostel complex in Ifugao. The TIEZA-owned property sits on a 5.3-hectare site overlooking the Banaue Rice Terraces and has 81 hotel rooms plus a 15-room youth hostel. TIEZA has been rehabilitating the aging property for years, which has remained temporarily closed.

The TIEZA-owned property sits on a 5.3-hectare site overlooking the Banaue Rice Terraces and has 81 hotel rooms plus a 15-room youth hostel. TIEZA has been rehabilitating the aging property for years, which has remained temporarily closed. P301.07 million for the CBDC River Water System in San Vicente, Palawan. This is meant to provide a long-term potable water supply to tourism establishments and communities around Long Beach, one of the main clusters of TIEZA’s San Vicente Flagship Tourism Enterprise Zone.

This is meant to provide a long-term potable water supply to tourism establishments and communities around Long Beach, one of the main clusters of TIEZA’s San Vicente Flagship Tourism Enterprise Zone. P400 million for iLIPAD , TIEZA’s airport development program with DOTr. Launched in 2020, the program helps fund upgrades to provincial airports, particularly facilities needed for night operations and greater flight capacity.

Launched in 2020, the program helps fund upgrades to provincial airports, particularly facilities needed for night operations and greater flight capacity. P212.2 million for the construction of a waste water treatment facility in Coron. The project is aimed at addressing the environmental strain that tourism and development place on one of Palawan’s busiest destinations.

The project is aimed at addressing the environmental strain that tourism and development place on one of Palawan’s busiest destinations. P63.7 million for the construction of Sky Garden in Barangay Lucap, Alaminos City. The project, which Marcos himself broke ground for in May 2025, is envisioned as another attraction and gateway near Hundred Islands, with elevated gardens, viewing decks, walkways, parking, a commercial center, and a multipurpose hall.

The proposed allocations for the DOT and its attached agencies are not yet final, however, as Congress can still revise the 2027 budget before it is enacted. But so far, lawmakers have appeared receptive to calls for more tourism funding, repeatedly pointing to the country’s infrastructure gaps and the need for greater investment.

After all, one need only look at NAIA to see what years of underinvestment can do to a country’s main international gateway — and how quickly things can begin to turn once fresh capital finally starts pouring in. – Rappler.com

World.title: House probe sought into Altai Mining operations in Sibuyan Island
World.content:
Gabriela party-list Rep. Sarah Elago (left), ACT Teachers party-list Rep. Antonio Tinio and Kabataan party-list Rep. Renee Co are shown here in a file photo taken in November 2025 after filing a resolution in the House of Representatives. INQUIRER.net / KRIXIA SUBINGSUBING

CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — Lawmakers from the Makabayan Bloc on Wednesday (September 9) filed House Resolution No. 1437 seeking a congressional inquiry into the mining operations of Altai Philippines Mining Company (APMC) on Sibuyan Island in Romblon.

The resolution was introduced by Kabataan Party-list Rep. Renee Louise Co, Gabriela Women’s Party Rep. Sarah Jane Elago, and ACT Teachers Party-list Rep. Antonio Tinio during the second regular session of the 20th Congress.

READ: Mining-free Sibuyan gains ground as local opposition mounts

Article continues after this 

Under HR 1437, the Makabayan lawmakers directs the House Committee on Natural Resources to conduct an investigation, in aid of legislation, of APMC’s activities on the island.

The resolution highlights concerns over potential illegal mining operations, lack of proper community consultations, and environmental destruction in the region.

The resolution explicitly urges the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), through the Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB), to immediately suspend all approvals and activities linked to the nickel mining project until free, prior, and informed consent (FPIC) is secured from affected communities.

The measure also calls on the Philippine National Police (PNP) to pull out police forces deployed in the area and respect the residents’ constitutional right to peaceful assembly and protest.

Local residents and environmental groups have long opposed APMC’s operations on Sibuyan Island—often dubbed the “Galapagos of Asia” for its rich biodiversity—citing threats to forests, rivers, watersheds, and agricultural livelihoods. /jpv

World.title: Reward offered to find last missing passenger in Tarlac bridge collapse
World.content:
A portion of the Agana Bridge in Barangay Tibag, Tarlac City, lies submerged in rushing waters on Monday, August 31, 2026. Heavy river currents triggered by relentless southwest monsoon or habagat rains undercut the infrastructure, causing the section to collapse on Saturday, August 29. INQUIRER PHOTO / GRIG C. MONTEGRANDE

TARLAC CITY – Tarlac City Mayor Susan Yap has offered a P100,000 reward for information that could help authorities locate the last missing passenger of the SUV that plunged into the river as a section of the Agana Bridge collapsed on August 29.

Search and rescue teams have yet to find Paul Harvey Collado, the SUV’s owner and a supervisor nurse at Jecsons Medical Center. Despite the passage of more than a week, rescuers have not given up the search.

READ: Bodies of 2 SUV passengers found after Tarlac bridge collapse

Article continues after this 

Yap addressed the public in a social media post on Wednesday night, September 9, appealing for information that could help locate Collado.

“Sa panahong puno ng pangamba, ang ating tulong at impormasyon ay maaaring maging daan upang muling makauwi si Paul Harvey sa kanyang pamilya,” Yap said on her official Facebook page.

(In moments of dread, all the help and information you provide may be the solution that would bring Paul Harvey home to his family.)

The bodies of Shanen Tuhao and Shiela Mae Taborlupa have been retrieved from the Bayambang town in Pangasinan where they were located separately on September 1 and on September 5. The remains of James Patrick Taborlupa was found earlier on August 31, off the coast of Lingayen town also in Pangasinan.

The youngest passenger, 20-year old Nataniel Dion, was the only survivor.

Article continues after this 

James Patrick and Shiela Mae Taborlupa, who were siblings, were buried on Tuesday (September 8) at the Loyola Eternal Memorial Park in Tarlac City.

In her post, the mayor also encouraged nearby municipalities and provinces to coordinate with the city government of Tarlac should they receive any information that will help locate Collado. /jpv

World.title: ACT: Higher Pisa scores due to sacrifices made by teachers, students, parents
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — Despite the country’s improved scores in the latest international learning assessment, the Alliance of Concerned Teachers (ACT) said these fail to account for the socioeconomic conditions of learners and educators and ignore how poverty directly undermines learning outcomes.

“The socioeconomic conditions of teachers and students while teaching and learning cannot be separated. It’s difficult to learn while your stomach growls and you’re thinking how you can afford the next meal,” ACT chair Ruby Bernardo said in a statement on Wednesday.

Bernardo added that the improvement in scores should not be credited to the Marcos administration but to the sacrifices of overworked and underpaid teachers, students and parents who “carry the burden of the education system despite systemic neglect.”

Article continues after this 

READ: PH improves rank in international education assessment

In the latest Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) scores released on Tuesday, the Philippines improved its ranking in science, mathematics and reading, outranking 14, 16 and 18 countries, respectively.

ACT, however, warned the public against being obsessed with international rankings, pointing out that the framework of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation (OECD) and Development did not capture local realities due to its “westernized” and “colonial” perspective on education.

“Our conditions are not the same as other countries. There is a difference to our educational system, and the rankings will not mirror our improvement. We must measure our improvement based on the actual situation and needs of our country,” Bernardo said.

READ: Dy credits teachers for PH rise in global student performance

Article continues after this 

ACT urged the government to overhaul the current “colonial, commercialized and repressive” education system and reject foreign-dictated curriculum frameworks.

It also told the government to prioritize a nationalist, scientific and mass-oriented education system grounded in national culture and social needs.

Article continues after this 

Low budget

ACT further criticized the Department of Education (DepEd) for having the lowest national education budget worldwide, which the group claims has neglected the need for schools to have good facilities and equipment. It also said the budget was embarrassing and nothing to be proud of.

The Department of Budget and Management has touted the P1.326 trillion allocated for basic and higher education in the proposed 2027 national budget as a reflection that the education sector ranks among the government’s top spending priorities.

ACT, however, said the education budget only falls under 3 percent to 4 percent of the country’s gross domestic product, “far from the amount needed to fulfill the needs of the country such as the amount of teachers, classrooms, education support personnel, and equipment.”

“That’s why alongside additions to the education budget, we should improve the state of living in the country, raise the salary of teachers and other personnel, and provide proper support to learners,” Bernardo said.

DepEd’s next step

The DepEd, in wake of the improved scores, said it would roll out Pisa for Schools, an OECD assessment service that provides school-level performance benchmarked against international standards.

“This can help us understand more clearly what is happening inside our schools and where support is most needed,” said Education Secretary Sonny Angara in a statement on Wednesday. “The objective is to turn better data into better decisions, so that improvements in our national results are felt by learners in the classroom.”

According to him, the service generates internationally comparable results for individual schools, measuring the same core competencies of 15-year-old students in reading, mathematics, and science.

“Our goal is not to create another ranking. It is to give schools information they can act on. If we know more precisely where learners are struggling, we can better target interventions, strengthen teaching, and direct resources where they can make the greatest difference,” said Angara.

World.title: Higher September power bills seen in VisMin
World.content:
Composite image from Inquirer file

MANILA, Philippines — The forced shutdowns of several coal power plants in the Visayas and Mindanao have led to record-high spot power prices, with consumers set to pay more for their electricity bills this month.

In a media briefing, Independent Electricity Market Operator of the Philippines (IEMOP) said power traded at Wholesale Electricity Spot Market (WESM) surged by 64.9 percent to P18.59 per kilowatt-hour (kWh) in the Visayas.

Higher rates were booked in Mindanao, hitting P19.56 per kWh, an 88-percent jump from a month ago’s P10.39 per kWh.

Article continues after this 

The hefty upward adjustments in WESM prices in the two main islands were attributed to the outages at major coal plants, forcing the market to rely on more expensive energy sources.

READ: VisMin consumers brace for power outages on Sept. 3

“We have outages that contributed a lot to the decline in supply in the Visayas. I think [the prices that] we’ve seen so far [are] the worst,” said Isidro Cacho, Jr., IEMOP’s head of trading operations.

“The P18 and P19 are actually the highest prices that I’ve seen in 20 years of WESM operations,” he added.

IEMOP is the operator of WESM, an avenue where power is traded between producers and distributors to boost their supply.

Article continues after this 

For months now, the Visayas has been under numerous yellow and red alerts due to tight electricity supply. Mindanao is likewise facing a power crunch due to the forced shutdown of some of its coal facilities.

During the billing period, which covered July 26 to Aug. 25, the supply in the Visayas and Mindanao declined by 2.6 percent and 7.3 percent, respectively.

Article continues after this 

Demand, on the other hand, went up by 0.7 percent for the Visayas and 5 percent for Mindanao. Luzon, meanwhile, saw its WESM prices drop by 34.2 percent to P4.80 per kWh. /cb

World.title: DENR: 339 illegally traded wildlife seized since January
World.content:
ENDANGERED Two juvenile Southern Rufous Hornbills were seized by the DENR and Philippine National Police in an entrapment conducted in General Santos City in July. —Photo courtesy of DENR-Soccsksargen

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) said that from January to August, it seized 339 illegally traded animals and exotic species nationwide, including poisonous snakes and “rarer exotic species” such as bearcats or “binturong.”

In a statement, the DENR said the seizures included 220 birds, 97 reptiles, 31 amphibians, and nine specimens of mammals, arachnids and insects.

“Feathered species made up nearly two-thirds of the total confiscations, with parrot varieties—such as cockatoos, cockatiels, and macaws—dominating seizures in Visayas and Mindanao,” it said.

Article continues after this 

“Meanwhile, the Central Luzon and Cagayan Valley regions accounted for the bulk of confiscations of lovebirds, which is common in many households,” it added.

Snakes, lizards

Among the confiscated reptiles, according to the DENR, were 79 lizards, primarily iguanas and geckos, and 17 snakes, among these venomous vipers and pythons.

It noted that separate enforcement activities in Central Visayas resulted in the seizure of 15 iguanas, while a total of 60 dried geckos and 50 endangered radiated tortoises were found in various airport shipments.

Also among the confiscated wildlife were “rarer exotic species,” the DENR said, adding that an illegal wildlife trader in Soccsksargen was apprehended for carrying two bear cats and four gibbons.

Nine tarantulas across five different species were likewise seized by authorities in Calabarzon (Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, Rizal and Quezon) region.

Article continues after this 

The DENR said that aside from wildlife, it also confiscated over 300 wild fauna and apprehended 55 illegal wildlife traders after conducting 71 enforcement operations from January to August.

Last year, the agency confiscated various heads of animals and insects. These included 976 heads of snakes, lizards, sugar gliders, scorpions, millipedes, as well as those from a Visayan leopard cat (“maral”) and Philippine palm civet (“alamid”).

Article continues after this 

During the same period, DENR personnel at Ninoy Aquino International Airport also seized nearly 7,000 orchids and 255 tropical plants.

The DENR, meanwhile, urged the public to help protect the country’s wildlife by “reporting suspected illegal collection, possession, sale, or trafficking of wild animals, including transactions conducted through online platforms.” /cb

World.title: 3 ex-soldiers in Degamo slay case convicted for gun, bomb possession
World.content:
Slain Negros Oriental Governor Roel Degamo (left) and detained ex-Rep. Arnolfo “Arnie” Teves Jr. —Photo from Facebook/Inquirer files

MANILA, Philippines — Three former Army soldiers have been found guilty beyond reasonable doubt of illegal possession of firearms and explosives in connection with the assassination of former Negros Oriental Gov. Roel Degamo in March 2023.

In a decision handed down on Aug. 18 and made public only recently, the Manila Regional Trial Court’s Branch 40 convicted Joric Labrador for unlawful possession of a firearm and ammunition, and coaccused Joven Javier and Benjie Rodriguez for one count each of unlawful possession of explosives.

Labrador was sentenced to up to 10 years in prison, while Javier and Rodriguez were handed down a prison term of reclusion perpetua, or up to 40 years.

Article continues after this 

The three convicts, along with expelled Negros Oriental Rep. Arnolfo “Arnie” Teves Jr., are facing separate charges for multiple murder, frustrated murder and attempted murder charges before the Manila court for the killing of Degamo.

READ: Court grants Teves bail, but he stays in Taguig jail

The court, meanwhile, ordered the custodians of the .45 cal. pistol, two magazines, 14 rounds of live ammunition and two hand grenades seized from the three men to turn these over to the Philippine National Police.

Discharged from Army

Labrador, Javier and Rodriguez were already discharged from the Army for going on unauthorized leave before they were charged in court three years ago over the killing of Degamo.

Labrador was a member of the Mechanized Infantry Battalion of the 4th Infantry Division while Javier was with the Light Reaction Battalion. Rodriguez, on the other hand, was assigned to the 35th Infantry Battalion of the 11th Infantry Division.

Article continues after this 

According to the Department of Justice, which transferred the case to the City of Manila, the court also upheld the validity of the accused’s warrantless arrests, noting that the seized pieces of evidence were properly identified and handled, as testified to by the police and other witnesses.

“Impunity should never triumph over justice. We shall hold accountable anyone who transgresses the rule of law,” Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida said in a statement announcing the Manila court’s ruling.

Article continues after this 

Degamo and nine others, including his driver and bodyguard, were killed by armed men on March 4, 2023, during the distribution of aid at his house in Pamplona, Negros Oriental.

Teves’ denial

Amid accusations, Teves, his longtime political rival, denied he masterminded the 56-year-old governor’s assassination. At the time Degamo was killed, Teves was on medical leave from the House of Representatives, supposedly seeking treatment in the United States.

In August 2023, the majority of House lawmakers voted to expel the lawmaker for disorderly behavior and violations of the chamber’s code of conduct. They cited his refusal to come home to face the charges against him and his attempts to seek political asylum in Timor-Leste.

World.title: PNP: Hunt for Dela Rosa still on despite negotiations with ‘powerful protectors’
World.content:
Fugitive Senator Ronald “Bato” Dela Rosa —Inquirer photo/Niño Jesus Orbeta

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police said on Wednesday there is no letup in its efforts to arrest Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa amid ongoing government efforts to negotiate with his “protectors” over his surrender.

“It will take as long as it will take,” PNP public information chief Col. Allen Rae Co said at a press briefing in Camp Crame on Wednesday.

“Our efforts did not wane, will not wane, and we will not deviate from serving the warrant of arrest,” Co told reporters.

Article continues after this 

The International Criminal Court (ICC) has ordered the arrest of the senator for his role in the drug war waged by former President Rodrigo Duterte as Davao City mayor and later on, as president. The tribunal, which already has Duterte in its custody at The Hague, the Netherlands, identified Dela Rosa, a former PNP chief, as a “co-perpetrator.”

On Tuesday, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla told One News’ Storycon that the government was in negotiations with Dela Rosa’s “protectors,” whom he did not identify but described as “powerful people.”

READ: Remulla: Negotiations underway with Bato dela Rosa’s ‘protectors’

He also justified the negotiations, saying: “We don’t want casualties involved. That’s number one. They have to surrender peacefully.”

“And we will use all the levers of the government to get him out of his hiding, using all the economic and military levers that we have in order to force him out,” Remulla said.

Article continues after this 

91 guns unaccounted for

The senator’s legal counsel, Israelito Torreon, however, denied any personal knowledge of Dela Rosa’s powerful protectors, saying that his client was a “deeply prayerful man” who considers God his “one and only protector.”

Co, meanwhile, said the PNP’s efforts to locate Dela Rosa are ongoing although he refused to provide further details, citing operational matters.

Article continues after this 

He noted that 91 of the 117 firearms registered to the senator remain unaccounted for.

“Our FEO [Firearms and Explosives Office] is continuously coordinating with the [senator’s] family for the surrender of the guns. Legal police action will be initiated,” Co said.

The PNP FEO revoked the firearms licenses and gun registrations held by Dela Rosa in June in line with the ongoing campaign to catch him.

The senator was last seen in public on May 14, leaving the Senate premises early in the morning.

Three days before that, he suddenly surfaced at the chamber after being in hiding for over six months following rumors the ICC had ordered his arrest.

Remulla previously said that Dela Rosa’s last known location was in Mindanao. /cb

World.title: QC prosecutors junk VP husband’s complaint over release of bank records
World.content:
Manases “Mans” Reyes Carpio —Inquirer file photo/Grig C. Montegrande

MANILA, Philippines — Quezon City prosecutors have dismissed for lack of jurisdiction a complaint filed by Manases Carpio, the husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, against several lawmakers and ex-officio members of the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) for making the couple’s bank records public.

The Office of the City Prosecutor recommended dismissal albeit “without prejudice,” saying it could not act on the matter because all the respondents are public officials with Salary Grade 28 or higher.

The Sept. 7 resolution said the acts cited by Carpio—including the House subpoena for AMLC reports on alleged suspicious transactions involving Duterte, and the lawmakers’ statements during her House impeachment proceedings—were performed in connection with their official duties.

Article continues after this 

READ: Solons say ‘good’ that Carpio complaint close to being junked

Named as respondents in the complaint filed in April were Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro, chair of the House justice committee; Akbayan Representatives Percival Cendaña and Chel Diokno; Mamamayang Liberal Rep. Leila de Lima; Bicol Saro Rep. Terry Ridon; ACT Teachers Rep. Antonio Tinio; Kabataan Rep. Renee Co; and Manila Rep. Joel Chua.

Also named were AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura; Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Governor Eli Remolona Jr.; Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Francisco Lim; and Insurance Commission chief Reynaldo Regalado.

Carpio accused them of acting in conspiracy to illegally disclose his and his wife’s bank records without their consent.

He cited the April 14, 2026, House committee hearing where Cendaña sought a subpoena ordering the AMLC to provide reports on Duterte’s bank transactions from 2006 to 2025. Diokno supported the request and said he had sought similar reports involving other members of the Vice President’s family.

Article continues after this 

Carpio also cited the remarks lawmakers made in arguing that the Vice President was not protected by laws on the disclosure of AMLC reports.

No ruling on merits

The prosecutors, however, said the subpoena and the lawmakers’ manifestations were made in performance of their official duties.

Article continues after this 

“By no stretch of the imagination could we rule that these acts of the respondents were done in their private capacity,” the resolution said.

The dismissal did not determine whether Carpio’s allegations were substantiated or not, but only ruled the complaint was filed before a body that had no jurisdiction on the matter.
