World.title: ACT sets out plan to wind up Waitangi Tribunal
World.content:
The ACT Party wants to wind up the Waitangi Tribunal, saying its contemporary inquiries have become increasingly ideological and expansive.

The party is campaigning on four reforms that it says will end the tribunal's contemporary jurisdiction, and move the country on.

ACT leader David Seymour, who has previously branded the tribunal as "increasingly activist", said while the tribunal had made an important contribution, particularly in helping address historical grievances, the tribunal that existed today was different to the institution established in 1975.

"Through urgent and kaupapa inquiries, the tribunal now passes judgement on day-to-day government policy. It proposes alternative policy settings and seeks to steer decisions that properly belong to elected governments and Parliament. This is not the tribunal's role and never was," Seymour said.

ACT's policy document stated every historical claim before the tribunal should be heard and resolved, limited to claims lodged by the statutory deadline of 1 September 2008.

This would end the tribunal's power to inquire into contemporary government policy, conduct, and decisions.

"The Tribunal should not operate as a parallel policy institution, producing its own prescriptions for how elected Governments should exercise their mandate," the document said.

The government has already launched a major review of the Tribunal's functions, but it is yet to be released publicly.

The review, which was part of National and New Zealand First's coalition agreement, promised to "refocus the scope, purpose, and nature" of the tribunal's inquiries back to their "original intent".

Lecturer for Māori Laws and Philosophy at Te Wānanga o Raukawa Carwyn Jones previously told RNZ that by examining contemporary issues, the tribunal was focused on what the legislation intended, and it was unclear what the government meant by original intent.

Carwyn Jones. RNZ / Mark Papalii

"The historical claims are, of course, winding down, and in fact, the tribunal can no longer accept claims which relate to historical matters. So the tribunal, when it was originally set up, was designed precisely to assess contemporary Crown policy, law, action, through the lens of the principles of the Treaty," he told RNZ in August.

Newsroom has reported the unreleased review does not recommend a curtailing of the tribunal's ability to launch kaupapa inquiries.

In contrast to the government's plans and ACT's proposal, Te Pāti Māori wants to amend the Treaty of Waitangi ACT 1975 to make Waitangi Tribunal recommendations binding on the Crown, giving the tribunal more power to investigate and enforce breaches.

World.title: Department of Conservation begins enquiries into man who threw dead fish at leopard seal
World.content:
The Department of Conservation has made contact with a man who threw a dead fish at a leopard seal on Petone Beach.

Footage of the man emerged online earlier this week, showing him going close to the animal amongst shouts telling him to "leave it alone".

Marine reserves ranger Breanna Hindmarsh said DOC had been in contact with the man in question and he was assisting with enquiries.

"DOC strongly discourages this type of behaviour when marine mammals come ashore."

Under the Marine Mammals Protection Act, DOC can lay charges for those disturbing protected marine animals, costing someone jail time or fines up to $250,000.

"We continue to encourage people to keep at least 20 metres away from marine mammals like this leopard seal, keep dogs on a leash, and enjoy it from a distance," Hindmarsh said.

A leopard seal on a Lower Hutt was harassed by dogs and people throwing fish at it. Supplied

Local Carrie was one of several yelling at the man to stop, heard in the background of a video shared to social media.

"I heard him saying to his kids, 'Let's go feed it'," she told RNZ.

"He hopped the little fence, and got the fish, and threw it at the seal."

Carrie said the man then looked at the crowd of about 20 people and yelled at them to "feed the bugger".

Carrie said she had left quite concerned that something would happen to the seal, after seeing teenagers daring each other to go up to it.

Marine biology student Ivan Raynaud earlier told RNZ he saw multiple people shine flashlights in the seal's face.

"When the torches and flashes shone on the seal he was starting to get more disturbed and agitated, rolling over more, yawning and sort of trying to turn his face away."

Raynaud said he tried to tell people to stop, but he was told there were "no rules".

World.title: Explainer: How 9/11 changed how we fly in New Zealand forever
World.content:
Explainer - It only took one day for how New Zealanders fly to be forever changed.

This week marks the 25th anniversary of the 11 September, 2001 terrorist attacks in America, which left nearly 3000 people dead.

Two New Zealanders also were killed on that day - Alan Beaven, a New Zealand native and environmental attorney who died on the hijacked Flight 93, and John Lozowsky, a US-born New Zealander who had dual citizenship and who died in the World Trade Center collapse.

There had been plane hijackings and bombings before 2001, of course, but what happened that day was something new - and terrifying.

Fred Stein is the deputy chief executive of aviation security at the Civil Aviation Authority, which establishes safety and security standards in New Zealand through its Aviation Security Service, or AvSec.

"We had trouble imagining an attack like 9/11 before 9/11 and by we, I mean the aviation industry, right?," he said.

"And now the aviation industry not only can imagine something like 9/11, but we're actually open to the idea that things we've never experienced are still possibilities."

Pedestrians standing on the Brooklyn waterfront look across the East River towards the burning twin towers of the World Trade Center in lower Manhattan, New York on September 11, 2001. HENNY RAY ABRAMS / AFP

How flying used to be

Most people under 30 will have no idea how different air travel was before 11 September 2001. Domestic flights in New Zealand had no real security screening at all, and international flights had far more relaxed standards than they do now.

"There were very few airports with screening and that screening was just started and was quite limited," Stein said.

"The only real equipment was a walk-through metal detector and maybe a hand-held metal detector and the very simple x-ray machines. That was it."

People could walk up to boarding gates to greet family members, you didn't have to worry about carrying your water bottles through, or arrive hours earlier for international flights.

"You pretty much just showed them your ticket and boarded," one person posted in a recent Reddit thread reminiscing about travel in New Zealand pre-9/11.

Today, only regional domestic flights for planes with fewer than 90 seats don't have security screening, according to AvSec - mostly ATR turboprop planes.

Stein worked for 20 years at America's Transport Security Administration, which was formed in the wake of the 9/11 attacks, before he came to New Zealand to work with the CAA. The attacks using commercial airliners were on a scale that had never been seen before.

"That was really the first time that an airplane had become the weapon," he said.

While there were deadly incidents like the 1988 UK Lockerbie bombing that killed 270 people, "This was the first time that the people on the aircraft had the sole purpose of turning that aircraft into a weapon."

Jeff and Sandy Stewart of Pittsburg, PA, hug each other 11 August 2002 as they look at angels representing the passengers on Flight 93 at the temporary flight 93 memorial overlooking the crash site in Shanksville, PA. SHAWN THEW / AFP

The single biggest change after 9/11

Security bio-scanning, shoe checking, reinforced cockpit doors - these are all part of 9/11's impact, but the biggest change is more of a state of mind, Stein said.

It's all about how we view air travel.

"The exact style of attack that happened on 9/11 would be almost certain to fail today," he said.

"And a huge reason for that is because the passenger expectation has changed. Passengers wouldn't allow themselves to be turned into a weapon by people wielding knives."

One of the key events of that day was when the passengers of United Airlines Flight 93 fought back against the hijackers. The plane crashed in Pennsylvania instead of on its expected Washington, D.C. target, killing all 37 passengers and four hijackers. New Zealand-born Alan Beaven was one of those on that flight.

Flight 93 "was galvanising," Stein said. Its story was turned into movies and books and it helped change the image of passengers from just passive travellers to actually acting as another layer of security, he said.

"They have demonstrated again and again and again in aviation travel since then, that the passengers won't take it. They will actually rise up and protect themselves. That was never even a consideration (before)."

Many times in recent years passengers have gotten involved with fighting back, such as with "shoe bomber" Richard Reid who attempted to blow up a Miami-bound plane in December 2001 and was tackled by passengers after he grabbed a flight attendant.

As recently as last week, a disruptive passenger on an American Airlines flight who reportedly attacked others on board was subdued and duct taped to his seat with the help of other passengers.

Crew are now trained to be more proactive, Stein said.

"Crews carry zip ties and duct tape with them, they know that they can enlist the aid of the passengers when something really unusual and threatening happens.

"Even if it's not to the level of trying to truly hijack the plane, if they're putting the plane at risk, passengers are gonna respond."

The Civil Aviation Authority is "continually assessing the threat environment and working with domestic and international partners to ensure New Zealand's security settings remain appropriate and proportionate," Associate Transport Minister James Meager told RNZ.

A board at the Los Angeles Airport announces the closing of the airport following an alleged coordinated terrorist attack to the World Trade Center twin towers in New York and the Pentagon in Washington DC 11 September, 2001. GERARD BURKHART / AFP

How that all changed in one day

The 9/11 attacks happened early in the hours of 12 September New Zealand time. Prime Minister Helen Clark was on a flight to Hong Kong for a European visit which was quickly cancelled.

Former RNZ presenter Geoff Robinson arrived at work at 4.30am to find one of the century's biggest stories unfolding. He told Stuff in 2021, "I remember Kim Hill saying, 'it will never be the same after this', and she was absolutely right."

Flights all around the world were grounded and governments hustled to upgrade security at airports.

In a book the Aviation Security Service published in 2017 looking back at its first 40 years, it describes 9/11 as the day "aviation security changed overnight".

Cabinet ordered emergency domestic security screening nationwide at 11am, which required a major expansion of airport staff. Defence Force staff were called in to assist AvSec in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch.

AvSec staff, police and others worked nonstop to bring tighter screening in.

Not everyone appreciated the additional security screening or delays, AvSec wrote. People were bringing things onto flights that wouldn't be imaginable now.

"Avsec was collecting bin loads of every imaginable object - knives, scissors, hammers, box cutters and even guns," the book notes.

The events of 9/11 led to global standards for security, set by the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO).

"Their focus on security before 9/11 was so small, minimal, and now of course it's a major part of what they do and the rules they set for the international community," Stein said.

"Across all political spectrums, it doesn't really matter, security is kind of a common thread we all hold pretty dear."

Stein said 9/11 forced greater cooperation across nations to ensure air security.

"Very few attacks actually originate in the country that the attack is targeting.

"We're one world, and we've got to work together if we're going to keep each other safe."

By the end of October, then-Transport Minister Mark Gosche announced domestic screening would be permanent.

"Although the changes at our airports were the most dramatic in the country's history, AvSec moved swiftly and efficiently," Gosche recounted in AvSec's account of the day.

Other changes came with time in the wake of 9/11 - after a 2006 attempt in Britain to detonate liquid explosives disguised as soft drinks, strict new rules about liquids, aerosols or gels were added to most security screenings.

The airport experience has changed dramatically since 2001. RNZ / Kim Baker-Wilson

How security keeps changing

The changes over the past 25 years have ranged from the visible - those full body Advanced Imaging Technology or AIT scanners, where you get to raise your arms over your head and get the total treatment - to less obvious changes in how bags are screened behind the scenes.

After cockpits were stormed, hardened cockpit doors and secondary barriers were added. "Behaviour detection officers" are now trained to look for what Stein calls "indicators of deception."

"We are lucky that we are in a different threat environment than almost anywhere else in the world," Stein said.

But that hasn't made New Zealand immune to air security incidents.

In 2008, Somali refugee Asha Abdille attempted to hijack an Air New Zealand flight from Blenheim to Christchurch. That led to a Ministry of Transport review and recommendations to further improve security.

"The threats don't stop evolving," Stein said.

Things nobody imagined in 2001 - drone attacks on planes, hacking or other threats from artificial intelligence - now need to be considered.

Organisations like AvSec need to address the threats "but to do it at the right proportion and without impacting legitimate activities. So it's a balance, like the rest of security. It's just a new frontier that we are learning to grapple with and trying to stay ahead of."

In 2011, US Transportation Security Administration supervisor Nick Fox (R) and another TSA employee demonstrate an advanced image technology (AIT) scanner in Las Vegas, Nevada. ETHAN MILLER / AFP

For instance, those slow body scans will soon become much faster.

"We're not far from that being a walk-through AIT, so it'll have the speed of the walk-through metal detector, but the effectiveness of the AIT," Stein said.

"The future technologies are continuing to change and they're definitely going to improve security, but hopefully also improve the passenger experience."

Meager told RNZ that the CAA and AvSec are constantly working to make flying safer.

"Over the past 25 years, aviation security in New Zealand has continued to evolve to keep pace with modern technology, most recently with work in the Civil Aviation Rules Update Programme, launched in April.

"A key project includes work to implement rules which address issues raised within International Civil Aviation Organisation audits. These improvements to security, safety and efficiency will create consistency with other like-minded countries and confirm New Zealand as a safe and highly respected international aviation destination."

Grant Morris, associate professor of law at Victoria University, said the changes to flying after 9/11 aren't going anywhere.

"They are here to stay for two main reasons," he said.

"Firstly, the threat of terrorism remains. Secondly, if measures were significantly reduced and then a terrorist attack occurred, authorities would be blamed for reducing the measures."

"New Zealanders should have confidence that agencies continue to work closely together to keep our aviation system safe, secure, and proportionate to the risks we face," Meager said.

What happened 25 years ago forced security authorities to think bigger and smarter, Stein said.

"The idea that people would get on a plane, and be willing to kill themselves and turn that plane into a weapon, all those things were so new in 9/11 ... and are now, just an ingrained part of how we approach security.

"There is just an awareness of the possibilities," he said.

"I think we're just collectively more open to using our imagination and knowing that the bad guy will use their imagination."

World.title: Average KiwiSaver balance cracks $40k
World.content:
New Zealanders' average KiwiSaver balance has ticked over $40,000 for the first time, but there are still more than a million members not contributing to the scheme at all.

The Financial Markets Authority has released its latest KiwiSaver report, which shows there were 3.4 million members in the year to March, with an average balance of $40,340.

FMA head of investment management Emelie Jensert said that was a milestone for the scheme, but it came with responsibilities for providers and members.

"As average balances, as well as the overall balance, goes up, what we expect from providers is that they have good governance, they have clear disclosures and the members understand what they are getting out of KiwiSaver.

"I think the flip side of that is it also puts responsibility on KiwiSaver members to make sure that they engage in a way that's appropriate for them and their own financial circumstances."

There was a total of $138.8 billion in KiwiSaver funds under management, an amount that has more than doubled since 2020.

When can I stop giving money to my kids? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

There was $13.2b contributed to the scheme in the year, a record level, and $10.7b was made in investment returns. But 1.4 million members were not contributing regularly.

"I think it's important to notice it includes a very wide range of individuals," Jensert said.

"It includes people who are under 18, it includes people who are retiring. So now more people are starting to age out of KiwiSaver and retire ... it includes people who are parenting, potentially on parental leave, people who are outside paid work. It doesn't necessarily reflect people who have stopped saving by choice. We do continue to encourage members to review whether contributions are the right thing for them to do at this point in time, for them."

Members withdrew $6.8b, including at 65, for first homes and hardship, as well as other reasons.

Withdrawals by members 65 and over increased 10.5 percent to $3.3b, almost half the withdrawals in the year.

But the number of members making a full withdrawal continues to fall, which the FMA said suggested more people were choosing to keep some or all of their savings invested.

The $531.5 million withdrawn for hardship reasons was up 19.8 percent year-on-year and first-home withdrawals hit record levels. More than 50,.000 people withdrew a combined $2.2b.

Members paid a total of $978.2 million in fees, up 12.6 percent from the year before.

"The fees as a proportion of the funds that are in the KiwiSaver system have stayed the same for the past three years," Jensert said.

"What the FMA will be doing for the year ahead is we will conduct some research into KiwiSaver provider fees and particularly around trends. Once we've conducted that work, we will then see what the next steps could potentially be."

Jensert the number of members switching between funds increased and the transfer volume between providers reached new highs.

Growth funds attracted the largest number of incoming switches, but cash and conservative funds recorded the largest net inflows by value, while balanced and growth funds experienced net outflows.

Jensert said there were three things she would encourage people to do. "The first one being review whether you're contributing or not and if the contribution rate is the right one for you. The second one being are you in the right fund? That might change over your lifetime and depending on your financial circumstances. And the third one being are you understanding the fees that are being charged and what you are getting back in return for those fees? And is the provider that you're with the right one for you individually?"

Commerce and Consumer Affairs Minister Cameron Brewer welcomed the report.

"Competition is a key focus for this Government, and this report shows it working. Members switched funds 460,000 times last year and $7.4 billion moved between providers, up from $5.5 billion. If your provider isn't delivering, you can move, and hundreds of thousands of Kiwis did exactly that," he said.

"Check what fund you're in, check what you're paying, and don't be afraid to shop around. This Government's job is to keep that market competitive and well regulated so Kiwis have real choices."

World.title: RNZ election coverage: Multiple forms, on every platform
World.content:
From in-depth analysis, longform interviews and live reporting to summaries of key events and policy news, RNZ has announced its plans to cover Election 2026 at every level.

There will be reporting and interviews from RNZ's political journalists, led by editor Jo Moir, as well as presenters, specialist journalists, correspondents and regional reporters explaining the key issues in their parts of the country.

There will also be coverage of the contests for the Māori electorates as well as issues affecting te ao Māori. The RNZ Pacific, IndoNZ and RNZ Chinese teams will report the stories that matter to their communities and the region.

RNZ chief news officer Mark Stevens said RNZ's goal was to deliver comprehensive coverage that reflected its independent public media role.

"We'll have our multimedia election night broadcast hosted by John Campbell and Lisa Owen, with live crosses from around Aotearoa.

"We'll have significant digital coverage across the day on the website and our social media channels, including a Chinese-language live blog from the RNZ Chinese team and dedicated party vote and electorate results pages with real-time updates."

World.title: High school students were on platform when boy was fatally struck by train
World.content:
Latest from scene of fatal train incident in Auckland Morning Report Download MP3 2m

RNZ understands students at Mount Albert Grammar School have been told to gather for an assembly this morning, a day after a boy died at a train station in the central Auckland suburb.

Police say they have spoken to high school students who were at the Balwin Avenue Station when the boy was hit by a train at 3.28pm on Wednesday.

They have not confirmed whether the boy was a student at the school.

Auckland Transport says Western Line train services are operating as normal, although there may be occasional cancellations.

Police say they have spoken to a number of high school students who were on the platform at the time of the incident.

A westbound train passes the Rossgrove Terrace level crossing before stopping at Baldwin Ave station on Thursday morning. RNZ / Erin Johnson

Inspector Kerry Watson said police had notified next of kin "and the community will appreciate that this will be devastating news for them".

Family members were seen crying at the station on Wednesday night.

World.title: CNMI groups sue US over deep sea mining plan covering 67 million acres
World.content:
Two Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) groups have taken the United States federal government to court over its controversial plan to open more than 67 million acres of ocean around the Marianas to potential deep-sea mining.

Our Commonwealth 670 and PåganWatch, joined by the Conservation Council for Hawai'i and Center for Biological Diversity, filed a lawsuit 8 September in the US District Court for the District of Hawai'i against the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) and US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Earthjustice represents the four groups.

At the heart of the lawsuit is a 10 August NMFS finding that the proposed deep sea mining lease sale was "not likely to adversely affect" threatened or endangered species or their critical habitat.

The plaintiffs contend NMFS reached that conclusion without adequately considering what could happen after the leases are awarded-including mineral exploration, testing, development, and actual mining.

The Marine Minerals Administration (MMA), formerly the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM), proposes to hold the lease sale 16 December 2026.

According to the complaint, five leases covering more than 67 million acres would be offered. The leases would have primary terms of 20 years, which could be extended if they enter production.

The lawsuit comes after months of opposition to the federal government's deep sea mining push in the Marianas.



The area under consideration was expanded earlier this year after more than 65,000 comments were submitted during the federal review process. The complaint says the "overwhelming majority" opposed proceeding with leasing.

Our Commonwealth 670 and other local advocates previously criticised that expansion, while CNMI Governor David Apatang and Guam Governor Lou Leon Guerrero called for a moratorium and changes to the federal process.

CNMI Governor David Apatang and Guam Governor Lou Leon Guerrero. Facebook / CNMI Office of the Governor & Lt. Governor / RNZ Pacific / Eleisha Foon

In the new lawsuit, the plaintiffs allege NMFS considered too narrow a slice of the proposed activity before signing off on the lease sale.

They argue the agency should have considered not only the issuance of leases and preliminary surveys, but also the exploration, testing, development, and mining that could follow.

The complaint alleges those later activities are part of the overall federal action-or at least indirect effects of issuing the leases-and therefore should have been considered under the Endangered Species Act.

The plaintiffs also allege NMFS failed to adequately evaluate potential effects from vessel strikes, vessel noise and discharges, mooring lines, and buoys during preliminary work.

MMA's biological assessment itself identified possible effects from preliminary activities, including underwater noise, vessel collisions, entanglement, habitat disturbance, changes in prey, and accidental releases of pollutants and marine debris, according to the complaint.

The plaintiffs say those impacts were characterised as insignificant even though the assessment indicated the extent of several impacts could not be estimated.

The groups say endangered and threatened whales, sea turtles, sharks, manta rays, corals, and other marine species could be affected.

For the two CNMI plaintiffs, however, the lawsuit is also about the cultural relationship between the people of the Marianas and the ocean.

The complaint describes the ocean as central to CHamoru and Refaluwasch livelihoods and culture. It also notes that traditional Refaluwasch wayfinding uses marine animals such as individual whales and sea turtles as "sea marks" associated with locations around islands.

Our Commonwealth 670 is described in the complaint as an Indigenous-led nonprofit based in the CNMI whose members include ocean elders, teachers, youth, cultural practitioners, community advocates, environmentalists, and recreational paddlers.

PåganWatch is described as a Saipan-based grassroots nonprofit advocating for residents of Gani', the islands north of Saipan, and for the preservation of Indigenous culture.

The lawsuit raises two legal claims.

The first alleges NMFS' Letter of Concurrence was arbitrary and capricious and contrary to the Endangered Species Act and Administrative Procedure Act because the agency failed to properly consider the effects of the entire action.

The second alleges NMFS failed to issue a required biological opinion addressing the entire action if the agency was using an incremental-step consultation process.

The plaintiffs want the federal court to declare NMFS' Letter of Concurrence unlawful and set it aside.

World.title: Oil prices could reach $US120 - analysts
World.content:
Oil prices have spiked back over a US$100 with some leading analysts now forecasting the possibility of prices reaching $US120.

It comes after an escalation in conflict between the US and Iran over the few days with the US hitting a number of Iranian oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz in response to an Iran attack on a US warship.

The international benchmark Brent finished at up 3.4 percent today to US$101.21 a barrel after touching a high of US$101.58.

While US West Texas Intermediate crude was up 3.25 percent, to US$96.05 a barrel.

Both benchmarks closed at their highest since 22 May, according to Reuters news agency.

Bloomberg News has reported that investment Bank Goldman Sachs has said oil prices may rally to as much ​as US$120 a barrel if attacks ‌on shipping in the Middle East rise.

Oil prices had eased from early war highs in recent weeks after both Iran the US appeared to pull back on fighting.

However, according to Reuters, shipping volumes through the Strait of Hormuz still remain far below their pre-war peak.

The Strait is responsible for transiting about one-fifth of the world's oil and gas supply, making it key to the worldwide energy trade.

The rise above US$100 a barrel was unwelcome news for Wall Street, which fell as markets nervously await US inflation data due this Friday evening.

A higher CPI print, boosted by resurgent oil prices, could stoke fears that the Federal Reserve will have to hike interest rates this month, against a backdrop of rising bond yields globally.

30-year US bond yields have already hit their highest level since 2007 this week.

Meanwhile, prices for 91 unleaded petrol in New Zealand are sitting at just over $3 a litre.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold expected that could rise given the recent increases in international markets.

World.title: Women's tennis has a new world number one as US Open showdown looms
World.content:
Elena Rybakina ensured she will leave Flushing Meadows as the new world number one after a comprehensive win over Qinwen Zheng, despite top seed Aryna Sabalenka still being alive in her quest for a third straight US Open title.

Rybakina reached the semifinals for the first time and will face 2023 champion Coco Gauff, who beat fifth seed Mirra Andreeva 2-6, 7-6(9/7), 6-2.

The early program kicked off barely eight hours after Ben Shelton ‌beat Carlos Alcaraz in a five-set thriller that finished at 3:33 am, breaking the record for the latest ever finish at the US Open.

Zheng had cultivated a ‌reputation as one of the tournament's finest comeback artists but ran ⁠out of gas against Rybakina, losing 3-6, 6-1, 6-4 as ‌the Kazakh chipped away at her defences after ‌overcoming early mistakes.

"Becoming the WTA number one is something I've dreamed about since I was a young girl, it means so much to me," said Rybakina, who dethroned Sabalenka at the top of the rankings.

"I'm so proud of this moment. I want to thank my whole team for their support and being able to celebrate this achievement with me."

Meanwhile, Gauff got off to a dreadful start before ​recovering ‌to beat Russian 19-year-old Andreeva.

Gauff improved her level dramatically across the match, saving ‌match points in the ‌second-set tiebreak to move into the last four of her home slam for just the second time.

"Elena — she's the new world number one so it's going to be a tough match," Gauff said.

"I'm looking ‌forward to the battle. These are the moments you live for."

Sabalenka and American third seed Jessica Pegula are in the other semifinal.

Pegula is the only woman left without a grand slam title to her name, while Sabalenka is trying to win the US Open to avoid going major-less for the first time since 2022.

If Rybakina and Sabalenka progress, it will mark their second meeting in a major final this year, after Rybakina won the Australian Open title in January.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Overlooked by the whole AFL, Isaiah Dudley used the disappointment as fuel
World.content:
Isaiah Dudley's remarkable rise from state league footballer to the AFL finals has taken many onlookers by surprise, but those who worked closest with him always knew the Fremantle Docker could succeed at the highest level.

"For Isaiah it's never been about a lack of talent, he's got more talent in his football acumen than many, it was about just being physically ready for the challenge of AFL footy," said Paul Thomas, who coached Dudley at Central Districts in the SANFL.

"The value that we got out of him is exactly what you're seeing now in the Fremantle side."

Dudley has enjoyed a quick rise since making his AFL debut for the Dockers last season. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre/AFL Photos)

Dudley, listed as the shortest player in the league at 168 centimetres, was overlooked by all 18 clubs at the 2021 AFL draft.

That would have been enough for many footballers to give up their AFL dreams, especially when feedback from recruiters suggested his fitness and lifestyle were not up to scratch for professional football.

But for Dudley, it only served as motivation.

"They were the main two things, my lifestyle and my fitness, which kind of opened my eyes, realising that if I get them knuckled down, I can take my place anywhere," he said.

Dudley was a mature-age recruit for the Dockers. (Getty Images: Travis Hayto/AFL Photos)

Dudley gives a lot of the credit to his former coach.

"That's the thing with Thommo, he built good habits into me, and now the habits are living out and I've been playing every game, and I've been loving it," he said.

"I also became a better person, maturing, and then obviously with Thommo he drove me to become a better person and player.

"I'm a whole completely different person to what I was at SANFL level, not the one bloke who sits in the forward line just chilling.

"Now I'm up the ground working, bringing my talent and getting the most out of myself."

Hard yards pay off

But it was far from an overnight process, with Centrals putting added focus on improving Dudley's conditioning.

"The club put a little 10-week program into Isaiah, like a personal training type thing in the middle of a season, which then really took his game in leaps and bounds the following season," Thomas said.

Paul Thomas coached Dudley at South Australian club Central Districts. (ABC News: Che Corley)

It paid dividends, with Dudley's 2024 SANFL season catching Fremantle's eye.

He was invited to train with the Dockers before being picked up in the supplemental selection period on the eve of the club's first 2025 pre-season game against the Indigenous All-Stars.

By round three of his first year, he had already made his debut in the cauldron of a Western Derby against West Coast, kicking two first-quarter goals in Fremantle's victory.

Dudley's pressure has helped make Fremantle's forward line one of the most feared in the AFL. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

He played 16 games in his first year and has featured in all 24 of Fremantle's matches so far this season, kicking 28 goals.

As the Dockers look to bounce back against Geelong in a must-win semifinal at Perth Stadium tomorrow night, he admits he is living a dream that he sometimes has to remind himself is real.

Dockers wilt against masterful Hawthorn So good for so long this year, Fremantle chose an inopportune time to put in — by some distance — their worst shift of the season, going down by 32 points to a brilliant Hawthorn.

"I still pinch myself every day that I've gone from SANFL to now playing in an AFL finals series," Dudley said.

" It's a dream come true and I'm loving it. "

All while his former coaches and teammates watch on proudly from South Australia.

"I probably can't push enough just how much he makes us all smile still, when he does what he does on the footy field," Thomas said.

"He has the ability to light the crowd, he lights our locker room up as well.

"Seeing Perth Stadium come alight when he does something, and the commentators as well, isn't a surprise, but it certainly makes us all smile."

Dudley hopes his improbable story can inspire other footballers. (ABC News: Blake Kagi)

Dudley is hopeful his improbable story can encourage other footballers to overcome their setbacks and never give up on their dreams, and has a simple message for those who face disappointment in the draft.

"Always have a smile on your face, because if you don't get picked up from the draft, you've got many ways to get into the league.

"Lean into the coaches, the close network that you have, they're the people that are supporting you through the highs and lows."

World.title: Opals survive in last second after giving up 20-point lead at World Cup
World.content:
A short-handed Australian team is still alive and into the last eight at the FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup despite surrendering a 20-point three-quarter-time lead before ultimately beating Italy 82-80.

The Opals had a 69-49 lead heading into the final quarter of their qualification final against the Azzurre, but watched the Italians slowly chip away at it over the next eight minutes and 51 seconds before Costanza Verona's three tied the game at 77 with 1:09 left.

Zitina Aokuso made a lay-up off Izzy Borlase's drive to end a three-minute scoring drought for Australia and Ally Wilson's clutch free throws gave them a four-point advantage when Italy was forced to intentionally foul with eight seconds left.

The great escape appeared to be complete until a long-range bomb by Vittoria Blasigh off the inbounds pass left Italy trailing by just one point with five seconds remaining.

Borlase was then sent to the line but made only one of two free throws to give Italy a chance for one last play while down by two, and Francesca Pasa appeared to catch the defence napping by going for the tie rather than the win.

The speedy guard burst past Borlase and got her left-handed lay-up onto the backboard as the siren sounded, but the ball just rolled off the right of the rim and the Opals survived.

"We still have an opportunity to keep fighting and that's what we're going to do," coach Sandy Brondello said.

They moved into a quarterfinal against Spain, but will have to do it without some of their biggest stars.

Having already lost veteran Sami Whitcomb to a knee issue before the tournament and losing WNBA champion Alanna Smith to injury in their opening game against Puerto Rico, the Opals copped another huge blow against Italy.

Captain and star forward Ezi Magbegor played just four minutes of the clash before she went down during a drive to the basket.

Magbegor powered into a seam in the defence but was fouled from the side by Lorela Cubaj, causing her right knee to bend awkwardly inward.

Ezi Magbegor knew straight away she was in trouble. (Supplied: FIBA)

The Seattle Storm star immediately shouted in pain and hit the deck, appearing to be in tears on the floor before being helped off the court by training staff.

"It made my heart sink to see her go down," Brondello said.

"She's so impactful for us and we just pray that she's OK. We don't know. We'll see what the result is tomorrow. She's walking and that's a good sign."

Meanwhile, an ill Jade Melbourne played only three minutes.

The Opals are still alive and face Spain in the World Cup quarterfinals. (Getty Images: Mami Yasui/FIBA)

Borlase, a rookie guard with the WNBA's Atlanta Dream, picked up the slack and scored a game-high 30 points on 7/13 shooting from the field while knocking down 14 of 16 free throws.

The 21-year-old was named player of the match as she became just the fourth Opal to score 30 points at a World Cup.

"Something we speak about a lot is the Opals legacy," Borlase said.

"We really respect what the girls have done in previous tournaments. They've inspired us to want to play for Australia and I just hope I've inspired someone to tonight to want to play for Australia because there's no greater honour."

The tears were flowing for Italy after its second loss at the tournament by just one bucket, having missed a last-second three-pointer to lose 55-52 to reigning champions USA in the group stage.

World.title: Greyhound trainer handed lifetime ban for 'egregious' actions
World.content:
A greyhound trainer has been found "entirely unfit" to participate in the industry, with the governing body in South Australia issuing a lifetime ban and a $5,000 fine for dishonestly negotiating the transfer of an injured dog to another trainer.

Jack Clayton Trengove, who is from a prominent Broken Hill racing family, was already suspended for previous animal welfare-related matters.

In a sentencing decision handed down by Greyhound Racing SA (GRSA), an integrity hearings panel said Mr Trengove discussed the transfer of a greyhound named "Arctic Girl" to a trainer in NSW without disclosing an "unhealed hock fracture" on the dog's hind leg.

"We found that Mr Trengove knew of the fracture and that his failure to disclose it was dishonest," GRSA said in its decision.

"Arctic Girl was transferred to a trainer who was unaware of the true condition of her hock and commenced preparing her to race, thereby placing Arctic Girl at significant risk of catastrophic injury."

Mr Trengove pictured at the Broken Hill Racecourse last year. (Supplied: Broken Hill Racecourse)

The panel said that although the dog did not ultimately suffer such injury, "that outcome was due in significant part to the timely intervention and positive action of GRSA officers".

"This offending represents such an egregious example that stands in stark contrast to the standard and welfare expected within the industry," it said.

"Accordingly, the [panel] have concluded that this offending not only strikes to the core of the values upon which greyhound racing in South Australia operates, it has also concluded that his conduct makes him entirely unfit to continue participating in the industry."

The panel said it accepted the new owner's account that Mr Trengove had told her over Facebook Messenger that Arctic Girl had been off with a sore hock but was "good to go now".

It rejected Mr Trengove's account that he separately disclosed the fracture by telephone to the new owner.

The decision states the greyhound was returned to SA and rehomed.

SA greyhound trainer banned for dog's 'unnecessary suffering' One of SA greyhound racing's most prominent identities has been disqualified after a 12-month inquiry by the sport's controlling body.

Mr Trengove has been suspended since June 2025 when charges relating to animal welfare rule breaches were laid against him, after an investigation stemming from photos taken inside his kennel.

In the latest ruling, the panel also noted several racing-related infringements Mr Trengove had accrued in 2024 which included a failure to present a greyhound for veterinary examination, striking a greyhound and a failure to maintain a treatment record book.

In a statement, GRSA chief executive officer Brenton Scott said the organisation had adopted a zero-tolerance policy to animal welfare breaches.

"The vast majority of industry participants both love and care for their greyhounds and abide by the rules and welfare policies … but any variation to this is acted upon and considered seriously by our independent integrity process," he said.

In response to the outcome, Mr Trengove told the ABC he felt he was being targeted.

" I was not given a fair hearing … their process for the hearing panel is run very wrong. "

The statement from GRSA said Mr Trengrove did not attend the hearing and did not provide a defence, "despite being given a fair opportunity to do so".

The panel's decision document states Mr Trengove did not attend a hearing related to the latest counts on which he had been found guilty, but had attended other hearings related to separate counts.

In 2021, Mr Trengove was described by GRSA as having a "strong future ahead of him" in a since-deleted online blog.

GRSA said Arctic Girl had been "subsequently rehomed" as part of its own Greyhounds as Pets initiative.

World.title: 'Purpose I had is no longer': Hollands opens up on Blues axing
World.content:
Elijah Hollands is at peace with the end of his Carlton career, saying he realises there are more important things in life that he needs to focus on.

Hollands was one of seven players delisted by the Blues on Wednesday, with former GWS star Zac Williams, Jordan Boyd, Lachie Fogarty, Lewis Young, Flynn Young and Harry Charleson also among the casualties.

But it was Hollands' axing just months after suffering an on-field mental health episode that represented the biggest story.

Carlton was fined $75,000 for its handling of Hollands during a round-six loss to Collingwood.

Hollands tallied just one disposal for the match, with his erratic behaviour catching the attention of fans even before the game started.

The 24-year-old was hospitalised days later before deciding to step away from football to concentrate on his mental health.

It meant Hollands wasn't able to add to his 47-game AFL career, 14 of which were played at Gold Coast.

His brother Oliver Hollands remains at Carlton.

Elijah took to Instagram to share his thoughts about the end of his time at the Blues, which could also spell an end to his AFL career.

Loading Instagram content

"Football means an extreme amount to me," Hollands wrote.

"My dad played professional footy, my great-grandfather played professional footy, my brother plays professional footy — it is everything I have lived and breathed for as long as I can remember.

"I have only ever wanted to do one thing my entire life: copy what was done before me and play AFL footy. It was something that I just knew I was going to do when I was a kid and it was all I ever cared about.

"And now, unfortunately, that purpose I had is no longer.

"I love this game, but I have come to realise that there are things in my life that are far more important than footy right now and they're the things I will now prioritise."

Hollands's father posts heartfelt message Elijah Hollands's father, former AFL player Ben Hollands, posts on social media pledging to help lift his son up and urging others to check on their friends if they are struggling.

Hollands thanked the greater AFL community for its support since his mental health challenges became public.

"As an extremely confident 18-year-old, I certainly envisioned my career going a whole lot differently, but I am OK with accepting that it just isn't in the plans set for me," Hollands said.

"I'll be moving into the next chapter of my life, leaving what will feel like a big hole to fill, but I am excited about what can come from having my health and mind in much greater shape."

Carlton's other big delisting was Williams, who joined the Blues from GWS at the end of 2020 on a six-year deal believed to be worth about $5 million.

The soon-to-be 32-year-old managed only nine games this year, with his time at Carlton plagued by injuries.

AAP

World.title: Data centre builder's deal with AFL club defended by team boss
World.content:
Aligning with Tasmania's fledgling football club isn't enough alone to bolster the public image of the company behind multiple divisive data centre proposals, a marketing expert says.

Firmus Technologies has signed a major deal with the Tasmania Devils Football Club, which will see the company's logo emblazoned on player shorts and coach polos for six years.

AI company to become Tasmania's largest power user Artificial intelligence company Firmus Technologies will become Tasmania's biggest power user if its ambitions to establish three "AI factories" in the state come to fruition.

The company, which was founded in Tasmania in 2019, has been the centre of swirling debate this year over its plans to build three artificial intelligence (AI) data centres across the state.

While some have welcomed the sponsorship deal, others have decried it as an attempt to garner public support as Firmus looks to push through the divisive projects.

The agreement places Firmus among a collection of sponsors for the future AFL side, including some with deep roots in Tasmania — such as Cadbury, Blundstone and Devil's Corner Winery.

Deal could help company's image, experts say

Dr Ashlee Morgan says this deal can help Firmus Technologies build a social licence in Tasmania. (Supplied)

Flinders University associate professor of sports management Ashlee Morgan said sponsoring the Devils could give a company like Firmus visibility, legitimacy and social license to operate.

"Firmus isn't simply buying a logo placement; it is repeatedly associating its brand with the Devils, with Tasmanian identity and with the community around the club," Dr Morgan said.

" So basically, the public will develop positive affiliations towards that brand and will see that they're giving back to the community, in a way, through this sponsorship deal. "

David Fleischman says Firmus will need to "activate" the sponsorship within the Tasmanian community to build trust. (Supplied: David Fleischman )

David Fleischman, a senior marketing lecturer at the University of the Sunshine Coast, echoed this sentiment.

But, he said earning trust would likely take more than just a sponsorship.

Facing public backlash, Firmus moves to calm concerns about its AI factories Firmus has outlined its commitments to sustainable energy and water usage after its plans for three artificial intelligence companies in Tasmania were met with public concern.

"Another way to think about sponsorship, in this case, is it buys you a ticket to the dance, but it doesn't necessarily mean you're going to be a good dancer," Dr Fleischman said.

"So it's what they actually do beyond just simply appearing on the apparel.

" Who benefits? How are they investing in other ways in the region? How are they engaging with the community? "

The Tasmania Devils are due to enter the national league in 2028. (Supplied: Tasmania Football Club/Solstice Digital)

Dr Fleischman said the company would need to "activate" the sponsorship within the Tasmanian community to begin gaining trust from supporters.

He said this could be done in a whole range of ways, from promoting employment pathways to building social partnerships with grassroots sports.

Delivering clear messaging about why the Devils and Firmus were a good fit would also be crucial to bringing fans and stakeholders on board, according to the marketing lecturer.

Sponsorship a 'natural fit' says Firmus co-founder

Tasmania Devils CEO Brendon Gale says the club and Firmus are aligned in their values. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

In the media release announcing the sponsorship deal, both the football club and the AI infrastructure company spruiked parallels between the two parties.

"Tasmania gave us our start, so backing a new Tasmanian initiative that's going to go national, just like us, felt like a natural fit," Firmus co-founder Oliver Curtis said.

George Town Council recently approved a proposal from Firmus to build an AI data centre at the site of the former Gunns pulp mill. (Supplied)

Brendon Gale, the chief executive of the Devils, told 936 ABC Hobart the cost of the sponsorship couldn't be disclosed as it was "commercial in confidence".

He said the figure was an important consideration, as it was an "expensive exercise to participate in the AFL".

But he said the deal went much deeper than that.

"There needs to be sort of alignment of values and first principles," Mr Gale said.

" This is a homegrown company that is investing significantly in this state and in jobs, in an industry that is a global mega-trend. "

Mr Gale said he was mindful some supporters might object to the deal, but that there would be others who supported it.

He said the six-year deal showed Firmus was "in for the long-term" and that "considerable due diligence" was undertaken during the negotiations.

Firmus said it would not provide any additional comment on the sponsorship.

One expert cautions that while "die-hard" supporters may overlook sponsorships they disagreed with, others may not be so forgiving. (Tasmania Football Club)

'They just have to be careful' warns expert

Community scepticism towards the sponsorship reflected a larger trend within sports, according to Dr Morgan.

"Supporters, the media, and the public want to know more about the social, environmental and economic value of the organisations their clubs are associating with," she said.

Devils lose to Bombers in semi-final VFL clash A rainy North Hobart VFL semi-final has ended in disappointment for Tassie fans, with the Devils going down to Essendon by 27 points.

Dr Fleischman said while "die-hard" supporters may overlook sponsorships they disagreed with, it could drive away fans who are only passively engaged.

He said this meant it was especially important for the Devils to strike the right balance when selecting its sponsors, as the club's fanbase is still in its infancy.

"They just have to be careful in this particular case just because the team is new and the sponsorship is brand new," Dr Fleischman said.

" So they don't necessarily have that legacy of die-hard fans, aficionados, that are just rusted on to sort of ride that wave a little bit. "

The Devils just concluded their inaugural seasons in the Victorian Football League (VFL) and VFLW and are set to join the Australian Football League (AFL) for the 2028 season.

World.title: SA government backed a risky horse in LIV Golf — lucky it hedged its bets
World.content:
Spending at least $45 million to upgrade a golf course so it can host a tour that's filed for bankruptcy is a hard sell.

But that's the position the Malinauskas government would have been lumped with had it not secured hosting rights to the Australian Open golf tournament from 2028.

The announcement in May that the prestigious, traditionalist golf event would be coming to the redeveloped North Adelaide Golf Course has taken some of the sting out of what would otherwise have been a nasty political headache surrounding LIV Golf's financial demise.

The acquisition of LIV Golf until 2031 was the impetus for a controversional redevelopment of the North Adelaide Golf Course., (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

The breakaway tour filed for bankruptcy in the US overnight, four months after Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund announced it would be pulling its billions in funding.

LIV Golf chief executive Scott O'Neil said the move was intended to keep the league in business while transitioning to a player-first ownership model. It hopes to exit bankruptcy in early 2027.

But the optimism of the press release doesn't quash the uncertainty about what LIV Golf will look like next year and whether it can hold onto the top talent — and party-like atmosphere — that made it such a success in Adelaide.

The tour owes huge sums to creditors, including its star players. Jon Rahm is owed more than $10 million, Bryson DeChambeau nearly $8 million, and Australian Cameron Smith about $6.5 million.

They could all walk away if not convinced by LIV's new model.

Premier Peter Malinauskas went all in on the LIV Golf vision back in February 2025, announcing a six-year contract extension until 2031 and that it would be moving to a new Greg Norman-designed championship course at North Adelaide in 2028.

South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas announced the six-year LIV Golf contract extension in 2025. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The government has been consistent that there was more to the course upgrade than just LIV Golf, pointing out it will be used by the public outside of events.

But it's also hard to imagine a world where the $45 million upgrade gets green-lighted without LIV Golf in the picture; indeed, the premier indicated as much at the time, saying the 2031 extension "justifies the investment".

"We didn't want to invest heavily in North Adelaide and face the prospect of it [LIV Golf] being lost from South Australia," he said in February 2025.

" This gives us the security that it requires to be able to justify that investment. "

As the negative headlines about LIV Golf's finances piled up, so too did the questions about the justification for the course upgrade.

The development and its loss of 585 trees was always going to spark opposition from parklands advocates, the Greens and elements of Adelaide City Council.

Trees were cut down at the course in May. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

But the prospect of spending $45 million on an upgraded course without a major event connected to it risked a much broader backlash.

If you wanted a sense of the political importance of securing the Australian Open, you only have to look at how prominently it featured in the government's talking points about LIV Golf's bankruptcy today.

Can the SA government justify a $45m golf course upgrade without LIV Golf? The Malinauskas government took a calculated risk to redevelop the North Adelaide Golf Course in time for LIV Golf in 2028. It might not pay off.

"We've been focused on not just LIV Golf but other opportunities," Labor minister Clare Scriven said, "which is why we've been so keen to secure the Australian Open."

Cabinet colleague Nick Champion — who in April said the prospect of LIV Golf ceasing to exist was "just speculation" and "not a question we would ask ourselves" — said today that the state government was not "over-reliant" on one event.

"I appreciate that we're going to have endless media speculation about LIV Golf, but we're upgrading the golf course so that we can have a world class golf course next to a world class [Adelaide] Oval in a world class city," he said.

"And we've got the Australian men's and women's open."

The debate moves on

The fight over the North Adelaide course upgrade appears to have largely moved on.

That's partly due to the Australian Open announcement, but also because attention has shifted to the government's controversial MotoGP circuit in the eastern parklands, which will require the felling of at least 377 trees.

The government recently unveiled designs for the MotoGP redevelopment affecting another part of the parklands. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

Opposition leader Ashton Hurn was today asked whether LIV Golf filing for bankruptcy raised questions about the need for the North Adelaide Golf Course upgrade.

"It does, but I think that we're kind of past that point really when you look at how many trees have now been pulled out," she said.

" But certainly, when this massive project was announced it was done so really with the idea that LIV Golf would be the major project underpinning that. "

Liberal leader Ashton Hurn says LIV Golf was the primary reason for the North Adelaide redevelopment. (ABC News: Isabella Carbone)

Ms Hurn was more focused today on questioning whether South Australian taxpayers had any exposure in LIV Golf's demise — something the government denies.

"We are good at writing events contracts," Mr Champion said, "we don't provide support for events that aren't held."

Over to you, Kooyonga

If LIV Golf can get out of its current predicament, it is next due in Adelaide in March 2027 at the Kooyonga Golf Club.

The western suburbs club has been waiting on an advanced payment from LIV Golf to help prepare.

The status of that fee remains unclear.

Adelaide's next LIV event is scheduled for March. (ABC News: Will Hunter)

But Australian golf commentator Jimmy Emanuel believes LIV Golf will put on a tournament next year, even if it looks a little different.

"The cost of putting on a tournament in that scale to attract music acts like Fisher is a lot," he said.

"Just building grandstands, building hospitality, those are big commitments financially — the scale of the investment is not going to be the same as it was from Saudi Arabia.

" It might not be quite as grand, but I imagine it's going to be their biggest event still. "

What happens beyond next year is a matter of anyone's guess — but the government remains certain of one thing.

Even if LIV dies, the North Adelaide course upgrade is set to survive.

World.title: Lynagh makes timely return after Wallabies fly half Gordon breaks leg
World.content:
Tom Lynagh's timely return at number 10 for the Queensland Reds and Zac Lomax's move to the centres for the Western Force will have Wallabies ramifications in a pre-season Ballymore hit-out.

Super Rugby AUS starts on Saturday in Brisbane and there will be immense interest in how both fare ahead of next year's World Cup on home soil.

Lynagh, the starting fly half in all three British and Irish Lions Tests last year, managed just 18 minutes for the Reds because of a series of injuries last season.

Wallabies escape with draw against Pumas after late penalty try A penalty try close to full-time sees the Wallabies and Pumas finish in a 28-28 draw in Mendoza, giving the visitors a history-making series win on Argentine soil.

All going to script, he will get at least 40 minutes against the Force at Ballymore in new Reds coach Vern Cotter's first game in charge since his historic move from Auckland's Blues to replace Les Kiss.

Lynagh's return comes as Reds teammate and fly half Carter Gordon enters two months of rehabilitation after fracturing his fibula in last weekend's Test draw against Argentina in Mendoza.

Gordon had established himself as the Wallabies' first-choice fly half, leaving Kiss with some big calls ahead of a clash with South Africa and a two-Test Bledisloe Cup in the next six weeks.

"I'm really enjoying Tom in a playmaker role," Cotter said of the son of former Wallabies great Michael.

"He's got a great head on his shoulders, he sees the game well, he's calm and decisive.

"With the niggles he has had, we will probably be a bit careful with him, so it probably won't be 80 minutes, but certainly a good 40 minutes to start with.

"He's a great player in organised play but brilliant at unstructured (play).

"It's a good opportunity for Tom to get out there and boss the team around … pull a few strings and get some combinations."

Harry McLaughlin-Phillips, released by the Reds to join the Force this season, will oppose Lynagh and consider himself in the thick of Wallabies discussions after being part of their training camp earlier this year.

Kurtley Beale has been named on the bench for the Force, but new signing James O'Connor, another sure to be in Kiss's considerations, will not play.

Lomax, an Australian and NSW State of Origin rugby league winger, revealed this week he would be deployed in the number 13 jersey against the Reds.

A dominant showing there would add intrigue to Kiss's midfield selection headache after fellow code-hopper Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii's struggles to nail down the jersey in 24 Tests.

Japan-bound fullback Jock Campbell, replaced in the number 15 by Tom Wright after one Test in July despite a good showing against Ireland, will also get a chance to show something when he comes off the bench for the Reds.

Fellow Wallabies Matt Faessler, Zane Nonggorr and Josh Flook have been named, while Australian under-20s captain Tom Robinson will wear the number 6, and exciting fullback Will McCulloch will start.

NSW Waratahs lock Miles Amatosero, red-carded in his second Test appearance in Osaka, will mount his comeback against the ACT Brumbies on Sunday in Bungendore, east of Canberra.

Teddy Wilson and Max Burey, after earning an early release from the Force, will partner in the halves, while Sid Harvey will start at fullback.

Triston Reilly will wear the Brumbies' number 15 against his former club a week after piloting the First Nations and Pasifika XV to victory in Tonga, while Wallabies wing aspirant Corey Toole will add pace on the flank.

AAP

Tech.title: The black iPhone Pro returns
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple has seen reason: It has a black model in the iPhone Pro lineup again.

Last year, Apple went bold with its colors for the iPhone 17 Pro, offering a flashy orange, a shiny silver, and a dark blue. Don’t get me wrong, they looked nice. But there was no black (or dark gray) for the first time since the start of the iPhone Pro lineup, which Apple first introduced in September 2019 with the iPhone 11 Pro and Pro Max.

I care about this because I always buy the black phone. I learned my lesson with the iPhone 6: I got it in gold to mix things up and came to regret it. I don’t need something flashy — I need a phone that blends into the background and looks decent in whatever case I throw it into. After the iPhone 6, my next phone was the iPhone 7 in the excellent matte black (I wasn’t brave enough to endure the jet black model’s potential scratches), and I’ve only ever gotten the black or gray phones since.

My black titanium iPhone 16 Pro in a black Torras case (with a mostly black homescreen) still works very well, thank you very much, and I’m not in the market for a new phone. But when I make my annual mid-September visit to the local Apple Store to look at all the new iPhones, I won’t be rushing to see the iPhone 18 Pro in burgundy, blue, or silver. I’ll be beelining for the model in black.

Just look at this thing! It’s great!
