Tech.title: OpenAI adds a prominent AI doomer to its board of directors
Tech.content:
Paul Christiano, an influential AI researcher focused on keeping AI systems aligned with human interests and under human control, is joining the OpenAI Foundation board, the frontier lab said Wednesday.

“I now believe there is a meaningful risk that rapid acceleration in AI capabilities leads to catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term,” Christiano wrote in a social media post. “I do not think that the AI industry in general, including OpenAI, is currently on track to reduce this risk to an acceptable level. I’m joining because I believe that if OpenAI rises to the occasion we could significantly reduce risk.”

Christiano wrote that using AI models to train subsequent AI systems could result in an explosion of capabilities that their creators can’t control.

He joins the board as OpenAI faces renewed scrutiny over its safety procedures, following a series of incidents in which AI agents broke out of restraints and penetrated outside computer systems without the knowledge of OpenAI’s researchers. On Tuesday, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned his position to call attention to what he considers irresponsible AI development — and it seems to have worked.

Christiano will join the board’s Safety and Security Committee, led by Carnegie Mellon University professor Zico Kolter. The committee has the final say on whether OpenAI releases new models, like Astra, which was deployed last week. Kolter has not commented publicly on the recent security incidents. OpenAI has not responded to TechCrunch’s request for Kolter’s perspective on the company’s approach to safety following those incidents.

Christiano is one of the people behind reinforcement learning (RL) from human feedback, a key technique for training large language models that he developed while working at OpenAI. He left the lab in 2021, subsequently founding the Alignment Research Center to focus on how to determine if an AI model could threaten its human creators.

“We currently train our AI agents with RL to get as much reward as they can,” he wrote Wednesday. “It has long seemed theoretically possible that this could motivate AI agents to undermine human control, seek power and resources, and cover up their tracks in pursuit of misaligned goals correlated with reward. Public evidence from recent incidents suggests that this is not just a theoretical possibility.”

Sometime in 2024, Christiano became affiliated with the U.S. government’s AI Safety Institute, which later became the Center for AI Standards and Innovation. There, he plays a role in the U.S. government’s largely hidden effort to evaluate frontier AI models before their release.

According to the frontier lab’s announcement, Christiano will continue advising the government while serving in his new role as a board member, but will recuse himself from OpenAI matters and model evaluations. However, that will hardly quell widespread concerns about the AI industry’s influence over policymaking.

Tech.title: Massachusetts hits data centers with new clean power rules
Tech.content:
Massachusetts became the latest state to force data centers to bring their own power, but this time there’s a twist. A new state mandate would require developers building data centers larger than 25 megawatts to provide clean power or pay into a ratepayer protection fund.

Gov. Maura Healey’s executive order is the latest example of states turning against data centers. Just a few years ago, tech companies and data center developers were showered with incentives to locate facilities in a particular state. Now, they’re fighting a groundswell of public opposition as politicians seek to show voters they’re addressing their concerns.

Under Healey’s order, data centers larger than 25 megawatts of peak demand will have to bring their own power and guarantee that it adheres to the state’s clean energy requirements. Healey would prefer that they generate the clean power onsite, too. If not, they’ll need to fund the construction of new generation nearby or pay into a ratepayer protection fund.

Massachusetts is also directing communities to “avoid signing non-disclosure agreements,” according to the executive order. To give regulators time to implement the new restrictions, the governor is pausing applications for a data center sales tax exemption that went into effect last month.

Healey said data centers must meet the Massachusetts clean energy standard enshrined in state law, although it comes with some added strength. The state’s clean energy standard dictates that industry only generate a portion of their power using approved sources like wind, solar, and hydro. In 2030, for example, those sources must contribute at least 40% of the total. The amount varies by year, and it ratchets up over time. But the governor’s office clarified that data centers will be required to meet 100% of its electricity demand with clean energy generation.

With the new restrictions, Massachusetts becomes the third state in as many months to rein in data center development.

In August, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott announced that all new data centers in the state would need to submit to audits by the public utility commission and the grid operator, ERCOT. In July, New York’s governor stopped construction of new data centers 50 megawatts or larger.

With public sentiment shifting against data centers, the tech industry is starting to push back. Pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future — which is funded by Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz, and Greg Brockman — is buying ads that seek to sway voters in battleground states ahead of midterm elections.

Update: This article was updated with information from the Massachusetts governor’s office that clarified the executive order will require data centers to meet 100% of its electricity demand with clean energy generation.

Tech.title: Apple’s new CEO is reviving a Steve Jobs strategy from 25 years ago
Tech.content:
Apple CEO John Ternus wants you to know that the iPhone isn’t going anywhere.

Ternus threw his weight behind the venerable device on Wednesday during his first keynote as CEO, placing it firmly at the center of Apple’s product strategy for the AI era.

“There’s no product in the world better designed to be your intelligent personal hub than iPhone,” he said.

This contrasts with the approach taken by former CEO Tim Cook, who tried time and again to convince Wall Street that Apple was more than just the iPhone.

Ternus’ pitch is also a rebuttal to pundits who have recently cast doubt on the iPhone. “The smartphone’s days are numbered,” said one headline. “The Tim Cook era is coming to a close with an existential challenge for Apple: figuring out what comes after the iPhone,” said another article.

But it’s not just about the hardware. Ternus has put the iPhone at the center of his “intelligent personal assistant” strategy, a vision that could define the company for years to come. Steve Jobs did something similar in 2001 with the Mac, less than 10 months before he announced the iPod.

At the time, many observers thought the PC’s days were numbered. At a Macworld New York keynote, Jobs called out bearish quotes from industry wonks like Walt Mossberg and the leaders of Compaq and Gateway.

“This is what everyone else is telling us. That our PC is waning if not the hole being dug,” Jobs said at the time, pointing at a tombstone for the “Beloved PC” on the screen behind him. “We don’t think the PC is dying at all. We don’t think the PC is moving away from the center at all. We think it’s evolving, just like it has since it was invented.”

“We think the PC is on the threshold of entering its third great age,” Jobs added, a prediction driven by the proliferation of digital devices at the time, including camcorders, digital cameras, and DVD players.

The Mac would form the center of a “digital hub” that would connect these disparate devices and, in Jobs’ words, “add value” to all of them.

Later that year, Jobs pulled the iPod out of his pocket, a device seemingly developed to answer the question, “Why do you still need a PC?” The device turned out to be an enormous hit, driving Apple’s profits quarter after quarter and ultimately helping lead to the development of the iPhone.

Today, with the iPhone on the cusp of its 20th anniversary, Ternus is facing a version of the same question Jobs took on in 2001. We don’t know if Ternus is quietly sitting on an iPod-like product, one that will secure the iPhone’s position a Apple’s hub for years to come. But he is firmly rebutting the idea that the iPhone is past its prime.

“If you were designing the ideal version of this hub from scratch, how would you do it?” Ternus asked, before listing the ingredients: a powerful processor, high-resolution cameras, persistent networking, and on-device AI.

It helps that the iPhone is one of the most powerful personal computing devices around, giving it an edge in the compute-hungry AI era. Its portability and adaptability make it, for many people, the only computing device they need. Even among those who own laptops and iPads, the iPhone is often the one device they can’t live without. Plenty of people leave home without their laptops. Almost no one leaves without their phones.

That combination of power and portability has given Apple a privileged position in the AI world. Other companies have attempted to unseat the iPhone with all manner of wearable devices, but none have succeeded.

Instead of sidelining the iPhone in favor of the next flashy thing, Ternus is leaning into it instead. In a way, he’s bringing Apple around to what the rest of us already know: The iPhone is pretty great, and maybe we don’t need to replace it with something else. Yet.

Tech.title: Apple Watch’s new AI features are normalizing the idea that technology is always listening
Tech.content:
Apple is trying to get consumers to accept, and even welcome, a new reality: Your tech is always listening.

At Wednesday’s “Surprise and Shine” iPhone event, where the company introduced its new hardware lineup, the real surprise turned out not to be the foldable iPhone, but how the famously privacy-sensitive tech giant has decided its watches will now be able to process live audio and transcribe what was said.

Does this mean you’re always being recorded if the person you’re interacting with is wearing an Apple Watch? Not exactly — though it may make some people uncomfortable regardless.

It also raises the question of whether consumers actually want this technology, or if Apple forged ahead in this area because it was afraid that another company, such as OpenAI, would soon introduce a competitive AI device of its own.

Today, a number of startups are acting on the belief that AI-powered transcription is a key consumer use case for AI. So far, this more often involves transcribing meeting notes or recording lectures or interviews. Some companies, like the AI pendant Friend and Amazon’s Bee, ventured into other areas, too, with always-available AI companions that can help you remember your day by passively taking notes.

Apple decided to go a slightly different route. With its new watches’ “audio intelligence,” “Live Rewind,” and “Siri Recap” features, the company is straddling the line between accessibility and utility on one side, and what starts to feel like invasive technology on the other.

On its own, Audio Intelligence seems to be a useful feature for the deaf or hard of hearing, as it can alert Apple Watch owners to sounds like sirens, alarms, doorbells, babies crying, and more, using on-device AI. This can work even when the wearer’s iPhone is not with them and, in some cases, could provide life-saving assistance, such as when a fire alarm or carbon monoxide detector goes off. It’s doubtful anyone would take issue with this type of audio AI.

Image Credits:Apple

However, Live Rewind and Siri Recap move out of the assistive tech space and into a murkier area.

While Apple’s data protections may make these features more palatable to some, there’s still the possibility that normalizing listening technology may not be the best move for a privacy-conscious company. This is especially true given the broader consumer backlash against surveillance technology like Flock cameras, AI data centers, and AI apps in general.

For starters, the Live Rewind AI feature lets you go back in time 15 seconds and transcribe what was just said by double-pressing the watch’s digital crown. This transcription can then be saved to Apple’s new standalone Siri app so you can revisit the information later.

Image Credits:Apple

Apple suggests that this could be used to remember things like a “book recommendation, a colleague’s brilliant idea, or something you didn’t hear the first time,” but it also means that you can essentially catch anyone saying something they didn’t necessarily mean to have recorded and make a note of it.

This has implications around consent, not only from an ethical standpoint but from a legal one as well. AI device-maker Plaud, for instance, advises customers to obtain legally required consent before recording. Amazon’s Bee‘s terms of service remind users that they’re solely responsible for complying with the law around minors’ data privacy, not Amazon.

Since Apple isn’t saving audio, it’s unclear how the court system might handle these new, text-only transcripts. It’s possible the notes could be introduced as evidence in court, but their lack of audio could make them harder to authenticate or verify. Plus, the evidentiary rules around their use will also likely vary by state.

Beyond the legal issues, the idea that someone can always record from their watch has cultural implications.

Already, recording devices have impacted the way people behave in real life, studies have shown, as has social media and data surveillance culture. Knowing you could be recorded at any time has a dampening effect on how you interact with others and engage in self-expression.

Image Credits:Apple

However, recording a photo or video still requires a fairly obvious move on the recorder’s part: you have to hold up your phone and face it toward the action. Snapping up a bit of audio to turn into a transcript just by pressing the watch’s digital crown is arguably a much subtler gesture, even though it comes with an audible chime and full-screen animation of a microphone, as Apple says.

Another new Apple Watch feature, “Siri Recap,” uses ambient listening to “take high-level notes” of your conversations, which can be reviewed in the Siri iOS app. These notes will automatically generate a title, summary, and key points based on what was recorded and summarized by AI. They will not be exact transcripts.

Apple suggests this could make sense for recording meeting takeaways or key info from a parent-teacher conference, for instance.

The company also tried to assure users that it has approached these listening features with respect for user privacy.

Apple notes that Siri Recap doesn’t default to always being on like some other AI wearables are. Instead, you can choose when it’s enabled, like only at work or only during the day. Plus, you can turn the feature off and on at any time from Control Center.

Notably, Apple points out that it does not create or store audio recordings, and that the raw audio isn’t accessible, even to Apple. It also doesn’t identify or attribute the speakers, and it protects the generated transcripts and recaps with end-to-end encryption.

Whether that’s enough for consumers not to feel like the feature is creepy is another matter. Either Apple has found the right balance between utility and privacy, or it’s about to see some consumer backlash.

Tech.title: Everything Apple announced at its fall iPhone event, from the foldable iPhone Duo to an always-listening Apple Watch
Tech.content:
Apple on Wednesday unveiled its latest iPhones and Apple Watches at its first fall event under newly appointed CEO John Ternus. The main event was the tech giant’s highly anticipated first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo. Apple also announced its iPhone 18 Pro lineup, along with new AirPods, and more.

We’ve compiled all of the announcements from today’s “Surprise and Shine” event.

iPhone Duo

Image Credits:Apple /

Apple’s first foldable, the iPhone Duo, features a 7.6-inch Retina display when unfolded, while its outer display measures 5.4 inches. The company said that the new device was “Inspired by the versatility of iPad.” The inner display features an “under-display” camera that gives users an all-screen feel.

Apple says the iPhone Duo delivers up to 31 hours of video playback on its inner display and up to 44 hours on its outer display.

The phone features a 48-megapixel fusion main camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide camera with 2x optical zoom. As with other foldable phones, users can take rear-camera selfies and look at previews on the outer display.

The Duo’s hinge is made from Grade 5 aluminum and comprises more than 100 specially engineered components designed to ensure smooth opening and closing.

The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 with 256GB of storage and is available in two colors. Pre-orders for Apple’s new foldable open October 16, with the device hitting stores on October 23.

iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max

Image Credits:Apple /

The new iPhone 18 Pro lineup retains the same design as its predecessors, but its biggest upgrade comes in the form of enhanced cameras.

The new Pro series camera features a 48-megapixel sensor with a variable aperture controlled by six thin blades. This system is expected to improve low-light photography while also increasing shooting speed. The camera software also introduces new Pro controls, including white balance, shutter speed, aperture, and a histogram. In addition, new “Photographic Styles” offer greater customization with texture and grain controls.

The new camera can record 4K video in Dolby HDR Vision and apply cinematic effects after shooting the footage.

The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299, which is $100 more than last year’s models. Pre-orders will open Saturday, with both devices officially available on September 18.

Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4

Image Credits:Apple

A new “Sound Recognition” feature can listen for sounds such as sirens, alarms, doorbells, and a baby crying, providing helpful alerts for people who are hard of hearing. The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 aren’t getting a major hardware makeover, but they are getting some significant software updates.

Apple is taking aim at the growing wave of AI-powered wearables with new “Audio Intelligence” features that can rewind moments and help users remember details from their everyday conversations.

The smartwatches are introducing a “Live Rewind” feature that shows the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet, and a “Siri Recap” feature that’s designed to help you remember key moments from daily conversations, like takeaways from a team meeting or a parent-teacher conference.

A new “Sound Recognition” feature can listen for sounds such as sirens, alarms, doorbells, and a baby crying to provide alerts for people who are hard of hearing.

The Apple Watch Series 12 starts at $399, while the Apple Watch Ultra 4 costs $499. Pre-orders open today, with availability in stores beginning September 18.

AirPods 5

Image Credits:Apple

The latest generation of Apple’s wireless earbuds, the AirPods 5, introduces several upgrades, including improved audio quality, stronger active noise cancellation, and expanded Siri and Apple Intelligence features.

Apple says AirPods 5 can reduce background noise by 50% more than the previous generation. They also feature volume control on the stem, which was previously only available on Apple’s more expensive AirPods Pro.

Transparency mode on AirPods 5 has also been improved to allow users to hear nearby voices and ambient sounds more naturally.

The AirPods 5 offer up to five hours of listening with active noise cancellation on a single charge. The charging case brings total listening time to up to 22 hours.

AirPods 5 start at $129, while the version with a Wireless Charging Case costs $149. Pre-orders begin today, with the earbuds set to arrive on September 18.

Revamped Health App

Image Credits:Apple

Apple announced a redesigned Apple Health app that takes advantage of Apple Intelligence to make better sense of your health data.

The updates introduce a new Insights tab with a summary of the most timely health information, along with personalized guidance, assessments, a new “Readiness” score, and a calculation of your “Health Age.” The updates also introduce a new Longevity tab that uses metrics from your Apple Watch and iPhone to assess your overall health across factors such as sleep, movement, heart health, and more.

The revamped Health app rolls out later this year, starting in U.S. English.

Tech.title: There are new shiny iPhones, so Apple is making you pay more for older models
Tech.content:
Apple on Wednesday unveiled its new iPhone 18 and its first foldable iPhone, the iPhone Duo. But amid all the attention on Apple’s newest and most expensive devices, there’s another change: Apple is raising the price of its existing iPhone models by $100.

Starting today, customers will notice a price hike for existing models on Apple’s online store, including starting prices for iPhone 16 at $799, iPhone 17e at $699, iPhone 17 at $899, and iPhone Air at $1,099.

The price increases are even steeper in some international markets. In India, for example, prices have reportedly risen by around 20.5%. The company also discontinued the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max.

The strategy is an unusual one for Apple. Traditionally, the arrival of a new generation of iPhones means older models become cheaper.

However, the price hike wasn’t entirely unexpected. Speculation had been building that Apple could raise prices as it introduced its next-generation iPhones. One of the biggest pressures is a global shortage of memory and storage chips. Demand for those components has surged as AI companies and cloud providers build out increasingly massive data centers.

In a June interview with The Wall Street Journal, former Apple CEO Tim Cook acknowledged that rising component costs could eventually force the company to rethink its pricing strategy. He said Apple could no longer fully absorb the rising costs of memory and storage chips.

About a week after those comments, the company raised prices across its Mac and iPad lineups.

Other reasons Apple may consider increasing iPhone prices are to remain competitive with rising prices from rivals like Samsung and Google. Additionally, Apple might feel that its new Upgrade program, which allows customers to spread the cost of an iPhone through manageable monthly payments, could cushion the impact of a price hike, making it less noticeable to consumers.

Tech.title: The hinge for Apple’s new foldable phone was built with AI
Tech.content:
In Brief

Apple’s long-awaited foldable phone, the Duo, contains a number of surprises, including a critical hinge that was designed and built with the help of AI and 3D printing.

The new phone represents Apple’s first entry into the foldable phone genre — a category of devices that has seen significant consumer enthusiasm, but whose form factors haven’t always lived up to that enthusiasm. As you might expect from a product that, by design, undergoes twice as much wear as a traditional device, most foldables suffer significant degradation and don’t have the durability of other smartphones.

Apple claims that it has integrated innovative protections into the Duo’s design to keep the phone from falling prey to the typical wear and tear associated with foldables. That includes the hinge, according to Johny Srouji, the company’s chief hardware officer.

“During manufacturing, we use AI algorithms to precisely match each individual hinge with its best-fit housing to ensure perfect alignment, and a confocal laser progressively scans the topology of every single unit, and 3D prints up to 25 micro layers of a custom photopolymer to eliminate residual waviness,” Srouji said during Apple’s Surprise and Shine event on Wednesday.

Srouji also shared that Apple gave the foldable phone “a custom nano-texture finish that significantly reduces glare and reflections” as well as a multi-layer lamination strategy designed to increase the device’s durability. Of course, it remains to be seen whether those protections will be enough to keep the Duo in peak physical condition in the long run.

Tech.title: Apple Watch’s new feature listens to your chats and recaps them
Tech.content:
Apple launched a meeting notetaker on Wednesday for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, one of a series of new audio intelligence features that can listen to sounds through your Apple Watch.

The feature, called Siri Recap, uses ambient listening to take high-level notes of your conversations, according to the company. Apple Intelligence will automatically generate a title, summary, and key points from the conversation, which can then be reviewed in the Siri app.

Apple said that you can choose to keep this feature always on, set up a schedule, or turn off completely.

The notetaker wasn’t the only audio-focused feature introduced for the Watch during the event. Apple’s new audio intelligence features also include Shazam, which can identify songs instantly. This means Apple has finally caught up to Google’s Now Playing feature. The Watch can recognize loud sounds like sirens, alarms, doorbells, or a baby crying and notify users.

Apple also introduced a feature is called Live Rewind, which lets users recap 15 seconds of conversation when they double press the digital crown.

Apple emphasized that the features don’t store recordings and that raw audio is inaccessible. The Siri Recap feature doesn’t identify speakers either. Users can access Live Rewind recaps, which are end-to-end encrypted. Despite these guardrails, an always-listening feature will likely raise privacy concerns because Siri Recap may still capture sensitive information in its summaries.

Besides some of the privacy features, Siri Recap sounds similar to other notetakers like Granola and Circleback, which also have Apple Watch apps.

Tech.title: The AI Researcher Who Just Quit Anthropic Says It’s ‘Crunch Time for Humanity’
Tech.content:
Artificial intelligence researcher Jacob Coxon sent shock waves through Silicon Valley and beyond on Tuesday by announcing his resignation from Anthropic and delivering a grave warning that the AI race is putting all of our lives at risk. In his post on X, which now has more than 100 million views, Coxon wrote that many of the people building AI share his views and believe time is running out to ensure AI systems are built safely.

“The consensus is that the next year or two is crunch time for humanity,” Coxon, who worked on the pretraining stage of AI development, said in an interview with WIRED. “These are actually just literal quotes from my colleagues at Anthropic. They'll say things like ‘endgame’ or ‘crunch time,’” he says. “From their perspective, this is when Anthropic and its competitors decide the fate of humanity.”

It’s far from the first time someone has sounded the alarm about AI, but it comes at a delicate moment. Silicon Valley is scrambling to reckon with the safety and security concerns of advanced AI models. OpenAI has rushed to respond to a security incident in which its agents hacked the platform Hugging Face. Meanwhile, Anthropic is trying to assure investors it has these concerns under control as it reportedly prepares to file for what could be the largest IPO ever.

Got a Tip? Are you a current or former Anthropic employee who wants to talk about what’s happening? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at mzeff.88.

What’s become clear in the response to Coxon’s post is that his views are indeed shared by many of his peers. Evan Hubinger, the AI alignment lead at Anthropic, predicted in a post on X that there’s a greater than 10 percent chance that AI could kill all people in the next decade. That post was reposted by current and former researchers from OpenAI and Anthropic, some of whom said it was a common sentiment in the industry.

What’s less obvious is how exactly these AI fears will come to pass and what the world is supposed to do about the concerns being raised by the people building AI. Coxon, who also worked at OpenAI, tells WIRED that threats could manifest through AI-enabled biological threats or cyberweapons. As a first step, he recommends that OpenAI and Anthropic coordinate on limiting recursive self improvement—the industry term for when AI is used to build new AI systems. Down the line, he thinks coordination among international power players, including the US and China, will be necessary.

Coxon notes that incidents like the Hugging Face hack factored into his decision to raise alarm bells on the AI race. He also cites the explosive growth of the industry: It now underwrites a meaningful share of US economic growth and has billions of users, while data centers have turned it into a political problem in a dozen states.

He claims that, in his experience, Anthropic operates more responsibly than OpenAI, but he expects both companies could cut corners in the future if nothing is done to slow their race for dominance.

OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately return WIRED’s request for comment.

Read our conversation with Coxon, which has been lightly edited for clarity and brevity, below.

WIRED: You’re not the first person to raise concerns that AI models could lead to an extinction event. People have been talking about this for years, and some for decades. Why do you think your message broke through?

Tech.title: San Francisco Orders Meta to Stop ‘Allowing’ AI Child Abuse Ads
Tech.content:
San Francisco’s city attorney has hit Meta with a cease-and-desist letter telling the company to stop “allowing” paid s that include AI-generated child sexual abuse content and asked it to explain how the ads repeatedly ran on its platforms.

On Tuesday, WIRED reported that Meta has run more than 350 ads in recent months that transformed still images of minors—some of them confirmed as real individuals, including a member of a European royal family—into short videoclips that can depict them performing sexual acts. When clicked, these ads would direct people to download AI image- and video-generation apps, some of which could be used to digitally undress people or create other nonconsensual intimate imagery.

The ads, which were discovered by researchers at the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), included some identical ads that had been uploaded multiple times, and in total they reached more than 29,000 accounts in countries in the European Union. The ads that were shown across Facebook, Instagram, and Threads also targeted accounts in the US, Australia, and India. WIRED initially reported on a batch of 53 of the ads at the start of August, but more than 250 of the total number of ads ran on Meta’s platforms after this initial report.

“Meta has failed to address a known issue of AI-generated child sexually explicit ads, while profiting from them," San Francisco city attorney David Chiu says in a statement to WIRED. “These ads are deeply disturbing and cause harm to real children. Meta claims to have zero tolerance for child exploitation, yet the scale and persistence of these issues suggest current efforts are woefully inadequate. This is unacceptable, and Meta must do better.”

“No company—particularly one that claims all s are reviewed and approved prior to distribution and then accepts payment for that distribution—should permit its advertising systems to be used in this manner,” Chiu writes in the four-page letter his office sent to Meta’s lawyers.

The letter raises a host of questions about how Meta’s ad policies and safety systems operate and asks that the company’s legal, child-safety, and advertising staff engage in “prompt discussions” with the city office. “These findings are especially troubling because they do not appear to reflect an isolated failure that Meta corrected when first alerted to the problem,” Chiu writes.

Meta says there is “no indication” that the ads were displayed in San Francisco and this means they are “outside the city attorney's jurisdiction.” While Meta’s ad library, which is a repository of ads, includes some data about ads published in the US, it does not break down where in the US ads may have run.

In response to Meta's jurisdictional claims, City Attorney's Office spokesperson Alex Barrett-Shorter tells WIRED that, because “San Francisco consumers can access the unlawful ads through Meta online spaces,” the matter is the the city of San Francisco's business.

“We find Meta’s response astonishing. Meta appears less concerned about whether they’re guilty of exploiting children than whether San Francisco should say anything about it,” Barrett-Shorter says. “Meta has bigger problems to solve here than determining our jurisdiction.”

Meta previously told WIRED that many of the ads identified by the TTP researchers had already been removed before they were reported—all of them have now been removed for violating its policies—and most had “fewer than 200 impressions” from accounts. “We don’t tolerate nudify apps or any kind of child exploitation, whether real or AI-generated,” a Meta spokesperson previously said. The company said the “total ad spend” for the 300-plus ads found by the researchers was “under $5,000.”

Tech.title: A Year After Charlie Kirk’s Death, Turning Point Plans to Spend Big on the Midterms
Tech.content:
A year after the assassination of cofounder Charlie Kirk, Turning Point plans to pour tens of millions of dollars into the midterm elections to help Republican candidates in key congressional and gubernatorial races, according to sources familiar with the matter.

The conservative grassroots group is expected to prioritize three states in the midterms—New Hampshire, Arizona, and Nevada—but will also deploy full-time field staff in seven other states where Democrats could pick up seats.

The precise amounts could change, but sources tell WIRED that Turning Point's super PAC is looking to spend $15–$20 million in ads across the three priority states. Turning Point's field operation spending couldn't be learned, as it is run by a 501(c)(4) nonprofit, but it is estimated to be tens of millions more.

The planned cash injection will pay for both a field operation as well as digital ads, and would only add to the advantage for Republicans in funding through a constellation of outside super PACs and party committees.

The most closely watched race for Republicans in New Hampshire is the Senate seat vacated by the retiring Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, where former Republican senator John Sununu is running against Democratic representative Chris Pappas to flip the seat.

The New Hampshire Senate race is a crucial battleground for both parties, as many of the possible paths to Democrats taking the Senate majority require the party to keep the seat, which the Cook Political Report rates as "Lean Democrat."

Turning Point has also been particularly focused on the race for governor in Arizona, where Democratic incumbent Katie Hobbs is running against Representative Andy Biggs, who endorsed President Donald Trump's claims of a stolen election in 2020.

These maneuvers come as Republican groups have started a massive cash injection to counter a wave of discontent from voters over the Iran war and high prices, and burgeoning Democratic momentum that has opened up the possibility of a Democrat-controlled Senate.

Tech.title: Everything Apple Announced: iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, Apple Watch, AirPods 5
Tech.content:
It’s a brand-new era for Apple. The company is turning over leadership for the first time in 15 years, with former CEO Tim Cook handing off the reins last week to the new CEO, former Apple VP of hardware John Ternus.

At the first Apple product soiree hosted by Ternus, the company made an even bigger change: it announced its first ever folding device, the iPhone Duo.

The company also announced its new line of iPhone 18 Pro phones, some updates to its Apple Watch line, new AirPods, and new software capabilities powered by Siri AI.

Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

As expected, there were no base-model iPhone 18 announcements; those are likely coming early next year. There was also no mention of Vision Pro, iPads, or Macs. Apple touted new desktop Macs in August.

Here’s everything Apple showed off today.

Apple iPhone Duo

Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Apple’s first ever folding device is the Duo, a “passport sized” foldable iPhone. It starts at $1,999 for a model with 256 GB of storage.

It’s a product category that Apple has been working toward for a decade. Now, it hopes to do that very Apple thing where it may not be the first company to the new tech party, but it definitely aims to be the snazziest.

The Duo is a landscape style foldable, meaning it has a vertical magnetic hinge that lets you open the device like a book. Closed, it has a 5.3-inch screen on the outside. Open it up, and the landscape display is 7.7 inches. The Duo is also heavy, weighing in at 254 grams, which might be a little too hefty for some users.

Tech.title: Apple Doesn’t Want You to Worry About the New Apple Watch’s Listening Features
Tech.content:
The new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 come not just with better fitness tracking and upgraded noise reduction, but also a whole new way to listen.

Apple announced on Wednesday that the two smartwatches come with four opt-in “audio intelligence” tools that are powered by audio gathered by the watches’ microphones. They include sound and music recognition, a conversation recap feature, and “Live Rewind” so a user can see a transcription of anything that was said in their environment in the previous 15 seconds.

Seemingly wary that the features could make it feel like the walls have ears, Apple is emphasizing that all of them are built to prioritize privacy and security using the extensive infrastructure the company has developed to protect its other Apple Intelligence and Siri services. As more and more of these types of features debut, though, the audio intelligence announcements are a reminder that AI-powered tools are becoming increasingly universal in all areas of computing and life.

“These features do not create or store audio recordings, and raw audio used for processing is completely inaccessible to the operating systems, apps, the user, or Apple,” the company wrote in a report shared with WIRED.

The new Apple Watch features are designed to process as much data locally on devices as possible, so potentially sensitive data doesn’t go to the cloud. Sound Recognition, for example, alerts users about sounds in their environment—including doorbells, sirens, alarms, or, say, a baby crying—without sending any data off the watch. The tools that do send information out to the cloud preprocess the data so it isn’t raw audio files, then use Apple’s Private Cloud Compute infrastructure.

Apple emphasizes that its on-device capabilities for Apple watches have expanded thanks to the company’s new S11 chips. The chips include a special memory-protected space that Apple calls the Secure Exclave. Designed specifically for sensor data, the exclave is an isolated buffer that is inaccessible to the rest of the operating system where Apple Watch can hold and process audio data in a protected space.

A new Shazam feature “listens” for music and will generate a signature of a song that is stored in the Secure Exclave. If the user navigates to Shazam to find out what the music is, the tool will send that signature—not an audio file—to Shazam’s servers for identification. (Shazam is an Apple-owned service.) If the user doesn’t prompt to identify the music, or as soon as they do, the special signature is “immediately” deleted from the watch.

The recap feature, known as Siri Recap, can be set to be on all the time and generate recaps of any substantive conversation, or it can be given a schedule to listen in at certain times during the day. A dedicated AI model determines when speech is occurring without recording or transcribing any data. If it detects a conversation, audio goes into a protected buffer within the Secure Exclave on the Apple Watch, the watch encrypts it, and then transmits it using Apple’s special secure Bluetooth pairing to the Secure Exclave on a user’s iPhone. Then the audio is immediately deleted from the Apple Watch.

The iPhone uses local speech recognition and language models on-device to transcribe the audio and then generate a minimal version of the transcript that removes nonessential elements like extra words and repeated phrases. Then the raw audio is immediately deleted from the iPhone as well. The last step on the iPhone is a safety model that “screens the text to omit potentially harmful terms,” according to Apple. From there, the distillation of the conversation is encrypted, and the iPhone sends it out to Private Cloud Compute.

Tech.title: UK Lawmakers Are Freaking Out Over AI’s Summer of Chaos
Tech.content:
A leading British politician has urged the United Nations to intervene in “the unsafe development of super intelligence” after an Anthropic team leader posted: “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!”

Whether “marketing hype” or signposting of a genuine extinction threat, “governments must step in,” Labour MP Darren Jones wrote in an open letter also addressed to the UK prime minister and international Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.

Jones is the latest lawmaker scrambling to find ways to protect the British public from AI threats to safety. Just one day earlier, Labour MP Alex Sobel had introduced a parliamentary bill proposing to ban the “development, deployment, and operation of artificial superintelligence”—systems which can fully replace and outmatch humans at any task. The legislation would also give the government powers to monitor and control the development of the technology at different points in the supply chain, including at chip level.

“We are not alone in this effort,” said Sobel while introducing the bill, pointing to the US government’s temporary export ban on Anthropic’s Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models in June. "If the Trump Administration, who are perceived as historically against AI regulation, can contemplate drawing a line on models that are too powerful and dangerous, it would be strange for us not to ask what our response should be," he argued.

MPs from across political parties put their names on the bill, including Labour MP Jess Asato, who is suing Elon Musk’s xAI after its Grok chatbot was allegedly used to generate fake sexualized images of her. Lawmakers have become increasingly worried about the threat of AI to national security after a string of incidents of AI agents going rogue in recent months. They want to introduce guardrails against worst-case scenarios, such as these systems seizing control of critical infrastructure and running sophisticated influence operations.

Tech.title: I Let an AI Agent Hack All My Gadgets—and I’d Do It Again
Tech.content:
As the author of a newsletter about artificial intelligence, I consider it my duty to experience the bleeding edge of this technology firsthand. This week, that meant embracing some agentic mayhem.

You’re probably aware that frontier AI models have attained advanced cybersecurity capabilities in recent months. They can find zero-day bugs in large codebases and scan computers for vulnerabilities at lightning speed. To make things even more exciting, cybersecurity agents sometimes go rogue, colluding with one another and hacking into outside systems to gain an edge.

To get a closer look, I decided to unleash one in my own home network. Over the course of a few days, I watched as my own rogue agent found vulnerabilities in various household devices, hacked into a PC, and showed me that several vibe-coded projects were—unsurprisingly—riddled with bugs. (My wife knew what I was up to, and rolled her eyes each time I proudly announced the discovery of a new vulnerability.)

But Will, you might be thinking, giving an impish, all-powerful cybersecurity agent access to your home network is batshit. And you would be correct! Nevertheless, I believe that a good way to understand the cybersecurity hellscape in front of us is to pay it a visit.

In the end, my experiment was revealing, but oddly reassuring, too. My little network gremlin showed me how vulnerable my home life would be to AI hacking, but it also told me how to make everything a lot more secure. In the end, I discovered that the best way to deal with AI hacking may well be having your own AI hacker.

Maverick Model

I got the idea for the experiment after discovering Abliteration AI, a startup that offers access to powerful AI models with the usual guardrails removed.

Most mainstream AI models will refuse to respond to certain queries, and they will certainly refuse to find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. But it’s possible to remove these restrictions by finding and modifying certain patterns within an open-weight model’s internal parameters. You can tweak the patterns that lead to refusals through a process known as abliteration.

Removing AI’s guardrails might seem risky, but it’s not uncommon. Academic researchers use these de-aligned models to better understand how AI actually works, while cybersecurity firms use them to probe software and systems for vulnerabilities. Technically speaking, Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s Astra work similarly: They’re basically conventional models that lack the usual cyber controls, with access limited to trusted customers for the time being. (The companies also offer wider access to models with a medium number of guardrails so that companies can vet their code and systems for problems.)

Abliteration AI offers several fully de-aligned models, the most powerful of which is a version of Z.ai’s latest agentic coding model, GLM 5.3. This puts similar cyber capabilities to Mythos and Astra right in your hands for as little as the cost of a pizza.

Devon, Abliteration AI’s CEO, believes that making de-aligned models widely available is smart defense: It will help good guys counter bad guys by probing systems for vulnerabilities and by mimicking the behavior of hackers, scammers, and, yes, rogue AI agents. (Devon asked that I use his first name only because his day job doesn’t know about his side project.)

“You have all these critical infrastructure companies, from airlines to banks, that are rolling out agents like crazy,” Devon says. “How do you make sure that a nefarious actor can't use some of these agents in a bad way?”

Tech.title: Apple Debuts the iPhone Duo, Its First Folding iPhone
Tech.content:
Apple says the hinge has a “custom variable torque profile” that precisely opens and closes the phone in an “effortlessly smooth” way. When it’s open, Apple says it’s the thinnest iPhone ever. As Samsung does with its “Flex Titanium” technology, Apple uses a carbon fiber metal plate below the display to better control the stress caused by bending the display. That, alongside a nano-texture finish, helps keep the display flat and “minimizes crease visibility.” An Apple-designed scratch-resistance coating sits on top.

Surprisingly, there is no Face ID sensor, likely to save space inside the phone for the folding components. Instead, like some of Apple’s tablets, the iPhone Duo brings back the fingerprint-sensing Touch ID integrated into the side power button. This is also the first iPhone to support the USB-C Apple Pencil later this year, though there’s no way to naturally store the stylus on the edges of the device like the iPad’s magnetic Pencil dock.

Apple says the Duo has the biggest battery ever in an iPhone. Like most book-style folds, it’s a split system where a battery rests on both sides. That will net you up to 31 hours of video playback with the inner display and 44 hours with the outer display—or 24 hours of mixed overall use per charge. It also sports Apple’s new custom C2 modem (with mmWave 5G support in the US) and the A20 Pro, the same chip powering the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max.

Video: Courtesy of Apple

There are only two cameras on the back—a 48-megapixel primary camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide. The lack of a telephoto zoom option is a sacrifice even Samsung made on its latest Galaxy Z Fold8. Like most book-like folds, it has two selfie cameras—a 12-megapixel camera on the outer screen and a second “FaceTime camera" on the inner display, though this one is hidden under the display.

There are familiar folding phone features here with the camera, like distracting a kid with a fun cartoon character on the outer screen to get them to look at the camera. Or your subject can preview the photo before you hit capture. The iPhone Duo can stand upright by itself, so you can set it down and it will automatically capture group photos if everyone stands at the ready.

Hardware is just one part of the story, though. The software needs to adapt and take advantage of the larger screen. Apple has been improving how apps adapt to different screen sizes for some time, making it easy for developers to scale apps from the iPhone to the iPad to the Mac, and even visionOS on the Apple Vision Pro. That means you’ll be able to enjoy iPad-like apps when unfolding the iPhone Duo.

Tech.title: Apple Debuts the iPhone Duo, Its First Foldable Phone
Tech.content:
It’s finally here: Apple on Wednesday unveiled its first foldable iPhone, called the iPhone Duo. It’ll start at $1,999 for 256GB in the US. Preorders for the iPhone Duo begin on Oct. 16, ahead of an Oct. 23 release.

Apple debuted the new device during its fall event in Cupertino, California, along with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

iPhone Duo design and build

Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

The iPhone Duo is compact, with a passport-size design and titanium frame. Apple says it’s the thinnest iPhone ever when open, measuring 5.2mm. It’s 11.3mm thick when closed.

The Duo has a 7.6-inch display on the inside and a 5.4-inch outer display. It fits squarely in my palm, with dimensions similar to Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, which has a 7.6-inch inner display and a 5.5-inch cover display.

One of the key differences in feel between Apple’s and Samsung’s phones is that the iPhone Duo has a matte, nano-texture finish on the inner display, which reduces the phone’s crease while also curbing reflections. It has a satisfying feel and really makes the crease virtually disappear when the screen is on.

Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

The Duos’ cover is made with Apple’s Ceramic Shield 2, while Ceramic Shield protects the back.

The iPhone Duo comes in two colors, dubbed star white and night sky, which is a navy hue. It’ll be compatible with the Apple Pencil. To unlock, it supports Touch ID, rather than Face ID.

Apple says a titanium plate helps to improve the iPhone Duo’s durability. The phone is powered by the A20 Pro chip.

iPhone Duo cameras

Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

The iPhone Duo has a 48-megapixel main camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide camera. Like the Z Fold 8, there’s no telephoto camera.

Apple’s foldable supports 4K video at 120 frames per second, as well as 4K time-lapse video. Dual capture in FaceTime lets you record video using both the rear and inside cameras. You can also turn on photo previews on the cover screen when the phone is unfolded, so your subject can see how the shot will look as you snap with the rear cameras.

iPhone Duo battery life

Apple says the iPhone Duo will give you up to 31 hours of video playback on the inner display, and 44 hours when using the outer screen. When using both equally, the company says you’ll be able to go 24 hours before needing to charge.

Considering how often I use both the cover and inside displays on the Galaxy Z Fold 8, I have a feeling my battery life would lean more toward that 24-hour mark. But we’ll have to see how the phone holds up in CNET’s battery tests.

Apple/Screenshot by CNET

A new foldable competitor

With the iPhone Duo, Apple enters an increasingly competitive foldable phone market, with key players including Samsung, Google and Motorola, as well as Chinese brands like Honor, Oppo and Huawei. Now, it’s Apple’s turn to further shape the space – and likely nudge it forward.

Analysts predict the iPhone Duo could give foldables, which remain a niche smartphone category, a significant boost. IDC forecasts that global foldable shipments will grow by more than 12% this year, with Apple’s entry driving much of that growth. The research firm also expects Apple to ship more than 17 million foldable iPhones by 2027, giving the company nearly 40% global market share by the end of next year.

Tech.title: IPhone Duo’s Under-Screen Camera: Invisible, but at What Cost?
Tech.content:
I love the idea of a phone or tablet with no camera cutout or bezel at all, where everything would be screen… and a camera hidden under the screen would handle the magic for you.

That’s exactly what Apple did with the inner camera on its new iPhone Duo, coming later in October. It’s a phone full of new tech specs to catch up on, but that new bonus camera (to go with the front-facing camera and dual rear cameras the Duo also has) fascinates me. And, based on the reported specs, concerns me.

Masked under layers of OLED pixels, the new camera has a much smaller spec list than the other three on the Duo. No megapixel count is listed. Apple promises 1080p video recording and FaceTime compatibility. It has Center Stage for auto-centering video calls, a feature I’ve found essential on iPads. It also has an f/1.8 aperture.

What it seems to lack are higher-res 4K recording features, an extra cinematic mode, slow-mo or time-lapse features, LED flash or portrait modes. It’s a more bare-bones camera, likely intended for use mainly for FaceTime and video chats.

Can you see the camera? Hint: it’s right above the left corner of the Find My widget. (Credit: Apple) Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Sure, if I were taking selfies on the Duo, I’d use the higher-end front-facing one (or the dual rear cameras flipped around to selfie orientation, something folding phones can do). Would that hidden camera step in well enough to be the FaceTime/Zoom/chat camera I need? If so, would that make it a great candidate for an under-the-screen camera on future MacBooks or iPads? Or…even an Apple Watch?

The compromise at play seems like a lot now, but it’s something the Duo can afford, since it has other cameras on other surfaces that can be invoked if needed. I’m glad Apple avoided camera notches or cut-outs on the inside, although I wonder how invisible the camera truly is when gaming or watching movies (or anything else).

It seems like an interesting experiment by Apple to slide its camera tech into smaller places. I want to try it. But I wonder if it’s ever going to replace cameras that are visible…and probably better.

Tech.title: For the Fourth Year in a Row, I Was Right. Here’s When iOS 27 Will Land on Your iPhone
Tech.content:
Apple announced iOS 27 at its Worldwide Developers Conference in June, and the tech giant has since released multiple beta versions of the software. The betas have brought Siri AI and a handful of other features to the iPhones of developers and beta testers, and you can expect many of those capabilities to land on your iPhone on Monday, just as I predicted.

Apple usually releases updates around 10 a.m. PT (1 p.m. ET), so that means your iPhone can get an updated Siri AI and more around then.

I accurately predicted iOS 26’s release in 2025, iOS 18’s release in 2024 and iOS 17’s release in 2023, too. Following a similar formula, here’s how I predicted iOS 27’s release date before Apple even announced it.

How my iOS 27 release date math works

Usually, Apple releases the next iOS update soon after the September event, and the company held its “Surprise and shine” event on Wednesday.

After most of Apple’s September events, the company releases the next iOS within a week. In 2025, for example, Apple’s event was held on Sept. 9, and the company released iOS 26 on Sept. 15. And in 2024, Apple’s event was held on Sept. 9 and iOS 18 was released seven days later on Sept. 16.

There’s only been one year over the past decade where it took longer than a week for Apple to release the next iOS version – 2019. That year, Apple released the next iOS version nine days after its September event.

In that same timeframe, most of the iOS releases were either five, six or seven days after the September event. Apple has also released the past five iOS versions on the Monday following its September events. This could be the new norm, with Apple releasing future iOS versions on the Monday after its September events moving forward.

That’s how I predicted Apple would release iOS 27 on Monday.

For more on Apple, here’s what to know about iOS 27, what to know about the iPhone Duo and everything Apple announced at its September event.

Tech.title: All iPhones — Not Just the Pro Models — Now Cost $100 More
Tech.content:
Apple has raised the prices of all iPhone models by $100. The price hike affects not just the new iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max models – announced at Wednesday’s live “Surprise and Shine” event — but also last year’s iPhone 17, iPhone 17E and iPhone Air, as well as the iPhone 16.

The iPhone 17 now starts at $929, the highest ever starting price for Apple’s base iPhone model. The entry-level iPhone 17E now starts at $699, while the iPhone Air starts at $1,099. The iPhone 16 is now back to $829 — the same price it had when it debuted in 2024.

While a price hike was expected for the newest iPhone models, the increase for older models is unprecedented. In previous years, older iPhones in the lineup either received a discount or maintained their original price.

Apple already raised the prices of several products in June, including Macs, iPads and HomePods, due to the global RAM shortage. Former Apple CEO Tim Cook called the price hikes “unavoidable,” citing a “100-year flood on the memory pricing.” RAMageddon caused companies, including Samsung and Google, to increase the cost of their new phones this year, but Apple spared the iPhone until Wednesday.

The cheapest new iPhone model, the iPhone 18 Pro, starts at $1,199; the most expensive new model is the $1,999 iPhone Duo. A base-model iPhone 18 wasn’t announced this week, but is expected to debut next spring.

That ruffled the feathers of a certain fictional owl: Duo, the mascot of language app Duolingo. (Duo’s used to wading into newsy issues — he once pretended to be murdered by a Tesla Cybertruck.)

“What an exciting Apple event!” Duo snarked on X. “I sure hope my brand doesn’t get infringed upon.”

what an exciting Apple event! i sure hope my brand doesn’t get infringed upon 💚 — Duolingo (@duolingo) September 9, 2026

Welp, guess what, Duo?

Tech.title: The iPhone 18 Pro Max’s Battery Is a Beast, but Is the Battery Worth the Upgrade?
Tech.content:
Apple just leveled up its battery on its new premium iPhone. Is it worth the leveled-up price tag?

As expected, Apple unveiled the pricier part of the iPhone 18 lineup at its “Surprise and Shine” event on Wednesday. The iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max have some serious upgrades, including faster performance from the A20 Pro processor, a new automatically adjustable camera aperture with built-in AI software, and a larger vapor chamber.

But the big “wow” factor is the battery. We saw a big improvement in the iPhone 17 Pro Max, which holds the crown as our current best-tested phone battery. But the iPhone 18 Pro Max is a pretty sweet upgrade for $100 more than its predecessor’s original price.

During the event, Apple said you can get 45 hours of video playback and 30 hours of usage per charge with the new premium version. It’s also expected to have faster wireless charging, and 15 minutes of wired charging should put the phone at 50%. By comparison, the iPhone 17 Pro Max promises 39 hours of video playback. And based on our testing, the phone’s battery life reached 49% in 20 minutes.

The 18 Pro Max seems to pack a powerful punch with its battery. And surprisingly, Apple’s not raising the price too much. The iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 for 256GB, which is only $100 more than the iPhone 17 Pro Max for the same storage. But are the battery upgrades worth the price? I don’t think so.

Sure, the iPhone 18 Pro Max has a better battery, but if you’re like me, you just want your phone to hold a battery for a day without rushing to a charger. If you’re not watching videos for days, you may not see much of a difference between the iPhone 17 Pro Max and the new model. Especially if you want a better battery on a budget. So if you have the iPhone 17 Pro Max, it’s not worth upgrading for better battery life. However, if you have an earlier model, it may be worth considering one of the latest models.

A recent CNET survey highlighted what US adults really want in a phone upgrade. Most (55%) want a cheaper phone, and next to that is better battery life (52%). Truthfully, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max price increase seems small (especially given the RAM shortage), you may be able to get a solid battery for less.

I have the iPhone 17 Pro Max, and I’m not sold on the new model’s $1,299 price tag when its predecessor is still available at select retailers. Shortly after Apple’s event, the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max disappeared from Apple’s site. But you still may be able to find the phones at other retailers and mobile carriers. We also noticed Apple quietly increased prices on other iPhone models, so it’s worth shopping around.

Apple’s Upgrade program and other mobile carrier trade-in programs may make the newer model cheaper. But if you’re buying outright or won’t get a deep discount, save yourself the money and look for the older model that still holds a charge for the day. And if you have the iPhone 17 Pro Max, don’t rush to upgrade for better battery life quite yet.

Tech.title: Missed the iPhone Duo Reveal? How to Rewatch Apple’s ‘Surprise and Shine’ Event
Tech.content:
Early September is when Apple likes to show off its biggest new products, and today’s “Surprise and Shine” event brought one of the company’s most revolutionary announcements — the unveiling of its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo.

Along with the Duo, we also saw a new Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 (with no price bump), AirPods 5 with new noise-canceling features, and the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max in black, silver, glacier and burgundy.

If you weren’t able to watch the live event earlier today, you can stream the whole show at your leisure on either the Apple website or on YouTube. The event runs 1 hour, 21 minutes and was Apple’s first major public event featuring new CEO John Ternus.

Tech.title: It’s iPhone Duo Users Who Will Want a Stylus
Tech.content:
“Who wants a stylus?”

Steve Jobs famously posed this question when he introduced the first iPhone in 2007. It was a jab at the other smartphones of the era with small screens that were better navigated with a skinny stylus than with a fat finger.

Jobs quickly answered his own question. “You have to get ’em and put ’em away, and you lose ’em. Yuck! Nobody wants a stylus.” The iPhone’s giant-for-the-time display was best navigated with nature’s stylus, Jobs argued, your finger.

Fast forward two decades, and we’ve come full circle with Apple announcing the iPhone Duo, which is not only the company’s first foldable phone but also its first phone to support – gasp! – a stylus.

iPhone Duo users, that’s who.

In the case of the Duo, it’s not about the display being too small, but about having a display so large when unfolded that it rivals an iPad’s. The Duo’s inner screen is 7.6 inches, which is within an inch of the 8.3-inch iPad Mini. And on that giant iPhone screen (as well as the Duo’s smaller 5.4-inch outer display), you will soon be able to draw, sketch, tap, write and swipe with an Apple Pencil.

In introducing the iPhone Duo at its fall event, Apple said that its new foldable will support Apple Pencil (with USB-C) later this year. A software update is needed to add pen support to iOS.

With the iPhone Duo starting at $1,999, perhaps the iPad-like pen support will help people justify the high price by viewing the Duo as two devices in one, acting as both a phone and tablet.
